0.title: Revelation: The Unveiling of the Victorious Lamb
0.overview:
Revelation is the most debated book in the Bible. Within a generation of its composition, Dionysius of Alexandria questioned whether it belonged in the canon — not because he doubted its inspiration, but because he could not make sense of it. In the centuries since, the book has generated more controversy, more speculation, more bad charts, and more genuine spiritual comfort than any other portion of Scripture. Before we open a single seal, we need to understand what kind of book we are reading.

The word that opens the book — apokalypsis — means “unveiling.” Revelation does not conceal the future in cryptic code to be cracked by clever scholars in the final generation. It unveils a reality that was always there but hidden from ordinary sight: the reign of the slaughtered Lamb over all of history. The book was written to be read aloud in congregations (1:3), probably by a lector standing in a first-century house church. Its images were designed to be heard, felt, and worshipped — not diagrammed. If your primary response to Revelation is to reach for a chart, you are already in danger of missing the point.

Revelation belongs to three overlapping literary genres simultaneously. As an apocalypse, it uses symbolic visions, cosmic imagery, and heavenly perspectives to reinterpret earthly events — a thoroughly Jewish genre with deep roots in Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, and the rich inter-testamental literature (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch). As prophecy, it speaks the word of God into a specific historical crisis, calling the church to faithfulness and warning the world of judgment. As a letter (1:4; 22:21), it is addressed to real congregations facing real pressure, and it carries all the pastoral weight of Paul’s epistles. Missing any one of these three dimensions distorts the whole.

The author is John, exiled to the island of Patmos “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (1:9). Early Christian testimony overwhelmingly identified him with John the Apostle, the beloved disciple. The book was most likely written during the reign of Domitian (c. AD 95–96), when the imperial cult was being aggressively promoted in the province of Asia and Christians were being pressed to acknowledge “Caesar as Lord.” Seven actual churches — in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea — received this letter. They were living under the crushing weight of Rome’s total-sovereignty claim. Revelation is the pastoral response of an exiled pastor to congregations in crisis.

Four Frameworks for Reading Revelation

Faithful, Bible-believing, Christ-loving readers have understood the overall structure of Revelation in four main ways. This commentary works from the amillennial/idealist position — the historic Reformed mainstream — while flagging clearly at every major structural decision point what the other frameworks say. All four frameworks agree on the non-negotiables: Christ has decisively won. The church will endure to the end. History is moving toward a fixed and glorious goal. Jesus returns in visible, bodily glory. The wicked face final judgment. The righteous receive a new creation. Where they differ is in the timing, sequencing, and nature of the visions.

The Preterist framework holds that most — or all — of Revelation was fulfilled in the first century. The great tribulation is the Roman-Jewish War of AD 66–70, culminating in Jerusalem’s destruction. The beasts represent Nero and the Roman imperial system. “The things that must soon take place” (1:1) and “the time is near” (1:3) are taken with strict literalness: the book addresses events imminent to its first readers. The partial-preterist position (R.C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry, David Chilton) holds that chapters 1–19 are largely fulfilled while chapters 20–22 remain future. Preterism’s great strength is its seriousness about the book’s own time-markers. Its challenge is explaining how a largely-fulfilled Revelation speaks with permanent power to the church in every age.

The Historicist framework reads Revelation as a symbolic map of the entire sweep of church history from Pentecost to the Second Coming, with the seals, trumpets, and bowls charting the rise and fall of empires. The Reformers broadly held this view, identifying the papacy with the beast. Though now a minority position, historicism produced generations of courageous preaching by men who believed they were living inside the very story Revelation was telling.

The Idealist (Amillennial) framework — the home position of this commentary — reads Revelation as a profound symbolic portrayal of the cosmic conflict between Christ and Satan, the church and the world, that characterizes the entire period between the first and second comings. The visions do not map a sequence of datable historical events; they depict recurring spiritual realities — the pressure of empire, the suffering of the saints, the apparent triumph of evil, and the certain victory of God — that are enacted in every age. The seals, trumpets, and bowls are best understood as parallel series (recapitulation), each sweeping from the cross to the Second Coming with increasing intensity. This reading takes seriously both the first-century occasion and the book’s permanent relevance. Its great advocates in the Reformed tradition include Augustine (City of God), B.B. Warfield, Geerhardus Vos, William Hendriksen, G.K. Beale (whose NIGTC commentary is the definitive scholarly treatment), Richard Bauckham, Dennis Johnson, and Michael Wilcock.

The Premillennial/Futurist framework holds that most of Revelation (especially chapters 4–22) describes events still future, culminating in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return. Two major streams: Historic Premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) teaches that the church goes through the tribulation before Christ returns to establish his kingdom on earth, followed by the final judgment. Dispensational Premillennialism (John MacArthur, Charles Swindoll, J. Vernon McGee, John Walvoord, Charles Ryrie) adds the distinctive of a pre-tribulation Rapture — the church is caught up before a seven-year tribulation falls on an unbelieving world, with that period constituting God’s final dealings with national Israel. Shaped by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and widely popularized through the Scofield Reference Bible, this is the dominant eschatological framework in much of evangelical America. This commentary treats it with full respect as the honest, Scripture-rooted reading of millions of sincere believers, and will note its specific interpretations at every key junction.

How to Read This Commentary

Three principles will guide us. First, let the book’s own genre shape how you read it. Apocalyptic literature communicates through symbols, not newspaper reporting. When you read of a dragon with seven heads and ten horns, you are not meant to visualize a literal creature — you are meant to feel the horror of satanic power in all its many-headed, grasping form. Second, hear the book through first-century ears. Most of Revelation’s images come from the Old Testament — Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah, Exodus — and from the Roman world of the first century. When John’s original hearers heard “the great city,” they heard “Rome.” Third, read for comfort and courage, not for curiosity. Revelation was written to sustain the church’s witness under pressure. It was written to answer one question above all others: Is Jesus really Lord, or is Caesar? The answer, given in vision after dazzling vision, is: the Lamb who was slain is Lord of lords and King of kings. Everything else is footnote.

1.title: The Son of Man Among the Lampstands
1.overview:
The book opens with a triple identification of its nature: a revelation, a prophecy, and a letter. All three genres are in play simultaneously, and the reader who forgets any one of them will misread the whole. John does not ease us in gradually. Within three verses we have God the Father, Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit (the seven spirits), angels, and the entire church across time — the whole cosmic cast assembled on the opening page.

The chapter moves in three great waves. The Prologue (vv. 1–3) establishes the book’s source, content, and urgency. The Greeting (vv. 4–8) is a full trinitarian doxology that would have been recognized immediately as a counter-imperial manifesto — every title Caesar claimed for himself (“faithful,” “firstborn,” “ruler of kings”) is stripped from him and given back to Jesus. Then the Vision of the Son of Man (vv. 9–20) is the pivot of the entire book: before any seal is opened, any trumpet blown, or any bowl poured, John sees who stands at the center of history. Everything that follows is commentary on this one vision.

The vision of the glorified Christ is drawn almost entirely from Daniel 7 and 10. John’s first readers — Jews and Gentile God-fearers schooled in the Hebrew scriptures — would have felt the weight of every image. The white hair of the Ancient of Days, the eyes like flame, the feet like burnished bronze, the voice like many waters, the two-edged sword from his mouth: this is not a gentle Jesus meek and mild. This is the eternal Son in his glory, the conqueror of death, the sovereign over all history. The seven lampstands among which he walks are the seven churches — and the first thing any congregation needs to know about itself is that the glorified Christ walks among them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three verses, and the whole book is already positioned. Verses 1–2 give the chain: God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ, to show his servants what must soon take place; Christ made it known by sending his angel to his servant John; John bore witness to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus, to everything he saw. Nothing here originates with the writer. Verse 3 then pronounces the first of the book’s seven beatitudes, and it falls on three groups at once: the one who reads the words aloud, those who hear them, and those who keep what is written — because the time is near.

The word apokalypsis means an unveiling, a covering taken off something that was there already. That single word rules out the most popular use of this book. Revelation is not a code hiding the future from ordinary readers until a clever generation cracks it; it is the cloth coming off the throne, so that a church which can see only the magistrate and the temple of the emperor may also see who has been governing the world the whole time.

“Soon” (v. 1) and “the time is near” (v. 3) are the book’s first difficulty and are addressed at the verses themselves. In short: the Greek en tachei speaks of speed rather than of the calendar; the New Testament dates nearness from the cross, so that every generation since Pentecost has lived in the last days; and in any case a great deal of what this book describes fell on these very congregations within a few years.

The beatitude of v. 3 is the sentence that should govern how the book is used. The blessing is not attached to understanding it but to keeping it. And the picture behind the verse is a room, not a desk: one reader, many listeners, a scroll that had to be carried by hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Doctrine of Scripture in Two Verses

The chain in vv. 1–2 is a miniature of how God has always given his word. It originates with the Father, is mediated through the Son, is carried by appointed messengers, is received and attested by a named human author, and is addressed to the church. The divine origin does not flatten the human writer — John’s vocabulary, his memory of Daniel and Ezekiel, and his eye for detail are all over the book. The human writer does not dilute the divine authority — what he hands over is the word of God.

Necessity, Not Fate

“The things that must soon take place” uses dei, the word of divine necessity — the same word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 9:22). What follows in this book is not the churning of blind history and it is not a struggle whose outcome is undecided. It is a purpose being carried out. That is why the book can be read without panic even where it is terrifying.

A Book for Congregations

Verse 3 establishes that Revelation was written for public worship: the one who reads aloud is a lector standing before an assembly. This carries a real interpretive consequence. Whatever these visions mean, they meant something to ordinary first-century congregations who heard them once, at speed, without notes. An interpretation that could only have been discovered after the invention of the aeroplane or the internet has a case to answer.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A courier arrives in a market town with a scroll. On the first day of the week the congregation gathers in a house, most of them unable to read, and one man reads for an hour and a half while they listen. They are the first people ever to hear about the Lamb, the dragon and the city with no temple in it. Some of them will be dead within a decade for refusing to say three words about Caesar. The blessing of v. 3 is pronounced over that room.

Now: The same blessing is available on the same terms, and the terms are not scholarly. Revelation promises nothing to the reader who masters the interpretive debates and grows no braver. It promises everything to the reader who keeps it — who refuses the small compromise that would make work easier, who holds on when there is little strength left, who stays awake in a sleepy church. A useful test after any chapter of this book: did it leave you with an opinion, or with a resolve?

And “the time is near” has not expired. Every generation of the church is the last generation as far as its own members are concerned; none of us is more than a few decades from meeting him, and most of us have less notice than that. The posture this book cultivates — awake, obedient, hoping, holding on — is not an emergency setting for a final generation. It is the ordinary Christian standing position.

verseByVerse.quote: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book does not begin with John. It begins four steps above him. God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ; Christ made it known by sending his angel; the angel brought it to John; John bore witness to everything he saw; and the churches heard it read aloud. Five links, named in order, inside two verses. Before a single seal is broken the reader has been told exactly where this material came from, and it did not come from a lonely man’s imagination on a prison island.

That opening matters more than it looks. Everything strange that is coming — locusts with human faces, a woman clothed with the sun, a beast rising out of the sea — arrives with a chain of custody attached. Evidence is only admissible in court if someone can say who handled it, in what order, from the scene to the courtroom, with no unexplained gap. John opens with the chain of custody. The first name on it is God, and the last name on it is the congregation sitting on the floor of a rented room.

The title word sets the register for all twenty-two chapters. Apokalypsis means an unveiling — a covering pulled off something that was already there. It is what happens when the sheet comes off a statue, or when a surgeon finally opens a patient and sees what the scans could only suggest. Revelation is not God encrypting the future so that clever readers in the last generation can decode it. Revelation is God taking the cloth off the throne room so that a frightened church can see who has been running the world all along.

“The things that must soon take place” is the first hard sentence in the book, and smoothing it over would be dishonest. Nineteen centuries have gone by. Was John simply mistaken? Three things can be said, and all three are needed. The Greek is en tachei, which carries the sense of speed rather than of the calendar — when it starts, it will not drag. Luke uses the same phrase of a judge who gives justice speedily (Luke 18:8) in a parable that is explicitly about waiting a long time.

Second, the New Testament measures nearness from the cross and not from our diaries. The last days did not begin with a headline we are still waiting for; they began at Pentecost, and every generation since has lived inside them (Acts 2:17; Heb. 1:2). And third, the plainest point of all — a great deal of it did happen soon. Within a few years of this letter, Christians in the towns it names were losing their trade, their standing, and in some places their lives, exactly as the book says they would.

The small word must is doing quiet work too. Dei in Greek means necessity — the same word Jesus used when he said the Son of Man must suffer many things (Luke 9:22). It is not the blind necessity of fate. It is the necessity of a Father’s settled purpose. Nothing in the chapters ahead is a surprise upstairs. When the horses ride out and the seas turn to blood, no angel will be improvising.

See where the chain ends: his servants. The word is douloi, bond-slaves. John puts himself in that same category in the same breath — “his servant John.” The disciple who leaned back against Jesus at supper signs himself as a slave. That fixes the posture of everyone who comes after him. This book is not a document we stand over with a highlighter and a chart. It is a word we sit under, with our shoes off.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven times in this book a blessing is pronounced, and here is the first of them (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). Put the scene together before taking the sentence apart. It is the first day of the week, somewhere in Asia Minor, in a room that is somebody’s house on every other day of the week. Most of the people present cannot read. There is one copy of this scroll in the town, and it has just arrived by courier. A man stands up with it. For perhaps an hour and a half he reads, and nobody moves.

That is what the verse describes. “Blessed is the one who reads aloud” is singular — one lector, one voice. “Blessed are those who hear” is plural — the room. Revelation was not written to be studied privately with a pencil; it was written to be heard in company, which is why its images hit like hammer-blows rather than unfolding like an argument. If the book has ever felt airless to you on the page, that is because you are reading a script for a performance while sitting alone in a chair.

Then comes the sentence that ought to reorganise every approach to this book. The blessing does not fall on the one who understands. It falls on the one who keeps what is written. A man may hold every chart ever drawn of the seventy weeks and the seven years and miss the blessing entirely, while a widow who could not tell a seal from a trumpet walks straight into it. Revelation is not primarily an examination paper. It is a marching order.

Which raises a fair question: how do you keep a vision? You cannot obey a dragon. But the book answers this itself, two chapters later, and the answer is completely concrete. Keeping Revelation looks like refusing to say the words that would restore your trading licence (2:13). It looks like not eating at the guild dinner where the meat has been offered to Artemis, even though missing the dinner will cost you the contract (2:14, 20). It looks like holding on to what you already have when you have little strength left (3:8, 11). It looks like staying awake in a church where everyone else has drifted off (3:2). Every one of those is something a person can do this week without owning a single commentary.

There is a way of testing this tonight, and it costs nothing. Think of the last time this book came up in conversation. Was the subject a headline — a war, a technology, a politician, a date — or was the subject your own faithfulness? Revelation has been used for the first purpose for centuries, and the men who used it that way were often sincere and always eventually wrong. It was written for the second purpose, and it has never once failed at that.

The verse closes with the pressure that makes the whole thing urgent: “for the time is near.” The word is kairos — not clock-time ticking away, but the appointed moment, the hour that has been set. A soldier waiting for the order to move does not need to know the minute. He needs to know that the order is coming and that he must be standing where he was told to stand when it does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Greeting to the Seven Churches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What looks like a routine letter-opening is a declaration of allegiance. Verse 4 names the sender and the seven churches of Asia, and sends grace and peace from “him who is and who was and who is to come” and from “the seven spirits who are before his throne” — the Father in his eternal self-existence, and the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness. Verse 5a completes the trinitarian greeting with three titles for Jesus Christ: the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, the ruler of kings on earth. Prophet, priest and king — and every one of the three a title the Roman emperor claimed for himself.

At verse 5b the greeting breaks off into praise before it is finished: to him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. The tenses carry the doctrine. He loves — present, continuous, written to people who may not survive the year. He freed — past, completed, at the cost of blood. He made us a kingdom and priests — past, already done, so that the church’s royal and priestly standing is a present possession and not a future promotion (Ex. 19:6). Verse 6 closes the doxology with glory and dominion forever and ever, and the word for dominion, kratos, is an imperial word being handed to a crucified man.

Verse 7 is the announcement the book exists to make: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10 fused into one sentence — the same fusion Jesus made at his trial (Matt. 26:64). The coming is public, universal, and unmissable, and the wailing may be repentance or terror; the text leaves both standing, and the same sight will produce both.

Verse 8 gives God the Father the last word of the section in his own voice, which happens only twice in the book: I am the Alpha and the Omega… who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty. Pantokratōr — ruler of all — occurs nine times in Revelation and once in the rest of the New Testament. It was also carved on imperial monuments across the province of Asia. Only one of the two claimants is still ruling.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Name That Will Not Decline

“Him who is and who was and who is to come” (v. 4) is deliberately ungrammatical in Greek: John refuses to let the divine title change its endings after a preposition. It is his way of writing the name of Exodus 3:14 in a language that has no room for it. God’s sovereignty over time is his sovereignty over history — and the third term is not who will be but who is to come. What lies ahead of us is not simply more of God’s existence. It is his arrival.

A Kingdom and Priests, Already

The status granted in v. 6 is among the most neglected doctrines in the New Testament. The church is not a waiting-room for significance. It is a kingdom, and its members are priests — with access to God that needs no appointment, an intercessory office that carries other people’s names into the throne room, and sacrifices to offer in praise and generosity (Heb. 13:15–16). All of this belongs to the church now, in its weakness, under pressure, with the door watched.

Two Claims to One Title

The counter-imperial edge of vv. 5 and 8 is not a modern discovery imposed on the text; it is why the book was dangerous. Faithful, firstborn, ruler of kings, almighty: each belonged to Caesar in the public language of the province. John does not argue the case. He simply uses the words of Jesus, which is a far more serious act than argument, and it tells the churches where the line runs before a single letter is addressed to them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Pergamum the temple of Rome and Augustus stood on the hill above the city, the first of its kind in Asia. Trade guilds met over meals that opened with a libation to the emperor’s genius. A Christian who would not join in did not go to prison the same afternoon; he simply stopped getting work. Into that, a letter arrives whose opening line assigns every one of the emperor’s titles to a Galilean who was executed by a Roman governor.

Now: Every age has its own version of the demand, and it is rarely as clear as a temple on a hill. It is the sentence you are expected to agree with in a meeting; the opinion that has to be held before you can be considered reasonable; the ultimate loyalty quietly claimed by a career, a party, or a family. The greeting answers all of it in the same way: grace and peace have already reached you from a throne none of these things can approach, and the one who holds it loves you, present tense, today, in the middle of whatever is currently costing you something.

And the present tense in v. 5 is the pastoral heart of the section. John writes from exile to congregations facing economic exclusion, public ridicule and the risk of death, and the first thing he says about their Lord is not that he will reward them later but that he loves them now. Endurance is not squeezed out of Christians by threats. It grows out of that sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the majestic prologue, the ordinary furniture of a letter: sender, recipients, greeting. That in itself says something. Whatever else Revelation is, it is mail. It was addressed, carried, and delivered to seven congregations in seven real towns, and those towns sit on a road. A courier landing at Ephesus would go north up the coast to Smyrna, then further north to Pergamum, then turn inland and swing south-east through Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea — a rough circle of about three hundred miles. John lists them in exactly that order (v. 11). This is a postal round, not a numerological code.

Seven, all the same, is the number that governs this book — seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls, seven beatitudes, seven spirits. In Scripture’s symbolic arithmetic seven means fullness, the complete set. There were more than seven churches in Asia; Colossae and Hierapolis were both within a day of Laodicea. So these seven stand for the whole church, in every age, which is why the letters keep saying “he who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” — plural, every time.

Grace and peace come from three sources, and John names all three. The first is “him who is and who was and who is to come.” In Greek this phrase is deliberately broken. The grammar requires the words to change their endings after a preposition, and John simply refuses to let them — he leaves the divine title standing in the nominative like a boulder in a stream. The effect is untranslatable and unmistakable: this name will not be bent to fit our sentences. It is the name given at the burning bush, I AM WHO I AM (Ex. 3:14), stretched across time. And the third term is a surprise. Not “who will be” — which is what the pattern demands — but “who is to come.” God’s future is not merely more existence. It is arrival.

The second source is “the seven spirits who are before his throne.” This is the Holy Spirit in his sevenfold fullness, and two Old Testament pictures stand behind it: the Spirit resting on the Messiah in a sixfold description crowned by the Spirit himself (Isa. 11:2), and the lampstand of seven lamps in Zechariah’s vision, interpreted with the words not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech. 4:2–6). Some readers have taken the seven spirits to be seven high angels. Against that stands the position they occupy: they are named between the Father and the Son, in a greeting that dispenses grace and peace. No angel has ever had grace to give.

The third source is Jesus Christ, and he gets three titles where the others get one. The faithful witness — the Greek is martys, the word from which we get martyr, and the slide in meaning happened because of men like the one described here. He testified to the truth in front of a Roman governor and it killed him (cf. 1 Tim. 6:13). The firstborn of the dead — not the first to be revived, since others had been raised only to die again, but the first through death and out the other side permanently, the eldest son and heir of a family that will eventually be enormous (cf. Col. 1:18). The ruler of kings on earth — present tense, written by a prisoner of the empire, about the man the empire executed.

Prophet, priest, king. The faithful witness speaks God’s word; the firstborn from the dead has passed through death on our behalf; the ruler of kings reigns. And every one of the three was a title Caesar had already claimed. Roman coins called the emperor faithful and trustworthy. The imperial cult called him the firstborn of the gods. Ruler of kings was simply a description of what Rome was. John takes the three off Caesar and hands them back to their owner, in a letter, in the opening greeting, before he has said anything the censor could object to.

verseByVerse.quote: To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something happens here that the English cannot quite show. John is in the middle of a sentence — grace and peace from the Father, from the Spirit, from Jesus Christ, who is this and this and this — and then the sentence breaks. He never finishes the greeting properly. The mention of Jesus derails him into worship, and by the time he recovers, six verses have gone by. The gospel would not wait its turn.

Three things are said about what Christ has done, and the tenses are the whole sermon. To him who loves us — present tense, a participle that keeps running. And has freed us from our sins by his blood — past tense, done, a single completed act. And made us a kingdom, priests — past tense again, already enacted.

Take the present tense first, because it is the one a suffering reader needs. John does not write “him who loved us,” looking back to Calvary as a historical kindness. He writes loves, and he writes it from a prison island to people who may be dead within a year. That is the tense that has to hold when a diagnosis comes back, when a congregation shrinks to nine, when the trade guild strikes your name off the list. Not he loved me once and I must make that stretch, but he is loving me now, in this, while this is happening.

Then the past tense: freed us from our sins by his blood. The vocabulary is the exodus. Israel came out of Egypt because a lamb died and its blood went on the doorframe, and the whole nation walked out of slavery in the morning. Christ is the greater Passover lamb, and the slavery he breaks is not Pharaoh’s but the one underneath it — the guilt that no change of address can escape. And see what purchased it. Not his teaching, not his example, not his miracles. His blood: the actual, physical, arterial cost of a real death.

And then the extraordinary third clause. He made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. That sentence is lifted straight off Sinai, where God told a nation of former brick-makers that they would be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Ex. 19:6; cf. 1 Pet. 2:9). Now it is said of shopkeepers in Thyatira and slaves in Laodicea. And it is said in the past tense. The church does not get promoted into royalty and priesthood at some future ceremony. It already is both, right now, in its weakness, with its dwindling numbers and its debts.

What does a priest actually do, if he is a man who fits doors for a living? Three things, and none of them requires a robe. He has access — he walks into the presence of God without an appointment and without an intermediary, which no ordinary Israelite could ever do. He carries other people in there with him: that is what intercession is, standing at the throne holding somebody else’s name. And he offers sacrifice — praise, and a life laid down for others, and the money that could have been spent elsewhere (Heb. 13:15–16). A man who prays for his neighbour on the way to work has performed a priestly act, whatever his payslip says.

The doxology closes with glory and dominion forever and ever. The word behind dominion is kratos — raw ruling power, the root buried inside words like democracy and autocracy. It was an imperial word. And here it is being assigned, forever, to a man who was flogged, stripped, and nailed up outside a city wall by the very power that thought it owned kratos. To him who loves us. To him who freed us at the price of his own blood. To him who has made peasants into priests. To him be the glory and the dominion, for ever and ever, and there is no second name on the list. Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the announcement the whole book exists to make, and John gives it in one sentence built out of two Old Testament texts welded together. The first half is Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion. The second half is Zechariah 12:10, where the inhabitants of Jerusalem look on the one they have pierced and mourn. John did not invent the weld. Jesus made it himself, under oath, in front of the high priest who was about to condemn him: you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven (Matt. 26:64). The court heard it as blasphemy and voted to kill him. This verse is that answer coming back.

Clouds in the Old Testament are not weather. They are the vehicle of God’s presence — the pillar that went before Israel, the cloud that filled the tabernacle so densely the priests could not stand up to minister, the cloud on Sinai. A figure who comes with the clouds is not travelling by an unusual method. He is arriving as God arrives.

“Every eye will see him.” It would be difficult to write a more comprehensive phrase in any language. This settles a question that recurs in every generation, because in every generation somebody announces that the Lord has already returned quietly and only the initiated noticed. Jesus dealt with this himself: as lightning fills the sky from one horizon to the other, so will the coming of the Son of Man be (Matt. 24:27). Nobody will need to be told. Nobody will be able to check whether it happened.

“Even those who pierced him.” A soldier at Golgotha put a spear into the side of a dead man because it was the standard way to confirm a crucifixion. He went home afterwards and had his supper. This verse says he will see him again. So will the men who held the hammer, and the ones who chose Barabbas, and the councillors who agreed the verdict at night. Nobody involved has been lost track of. And the Zechariah passage John is quoting is even more staggering than the English shows: there it is the LORD himself who says they shall look on me whom they have pierced. John applies the line to Jesus and offers no explanation at all, because he has not noticed a difficulty.

Then: all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. The verb is kopsontai — to beat the breast, the violent public grief of a funeral. Which kind of grief is this? Godly readers have taken it both ways, and the text does not force the question. In Zechariah the mourning is unmistakably repentance: God pours out a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, and the people weep as for an only child. In Matthew 24:30 the same mourning reads much more like terror. The honest answer is probably that both are in view, because the same sight will produce both. The face that one man has longed for all his life is the face another has spent all his life avoiding, and when it finally appears, neither of them will be able to look away.

So this single verse holds the two halves of the book together in advance. To the seven churches, hunted and outnumbered, it says: he is coming, publicly, and everyone who ever laughed will be standing there when he does. To everyone else it says: you will see him. That is not a threat thrown at an enemy. It is a fact laid on a table while there is still time to do something about it. John ends the line by saying yes twice, once in Greek and once in Hebrew — nai, amēn — as though one language could not carry the agreement on its own.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God, "who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the whole of Revelation, God the Father speaks in his own voice in the first person exactly twice: here, and again at the very end when he says Behold, I am making all things new (21:5–6). Two sentences, twenty chapters apart, bracketing everything. The first says who he is. The second says what he will do. Between them come the dragon, the beasts, the famine, the martyrs and the burning city — all of it inside those two brackets, none of it outside.

“I am the Alpha and the Omega.” First and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and therefore everything in between: every word ever formed, every sentence ever spoken, the whole alphabet of history. He is not merely present at the start and waiting at the finish, like a man who sets a race going and then walks to the tape. He is the letters the middle is written with.

The threefold name returns — who is and who was and who is to come — and the order rewards a second look. Our instinct would be to start with the past: was, is, will be. John starts with the present, because that is where a frightened church is standing. God is not principally a memory from Israel’s history or a hope for a future generation. He is, in the present tense, in the room where the letter is being read.

Then the last word of the verse, which is the heaviest: the Almighty. The Greek is pantokratōr — ruler of all, holder of all power. It appears nine times in Revelation and only once in the rest of the New Testament (2 Cor. 6:18). In the Greek Old Testament it was the word chosen to render LORD of hosts, the God who commands armies. And in the first century it was also carved on monuments to the emperor. Two claims to the same title were now circulating in the province of Asia, and one of them was engraved in marble at public expense while the other was being read aloud in a borrowed room by people who could be arrested for it. The marble has been in museums for a long time.

Set that against what the seven churches could actually see. They could see the temple of the imperial cult on the hill at Pergamum. They could see the magistrate who decided whether their case went further. They could see the empty chair where a brother used to sit. What they could not see was the throne. So God says it himself, out loud, in the first person, before the visions begin: whatever your eyes report, the one who holds all power is not the man with the seal-ring, and he has not been away.

He is the Alpha, before whom nothing existed and by whose word everything that does exist came into being. He is the Omega, after whom there is no further chapter and beyond whom there is no appeal. He is the one who is, and who was, and who is on his way. He is the Almighty, and there has never been a single second in which that was less than completely true. Let the seals be opened. He is not braced for what is in them; he wrote them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — The Vision of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before a seal is opened or a trumpet blown, John is shown a Person, and everything in the remaining twenty-one chapters happens under the authority of the one he sees here. Verses 9–11 set the scene: John, calling himself brother and partner rather than apostle, exiled on Patmos for the word of God, in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, hears a voice like a trumpet commanding him to write and to send the book to seven named churches. The three things he shares with his readers — the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance — are bound together in the Greek by a single article. They arrive as one package.

Verses 12–13 give the setting of the vision: seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of them one like a son of man in a high priest’s long robe with a golden sash across his chest. The temple’s single seven-branched lampstand (Zech. 4:2–6) has become seven separate stands scattered along a Roman postal road, and Christ is not above them or outside them but among them, doing the priest’s daily work of keeping the lamps burning.

Verses 14–16 describe him feature by feature, and every feature is quarried from the Old Testament: white hair (Dan. 7:9 — the hair of the Ancient of Days, given here to the Son of Man), eyes like flame (Dan. 10:6), feet like burnished bronze from the furnace, a voice like many waters (Ezek. 43:2), seven stars in the right hand, a sharp two-edged sword from the mouth (Isa. 11:4; 49:2), and a face like the sun at full strength (cf. Matt. 17:2).

Verses 17–18 give John’s collapse and Christ’s answer. He falls as though dead; the right hand that holds the stars is laid on him without letting them go; and he hears Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades. Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-identification (Isa. 44:6) is claimed by a man who died.

Verses 19–20 close with the commission — write what you have seen, what is, and what is to take place after this — and with Christ explaining his own symbols: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, the seven lampstands are the churches. The identity of the angels is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse; what is not disputed is where they are. In his hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Highest Christology in the New Testament

John does not argue for the deity of Christ in this chapter; he assumes it by the images he chooses. In Daniel 7 the Ancient of Days and the son of man are two distinct figures. John takes what Daniel says about the first — hair white like pure wool — and says it about the second, then moves straight on. He does the same with Isaiah’s I am the first and the last, a formula Isaiah uses precisely to exclude every other claimant. Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate, is the God of Israel.

The Sword Is the Word

The two-edged sword comes from Christ’s mouth, not his hand (v. 16), and it is the same sword that strikes the nations at 19:15. The conquest this book describes is achieved by speech — the truth proclaimed by people with no leverage, apparently defeated for long stretches, and finally irresistible. That is also the only weapon the church has been issued. Where a church reaches instead for political power or cultural prestige, it is not merely making a tactical error; it is exchanging the sword of the Son of Man for something he never carried.

Tribulation, Kingdom, Endurance

Verse 9 will not let the three be separated. The New Testament nowhere promises the church exemption from tribulation in the present age (John 16:33; Acts 14:22), and it never treats present suffering as evidence that the kingdom has failed to arrive. Believers differ about a specific future tribulation and about the timing of the church’s deliverance from it, and those questions are taken up where the text raises them. This verse concerns the one the seven churches were already inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An old man on a bare island of sixteen square miles, banished under Roman relegatio, with no congregation, no property and no way home, keeps the Lord’s day by himself because the Lord rose whether anyone on Patmos cares or not. Heaven finds him there. The exile that looked like the end of a ministry turns out to be the circumstance in which the church receives its most extraordinary book.

Now: Most of us carry a Jesus scaled to our comfort — warm enough to approach, never so glorious as to unsteady us. Chapter 1 exists to recalibrate that, and the recalibration does not work by making him less kind. It works by making him larger and then showing that the enormous one stoops. The face like the sun in full strength belongs to the same person who reaches down to a man lying on a rock floor and says Fear not.

Two practical things follow. The first is for a church that feels small: the lampstand generates no light of its own and was never meant to; it holds the lamp up. Faithfulness, not impressiveness, is the whole job description, and he is standing in the middle of the room while it is done. The second is for anyone who has stood at a graveside or lies awake afraid of dying. The keys of Death and Hades are not lost, and they are not held by death. They hang from the belt of the one who went in and came out, and he wept at a friend’s tomb before he opened it.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying, "Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He could have written I, John, apostle. He could have written the disciple whom Jesus loved, which is how the fourth Gospel refers to him. Instead: I, John, your brother and partner. The Greek is synkoinōnos — a fellow-sharer, someone holding the same thing you are holding. Before he tells them anything they do not know, he tells them he is standing where they are standing.

And what are they all sharing? Three things, and in the Greek a single article gathers them into one bundle: the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus. Not three separate items on a list — one package, delivered together. That arrangement is the theology of the whole book compressed into eleven words. The kingdom does not arrive after the tribulation is over and it is not an alternative to it. The three come in the same envelope, and the middle one is the one nobody expects to find there.

This needs saying plainly, because it cuts against something the human heart assumes by default. A Christian under pressure very naturally concludes that the pressure is evidence of God’s absence — that if the kingdom were really here, the tribulation would not be. John, who is in more trouble than any of his readers, says the opposite: he is in the kingdom and in the tribulation, and both are “in Jesus.” The Lord said the same thing without a single softening clause: in the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33), and the apostles told the young churches on their way home that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Whatever a reader concludes about a specific future period of tribulation — and sincere believers hold different views about that, which this commentary will set out where the text raises it — this verse is about the one the seven churches were already in.

The third word in the bundle is the one that gets the reader through: hypomonē, translated patient endurance. It is not resignation, and it is not the vague cheerfulness we mean by patience. It is a military word for holding a position — remaining under the weight rather than stepping out from under it. It appears seven times in Revelation, and every time it describes the saints. The great Christian virtue in this book is not brilliance or influence. It is still being there.

Patmos is a bare volcanic island of about sixteen square miles, roughly forty miles off the coast, close enough to Miletus that on a clear day the mainland is a smudge on the horizon. Rome used such islands for relegatio, banishment — not a labour camp so much as a life shrunk to nothing, no property, no assembly, no way home. John is careful to say why he is there: on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. He was not sent for a crime. He was sent for a sermon. His circumstances look like the end of a ministry, and they are in fact the beginning of the most-read prophetic document in the world.

“I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.” This is the earliest surviving use of the phrase kyriakē hēmera for the first day of the week, the resurrection day, and it is dropped in without explanation because the readers already knew it. Picture what it means in his situation. There is no congregation on Patmos. There is nobody to read to, nobody to break bread with, no lampstand in sight. And an old man keeps the Lord’s day anyway, alone, on a rock, because the Lord rose whether anyone else on the island cares or not. That is where heaven finds him.

One guard is needed here, because this verse has been used to make ordinary Christians feel second-rate. “In the Spirit” describes something God did to John, not a technique John had mastered. He was not meditating his way upward; he was keeping Sunday, and the trumpet sounded behind him. Nobody reading this should conclude that a normal Christian life — prayer that feels flat, a psalm sung badly, a sermon half-remembered by Tuesday — is a lower grade of the same thing. It is the same Spirit. The dullest act of worship performed this month was performed in him.

The commission is immediate and specific: write it down, and send it to seven named towns. Not treasure this experience. The vision is not for John’s private edification, and it never becomes his possession. Within a sentence of receiving it he is a courier.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me.” The ESV keeps the oddity rather than tidying it, and the oddity is the point. You do not see a voice. But this voice is so massive, so evidently coming from somebody, that John turns to look at it the way you would turn towards a shout in an empty house.

What he sees first is not the figure. It is the furniture: seven golden lampstands. Anyone raised on the Hebrew scriptures would place them instantly. In the tabernacle and the temple there stood a lampstand of pure gold with seven branches, the menorah, and it burned continually in the holy place before the veil. Zechariah saw it in a vision and was told what it meant: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zech. 4:2–6).

But something has changed, and the change is the point. In the temple there was one lampstand with seven branches. Here there are seven separate lampstands. The single light of Israel has been broken out and distributed — one in Ephesus, one in Smyrna, one in Pergamum, and so on up the road. The holy place is no longer a room in Jerusalem. It is a rented hall in a Roman market town, and another one sixty miles north, and the lamp is lit in both.

A lampstand makes no light. Sit with that for a moment, because it quietly settles what a church is for. The stand holds the lamp up so the room can see. It is not admired; it is not the point; it is judged solely by whether the light is high enough to be useful. A congregation that has become impressive at everything except that has misunderstood the shape it was made in.

And then, in the middle of them, a figure: one like a son of man. The phrase comes from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds into the presence of the Ancient of Days and receives a dominion that will never pass away. It is the title Jesus used of himself more than any other, and its power lies in its double edge — on the surface it means simply a human being, and underneath it means the figure Daniel saw receiving the worship of all peoples.

He is dressed. The long robe is podērēs, the very word the Greek Old Testament uses for the high priest’s garment (Ex. 28:4), and the golden sash is not round his waist where a working man would knot it, but across his chest — the way a man wears a sash when he is not labouring but presiding. The first thing John sees him doing is priestly work: tending the lamps. That was the daily task in the holy place, morning and evening, trimming the wicks and topping up the oil so that the flame never went out.

Which leaves the phrase that carries the weight of the whole vision: in the midst of the lampstands. Not above them, inspecting from a height. Not outside, waiting for results. In the middle of them, close enough to touch the gold. Take the smallest, coldest gathering your church has had in the last year — the wet evening when eleven people came and the singing was thin and nobody could think of anything to say afterwards. He was standing in the middle of that room. He was not disappointed at a distance. He was there, doing what he does, keeping a wick alight that anybody else would have written off.

verseByVerse.quote: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven details, and every one of them has a reference behind it. John is not describing a face; he is assembling a theology out of the Old Testament’s greatest visions, and each feature tells a hard-pressed congregation something it needs to survive the week.

The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. This is the most audacious sentence in the chapter, and it is easy to walk past. In Daniel 7 there are two figures in the throne room: the Ancient of Days, whose clothing was white as snow and the hair of his head like pure wool, and the son of man who is brought before him. John has taken the description of the first and put it on the second. He does not argue for the deity of Christ here. He simply hands the son of man the Ancient of Days’ own hair and moves on to the next clause. The white is not the white of decline; in Daniel it is the mark of one whose existence has no beginning to date.

His eyes were like a flame of fire. Fire does two things at once: it illuminates and it consumes. Nothing survives it and nothing hides from it. In four of the seven letters that follow, this Christ will tell a church something about itself that it had managed not to know — Sardis thinks it is alive, Laodicea thinks it is rich. The eyes of flame are why. And the same fact lands two ways depending on where you are standing. To a believer keeping faith in a town where nobody notices, it means that nothing done in obscurity has gone unrecorded. To anyone maintaining a respectable front over something rotten, it means the front has never worked for a moment.

His feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace. Bronze glowing from the fire, and therefore bronze that has already been through it. These are feet that have stood in the heat and come out harder. Any reader who knows Daniel will remember three young men in a furnace and a fourth figure walking about in the flames with them, unbound and unburnt (Dan. 3:25). Feet also crush; that image will return when the winepress is trodden (14:20; 19:15).

His voice was like the roar of many waters. Ezekiel heard exactly this sound and named it: the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory — the glory of God returning to a temple it had abandoned (Ezek. 43:2). Stand at the foot of a waterfall in spate and try to hold a conversation. You cannot. Every other sound in the valley is simply taken away. That is the volume at which this Christ speaks over the empire, the accuser, the rumour, and the voice in a believer’s head at three in the morning.

In his right hand he held seven stars. The right hand is the hand of power and possession. The stars are not orbiting nearby; they are held. Verse 20 will say who they are. And Roman emperors put stars on their coins to advertise that heaven itself was in their gift — the deified Julius had a comet, and imperial issues showed the emperor with stars in his hand. John has seen the real hand.

From his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword. Not in his hand; from his mouth. The weapon of this King is speech. Isaiah said the coming ruler would strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isa. 11:4) and that God had made his servant’s mouth like a sharp sword (Isa. 49:2). The church has therefore been given no other armament, and needs none: not political leverage, not cultural weight, not numbers, but the word, spoken by people with no power, which has outlived every empire that ever banned it.

And his face was like the sun shining in full strength. Three of the men who read this letter’s companion Gospels had seen it once before, on a mountain, for about a minute (Matt. 17:2). Here it is not a glimpse permitted and withdrawn; this is simply what his face is like now, permanently, and it is the last detail because nothing can be added after it. Every other feature has been an image drawn from somewhere. The face is just the face. He is the light that the lampstands were made to carry, standing in the middle of them, shining at full strength in a province that thought it had put the gospel out.

verseByVerse.quote: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He fell down as though dead. This is the man who leaned back against Jesus at supper and asked him a question about the person sitting across the table (John 13:25). Sixty years later he sees the same person and his body simply stops holding him up.

That reaction is the normal one, which is itself instructive. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up and said Woe is me, for I am lost (Isa. 6:5). Ezekiel fell on his face (Ezek. 1:28). Daniel fell into a deep sleep with his face to the ground (Dan. 10:9). Peter, in a boat with more fish in it than it could hold, said Depart from me, for I am a sinful man (Luke 5:8). Nobody in Scripture who actually sees the glory of God finds it comfortable. Which raises a question worth putting honestly: if a congregation always leaves a service feeling pleasantly warmed and never once leaves it undone, has it been near this Christ, or near a picture of him scaled down to a size that would not disturb anybody?

Then the response, and every word of it counts. He laid his right hand on me. That is the hand from verse 16, the one holding the seven stars. He does not put them down to reach for John. The hand that governs the churches is the hand that steadies one frightened man on the floor, and it does both at the same time without strain.

Fear not. The first words the glorified Christ speaks to his church in this book are the same two words he used in Galilee to men in a sinking boat. The voice like many waters says the gentlest thing in the vocabulary. And note the order carefully, because sentiment gets it backwards: the comfort does not arrive by reducing the glory. John is not told that he over-reacted. He is left flat on the ground, and lifted there.

I am the first and the last. In Isaiah, twice, this is how God distinguishes himself from every rival: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isa. 44:6; cf. 48:12). It is not a phrase that can be shared out. Jesus takes it, unedited, and applies it to himself — and then adds something Isaiah could not have said.

And the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore. Read that slowly, because no other being in existence can put those two clauses side by side. He does not say I was dead and now I am not, as though death had been an interruption to be got over. He says I am the living one — the one whose very definition is life, the source of it — and then, I died. Life itself went into the grave. And came out, not restored to a life that could be lost again like Lazarus, but alive into the ages of the ages.

And I have the keys of Death and Hades. Keys are not decoration; keys are authority. Whoever holds them decides who goes in and who comes out, and holds them because the door is his. Death here is the event and Hades is the realm, the state of the dead — the two things every human being fears in different ways, the dying and the being dead. Both sets of keys hang from one belt, and they were taken by the only man who has ever been inside and walked out under his own power.

Which means this, exactly and without softening. A grave is not a locked room with the key lost. Somebody has the key, and he loves the person inside. For anyone who has stood at a graveside in the rain and heard the earth go down, that is not a decoration on a hard fact; it is the hard fact. The one holding the keys is not a stranger who might be persuaded. He is the one who wept at a tomb before he opened it (John 11:35, 43–44). And for anyone who lies awake afraid of their own dying, the fear is not answered by being told that death is small. It is not small. It is answered by the keys, and by whose hand they are in.

Death has a master. He was killed by it, and he came back holding its keys, and he is alive into the ages of the ages. Every grave that has ever taken one of his people is now a locked room to which he alone has the key, and he is coming back for what is his.

verseByVerse.quote: Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this.” The instruction is plain enough; what has been argued about for centuries is whether it is also an outline of the book. Many readers take it that way, and the case is a real one: chapter 1 is what John has seen; chapters 2–3 are the things that are, the state of the seven churches; chapters 4–22 are what must take place after this — and 4:1 does open with almost the same words, come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this. This is the structural key in the dispensational tradition, worked out with care by teachers such as John Walvoord and John MacArthur, and any reader in a church shaped by that tradition will have met it. It is a serious reading of a genuine feature of the text.

Others hesitate, for two reasons that should also be given fairly. The same Greek phrase, what must take place, is used in verse 1 of the entire book, chapters 2 and 3 included — so it is not obvious that it marks off a section beginning at chapter 4. And the contents resist the split in both directions: the letters to the seven churches are full of the future (a crown, a hidden manna, a pillar in the temple, the coming of Christ himself), while chapters 4 to 22 are full of the present (a throne that is occupied now, martyrs who are already under the altar, a Lamb who has already conquered). On that reading, the three phrases are simply a comprehensive way of saying: write down everything, past, present and future.

It should be said plainly that nothing essential rests on which of these is right. The Christ who commissions the writing is the same either way, and so is what he commissions. Readers who differ here can and do sing the same hymns. Where the structural question genuinely does change what a passage means — at the seals, at Babylon, at the thousand years — this commentary will lay the options out again at the verse itself rather than settling them here by a decision about grammar.

Then Christ explains his own symbolism, and that fact is more useful than the explanation. As for the mystery of the seven stars… the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches. Twice in one sentence the pattern is: this image means that reality. A reader who wanted a rule for handling the rest of the book has just been given one by the author. The word mystērion in the New Testament never means a riddle nobody can solve. It means something that was hidden and has now been told (cf. Eph. 3:3–5). The visions are not locked; they are explained, sometimes on the spot, and almost always by the Old Testament.

The angels of the seven churches remain genuinely open, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Three readings are held by careful people. Some take angelos in its ordinary Revelation sense — a heavenly being, which is what the word means in all sixty-odd other occurrences in this book — and understand a guardian angel set over each congregation. Others point out that each letter is addressed to the angel and then rebukes him and calls him to repent, which is difficult to say to an unfallen angel; on that view angelos carries its plain meaning of messenger and refers to the human leader who received the letter and read it to the assembly. A third view treats the star as the congregation’s heavenly counterpart, its corporate character as heaven sees it. The text does not settle it, and the letters work under any of the three.

What is not ambiguous is where the stars are and where the lampstands are. The stars are in his right hand. The lampstands are around his feet. Whatever pressure is coming in the next twenty-one chapters — and a great deal is coming — it will arrive at churches that are already held and already surrounded. That is the chapter’s last word before the letters begin, and it is the reason the letters can be as searching as they are. He can afford to tell Ephesus the truth. He is not going to lose it.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place.<sup>2</sup>He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.<sup>3</sup>Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.<sup>4</sup>John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,<sup>5</sup>and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood<sup>6</sup>and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>7</sup>Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.<sup>8</sup>“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”<sup>9</sup>I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.<sup>10</sup>I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet<sup>11</sup>saying, “Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”<sup>12</sup>Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands,<sup>13</sup>and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.<sup>14</sup>The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire,<sup>15</sup>his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters.<sup>16</sup>In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.<sup>17</sup>When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Fear not, I am the first and the last,<sup>18</sup>and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.<sup>19</sup>Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this.<sup>20</sup>As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.”

2.title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
2.overview:
The seven letters of chapters 2–3 are the most immediately practical section of Revelation. Before the cosmic drama unfolds, the risen Christ pauses to speak personally to each congregation — by name, with specific knowledge, with diagnostic precision. These are not generic pastoral encouragements. They are surgical letters, each one calibrated to the exact spiritual condition of a real church in a real city.

Every letter follows a recognizable pattern: (1) a self-identification of Christ drawn from the vision of chapter 1; (2) “I know” — a statement of Christ’s comprehensive knowledge of the congregation’s situation; (3) commendation or absence thereof; (4) rebuke or absence thereof; (5) a call to repentance or endurance; (6) “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches”; and (7) a promise to “the one who conquers.” The word nikōn (conqueror/overcomer) is the key word of the seven letters. Every letter ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, and the nature of overcoming is not occasional spiritual performance but faithful endurance to the end.

The seven churches were not chosen arbitrarily. They formed a postal circuit in the Roman province of Asia, moving roughly in a clockwise direction from Ephesus. Any one of them could be a “hub” for distributing the letter to surrounding congregations. But the number seven also signals completeness — these seven represent the whole church of every age. Every congregation since the first century has found itself somewhere in these seven letters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — To the Church in Ephesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Ephesus was the first stop on the courier’s road: a harbour city of some quarter of a million people, home to the temple of Artemis, and the congregation Paul had spent three years building (Acts 20:31). Verse 1 addresses its angel and identifies the sender as the one who holds the seven stars and walks among the seven lampstands — both images sharpened from 1:13 and 1:16. He grips, and he is moving through the room.

Verses 2–3 are two full verses of commendation before a word of criticism, and it is genuine: works, toil to exhaustion (kopos), patient endurance, an unwillingness to bear with evil, false apostles tested and exposed, weight carried for his name’s sake, and no weariness after forty years. Paul had warned this very church that wolves would come (Acts 20:29–30) and they had acted on it.

Verse 4 turns: you have abandoned the love you had at first. The verb is not cooling but putting down and walking on. Everything in vv. 2–3 is visible from outside; what is missing can be seen only by the eyes of fire. Verse 5 gives the remedy in three ordered verbs — remember where you have fallen from, repent, and do the works you did at first — and then the threat: the lampstand removed from its place. Not salvation withdrawn; a congregation ceasing to give light. There is no church in Ephesus today.

Verse 6 returns to commendation before the letter ends: they hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which Christ also hates. Verse 7 sounds the refrain — he who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches — and promises the conqueror the tree of life in the paradise of God: the tree guarded since Genesis 3:24 and standing open in the street of the city at 22:2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Orthodoxy Is Not Enough, and Neither Is Warmth

Ephesus is the proof that a church can be doctrinally impeccable and in mortal danger. But the very next letters forbid the obvious conclusion. Pergamum and Thyatira are rebuked for the opposite fault — for tolerating the teaching Ephesus refused — and Thyatira is explicitly credited with love at the head of its commendation. Two churches forty miles apart, each excelling exactly where the other failed, and each corrected by the same voice. Neither warmth nor rigour is the safe direction in which to err.

The Order of the Cure

Verse 5 does not say feel more. It says remember, repent, and do the works you did at first — deeds identified by pointing back to ones the church can remember doing. Affection cannot be generated by being commanded, and trying to produce it directly ends in despair. Christ prescribes actions instead, and expects the heart to follow the hands. The same order runs through the New Testament’s ethics, and it is the mercy of it.

Hatred as a Commendation

Verse 6 commends a church for hating something, and Christ says he hates it too. Love that is incapable of hatred is not love but indifference. The object is stated with care, though: the works of the Nicolaitans, not the Nicolaitans. That distinction is the whole difference between the church of Ephesus and a mob.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation into its second generation. The founding members who had watched the magic books burn in the street (Acts 19:19) are mostly dead. Their children hold the same doctrine, meet in the same houses, and defend the same truths — and nobody would now take the kind of risk their parents took, because nobody in the room can quite remember what it felt like to be astonished.

Now: This is the most common condition in a long-established church and the hardest to detect, because every measurable indicator reads normal. A useful private test: list the things you would mention if someone asked how you were doing spiritually. They will almost all be observable — attendance, giving, service, convictions, a reading habit. Christ commends every one of those here. Now ask what would remain if the unobservable thing had gone.

And the remedy is deliberately concrete, so it can be started this week. Not try to feel more. Do the thing you used to do: the visit, the giving that cost something, the praying before anyone was awake, the conversation about Christ you used to be willing to begin. The love that was put down can be picked up, and Christ says so to a church he has just threatened.

verseByVerse.quote: "To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: 'The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven letters follow, and they are built to a pattern. Each opens with an address to the angel of a named church. Each then identifies the sender by lifting one feature out of the vision of chapter 1 — and the feature chosen is always the one that particular congregation most needs to see. Each says I know. Each gives a commendation, or a complaint, or both. Each issues a command. Each calls out “he who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” And each ends with a promise to the one who conquers. Once the pattern is in view, the variations start speaking: Smyrna and Philadelphia get no complaint at all, and Laodicea gets no commendation.

Ephesus was the first stop on the courier’s road and the largest city in the province — a quarter of a million people, a harbour, a theatre seating twenty-four thousand, and the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Paul spent three years here (Acts 20:31). Timothy pastored here. By the time this letter arrives the congregation is roughly forty years old and into its second generation.

And the sender identifies himself as him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands. Both halves are from 1:13 and 1:16, and both are sharpened. In chapter 1 he simply held the stars; the word here is stronger — he grips them. In chapter 1 he stood in the midst of the lampstands; here he walks among them, which is what an inspector does. He is not stationed at the front of the room. He is moving through it.

That is the picture a church needs before it is criticised, and the order is not accidental. Christ does not begin the correspondence by naming faults. He begins by saying where he is standing. Every hard sentence in the next twenty-eight verses is spoken from inside the room, by someone who has not left and is not going to.

The address to the angel of the church raises the question set out at 1:20, and it need not be resolved to read the letter. Whether the star is a guardian angel, or the human messenger who will read the scroll aloud to the congregation, or the church’s own character as heaven sees it, the letter is plainly for everyone present: it closes by telling whoever has an ear to hear what the Spirit says to the churches, plural. All seven letters were sent to all seven towns. Ephesus read Laodicea’s mail, and so do we.

One further thing follows from that plural. These are not seven private notes that happen to survive. Any congregation that has ever existed will find itself somewhere in this chapter and the next — correct and cold, poor and hunted, compromised, tolerant of what it should have confronted, asleep, weak and faithful, or comfortable and self-satisfied. Before reading on for the interesting question of who the Nicolaitans were, a more useful question is which of the seven letters was written to the church you belong to.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name's sake, and you have not grown weary.
