verseByVerse.commentary:
I know your works. Every one of the seven letters begins there, and it cuts two ways depending on what is in the works. To Ephesus it opens a commendation that runs for two full verses before a word of criticism.

What he commends is impressive by any measure. Toil is kopos, labour to the point of exhaustion — not activity, but the kind of work that leaves a person emptied. Patient endurance is hypomonē again, the soldier’s word for holding a position. They cannot bear those who are evil. They have tested men who arrived claiming apostolic authority, examined the claim, and found it false — which took nerve, because rejecting a self-proclaimed apostle in the first century meant a public fight. Paul had warned this very congregation, in tears, that after his departure fierce wolves would come in among them and that men would arise from their own number speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29–30). Ephesus took the warning and acted on it for forty years.

Then verse 3 says it again from a different angle, and the repetition is deliberate: you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary. They have carried the weight. They have done it for his name and not for their reputation. And they have not given up. If a modern church presented that record — hard-working, doctrinally alert, resistant to fashionable error, still going after four decades — it would be held up as a model, and the assessment would not be wrong. Christ says all of it before he says anything else, and he means every word.

Which makes what follows in verse 4 far more serious than it would otherwise be. If Christ had opened with the fault, a reader could dismiss the commendation as softening. He opens with the commendation, at length, in detail, and it is genuine. The problem at Ephesus is not that the good things are unreal. It is that a church can have all of them and still be in danger.

There is a warning here for anyone who has ever measured a congregation. Everything in these two verses is visible from outside — the workload, the doctrinal spine, the longevity, the discernment. A visitor could count all four in a single Sunday. What is about to be named cannot be counted at all, and only the eyes like a flame of fire could see it. That is why the same church can be commended by every observer and corrected by its Lord in the same letter.

And a personal test comes out of it easily enough. Take the things about your own Christian life that you would list if somebody asked how you were doing spiritually. Almost certainly they are things that can be observed: attendance, giving, service, sound convictions, a habit of Bible reading. Every one of them is good, and Christ commends every one of them here. Now ask what would be left if the thing that cannot be observed had quietly gone.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. One sentence, and it undoes the tone of everything before it.

The verb matters. It is not that their love has cooled by degrees, the way a room cools when the fire goes out. Aphēkas is the word for leaving something behind, letting it go, releasing it — the same verb used of the disciples leaving their nets. Ephesus has not lost its first love in the way a man loses his keys. It has put it down and walked on.

What is first love? Two answers are usually given and there is no need to choose between them, because the letter itself refuses to. Love for Christ, plainly — the astonishment of a person who has just discovered he is forgiven and cannot get over it. And love for one another, which is what the same apostle spends his first letter insisting cannot be separated from it (1 John 4:20). A church that has stopped marvelling at grace will, in short order, stop being gracious. The two go together, and they leave together.

Picture the difference concretely, because this is easy to nod at and hard to see. A young congregation in the fifties of the first century takes in a runaway slave and hides him at real legal risk, because they cannot get over the fact that they were themselves bought out of slavery. Forty years on, the same congregation, in the same city, correctly identifies a false apostle, writes a careful refutation, and is right in every particular — and nobody in the room would take a risk like that any more. Nothing has been believed that should not be. Nothing has been added or removed from the creed. The doctrine is exactly what it was and the temperature is not.

Christ’s remedy is three verbs, and they are in a deliberate order. Remember — from where you have fallen. Not try harder; look back. Recovery begins with an honest comparison between what you were and what you are, and it is uncomfortable enough that most people skip it. Repent — the word means turn round, and it means this is a sin and not a phase. Coldness towards Christ is not a temperament or a season of life; it is something to be confessed. Do the works you did at first — and here the order reverses what we expect. He does not say wait until the feeling returns and then act. He says act, and he specifies the actions by pointing back to ones they can remember doing.

That last instruction is the practical hinge of the letter, and it is enormously freeing. Anyone who has ever tried to manufacture affection for God by sheer effort knows that it does not work and that failing at it produces despair. Christ does not ask for the feeling directly. He asks for the deeds, and he identifies them from the record: the visit you used to make, the giving that used to cost you something, the praying you used to do before anyone was awake, the conversation about Christ you used to be willing to start. Do those. The heart is not reached by being lectured; it is reached through the hands.

And then the threat, which is severe and precise: If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place. Not I will remove your salvation — this is a letter to a church, and the lampstand is the congregation as a light-bearer (1:20). A church that keeps its doctrine and loses its love does not immediately close; it can run for years on organisation and memory. But the light goes out, and eventually so does everything else. There is no church in Ephesus today. There has not been for centuries. The harbour silted up, the city was abandoned, and the lampstand stands in a field.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. Christ returns to commendation before the letter closes — and this is a church he has just warned with the removal of its lampstand. The rebuke is not the last word even inside the same paragraph.

Who the Nicolaitans were, nobody knows with certainty, and honesty is better than invention here. Irenaeus, writing about eighty years later, linked them to Nicolaus, one of the seven chosen in Acts 6:5, but he offers no evidence and later writers simply repeat him. What the text itself supplies is more useful: verses 14 and 15 place the Nicolaitans alongside the teaching of Balaam, and Balaam’s teaching is defined there as eating food sacrificed to idols and practising sexual immorality. So the Nicolaitans were almost certainly not a doctrinal sect in the abstract. They were the party of accommodation — the people arguing that a Christian could keep his guild membership, attend the dinner, join the ritual, and privately not mean it.

Take the word hate seriously, because it is used twice and the second time Christ applies it to himself. This is a church commended for hating something. That sits awkwardly with a sentimental picture of Christian love, and it should. Love that cannot hate anything is not love; it is indifference wearing love’s clothes. A father who watched his child being fed poison and felt nothing would not be gentle. And the object of the hatred is stated with care: not the Nicolaitans, but the works of the Nicolaitans. Ephesus has got that distinction right while getting first love wrong, and Thyatira will get first love right while getting this wrong. Neither church is asked to trade one for the other.

Then the refrain: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The words are almost exactly what Jesus said repeatedly in the Gospels after telling a parable (Matt. 11:15; 13:9). And what the exalted Christ says, John reports as what the Spirit says — the two are not in competition, and the sentence assumes a unity between them that no one in the room felt the need to explain.

The promise is the tree of life. Trace it back and the reach of it becomes clear. The tree stood in the middle of the garden, and after the fall a guard was set on the way to it so that fallen humanity could not reach out and take and live for ever in its ruin (Gen. 3:22–24). For the whole of Scripture after that, nobody eats from it. It reappears in the last chapter of the Bible, in the middle of the street of the city, with its leaves for the healing of the nations and no sword barring the path (22:2). Here in verse 7 the exile is declared over. The way back is open, and the one who opens it is the one who was himself hung on a tree.

And the promise is to the one who conquers — ho nikōn, the participle that ends every one of the seven letters. It is a fighting word, and it will be defined precisely later in the book: they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). Conquering, in Revelation, is not winning an argument or outlasting an opponent. It is holding on to Christ, at cost, to the end. Which means the promise is not for a special class of Christian. There is no other kind.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — To the Church in Smyrna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Smyrna, thirty-five miles north, was the most beautiful and most loyal city on the coast — a temple to the goddess Roma from 195 BC and a temple to Tiberius won in competition against ten rival cities in AD 26. Verse 8 introduces Christ to this church as the first and the last, who died and came to life: of all the images in chapter 1, the two about death are handed to the congregation that is about to face it.

Verse 9 names three things he knows. Their tribulation. Their poverty — ptōcheia, the destitution of a beggar, in a wealthy city, and the invoice for their faith. And the slander of those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Into the middle of that sentence Christ inserts three words: (but you are rich). Laodicea will receive the exact reverse (3:17).

Verse 10 forbids fear without denying the suffering. The devil is about to throw some of them into prison — and the purpose clause that follows, that you may be tested, does not belong to the devil. The word is the one used of assaying metal; the striking hand is his, the assaying is not (cf. Job 1:12; 1 Pet. 1:6–7). The ten days are a bounded stretch, and the boundary was not set by the persecutor. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life — stephanos, the victor’s wreath, in a city whose own skyline was called the crown of Smyrna.

Verse 11 closes with the refrain and a promise stated negatively: the conqueror will not be hurt by the second death, defined at 20:14 as the lake of fire. Everything Smyrna’s enemies can do to it falls inside the smaller of the two categories.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Two Ledgers

Of the seven churches, the two that receive no criticism at all — Smyrna and Philadelphia — are poor and under pressure, and the wealthiest receives no commendation at all. Nothing in that says money is evil or that suffering is holy in itself. It says the instrument we habitually use to assess a church’s health is not the instrument Christ uses, and that on the same congregation the two readings can be exactly opposite.

“Synagogue of Satan”

This phrase has been quoted to justify appalling things and must be read for what it says. It is not a statement about Jewish people. John is a Jew; so is Jesus; so were the apostles; and the same apostle wrote that salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Paul makes the identical move in the other direction — no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly (Rom. 2:28–29). Satan means accuser, and the charge is functional: a specific group in one city was informing on its Christian neighbours, and whoever brings accusations against God’s people is doing the accuser’s work, whatever building he meets in.

What the Second Death Cannot Reach

Smyrna is not promised escape from the first death; several of them will not escape it. It is promised immunity from the second. That is a strange consolation until one notices it is the only kind that is true, and that it holds when the cell door shuts. Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more that they can do (Luke 12:4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: About sixty years after this letter, Polycarp, bishop of this same church and perhaps a young man when it was first read aloud, was brought into the stadium at Smyrna and urged to swear by the genius of Caesar. He answered that he had served Christ eighty-six years and Christ had never done him wrong, and asked how he could blaspheme his King and Saviour. He asked to be left unfastened at the stake, on the grounds that the one who gave him strength to endure the fire would give him strength to stay still in it.

Now: This letter belongs to every persecuted congregation in the world — in North Korea, in Nigeria, in Iran, in parts of China — and to them Christ says exactly what he said here: I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich). He knows. The poverty is real, the danger is real, and so are the riches.

And for the reader who is quietly frightened by all this and doubts he could stand: the question is not whether you feel able to face a prison today. Nobody does, and Peter, who was certain he could, could not (Luke 22:33, 57). Grace is not issued in advance for a trial you are not yet in. It is issued on the day, in the cell, at the fire (Luke 21:14–15). Smyrna was not asked to manufacture courage in the waiting weeks. It was told who would be there when the door opened.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: 'The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. "'I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty-five miles north of Ephesus lay Smyrna, and it was the most beautiful city on the coast — a planned city, rebuilt after centuries of ruin, with a paved processional street running from the harbour to the temple of Zeus and a ring of public buildings along the ridge of Mount Pagos that visitors called the crown of Smyrna.

It was also the most loyal city in Asia. Smyrna had built a temple to the goddess Roma in 195 BC, long before Rome was fashionable, and in AD 26 it won a competition among eleven cities for the right to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius. To be a Christian in Smyrna was to be conspicuous in the one town on the road where nobody wanted to be conspicuous.

Christ introduces himself to this congregation as the first and the last, who died and came to life. Every letter takes its self-description from chapter 1, and this one takes the two clauses about death (1:17–18) and hands them to the church that is about to face it. To a congregation being told to prepare for prison, the credential offered is not power in the abstract. It is that he has been where they are going. The one giving the orders has been dead.

Then: I know your tribulation and your poverty. The word for poverty is ptōcheia — not the modest means of a working family but destitution, the word for a beggar with nothing. In a rich city. That is not an accident of economics, and the letter has already hinted at why: a Christian who would not join the guild ritual lost the guild’s work, and a Jewish believer disowned by the synagogue lost the legal protection that exempted Jews from emperor worship. Their poverty was the invoice for their faith.

And into the middle of that sentence Christ inserts three words in brackets: (but you are rich). The parenthesis is the whole letter. He does not deny the poverty; he has just named it. He sets a second balance sheet beside the first and says the second is the real one. Laodicea, in a few verses, will get the mirror image: you say, I am rich… not realising that you are wretched, pitiable, poor (3:17). Two churches, two account books, and the figures inverted in both.

This needs saying plainly to anyone who has ever measured a church by its resources, or measured himself that way. Of the seven congregations, the two that receive no criticism whatever are Smyrna and Philadelphia, and both are poor and under pressure. The one that receives no commendation whatever is the wealthiest. Nothing in that pattern says money is evil or that hardship is holy by itself. It says that the instrument we habitually use to assess spiritual health is not the instrument Christ uses, and that the two readings can be exactly opposite.

The last clause is the hardest in the letter and must be handled carefully: the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. This is not a statement about Jewish people, and reading it as one has done terrible damage. John is himself a Jew. So is Jesus. So were the apostles. The same apostle wrote that salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22), and Paul, using the same logic, wrote that no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly (Rom. 2:28–29).

The charge here is against a specific group in one city who were, at that moment, informing on their Christian neighbours to the Roman authorities. Satan means accuser. The word is functional: whoever brings accusations against the people of God is doing the accuser’s work, whatever synagogue or church he attends. Sixty years later, at the martyrdom of Polycarp in this very city, it was a mixed crowd who called for his death, and the eyewitness account records that some of them ran to fetch the wood.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Not do not fear, you will not suffer. The suffering is confirmed in the same sentence in which the fear is forbidden. Whatever comfort this verse gives, it does not work by promising that the thing will not happen.

What follows is a remarkable piece of construction, and every clause moves the reader’s eye somewhere different. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison — so the agent is named, and he is real. This is not blind misfortune. Somebody is doing it. Some of you, not all — which is worse in one way, because it means the congregation will spend the coming months not knowing who. A Roman prison, incidentally, was not a sentence but a holding cell; you went in to await trial, and the trial ended in release, exile, or execution.

And then the clause that turns the verse over: that you may be tested. It is a purpose clause, and the purpose does not belong to the devil. He throws them in to destroy their faith; that is what he is for. The sentence says the imprisonment has another purpose running through the same event, and that purpose is the proving of something valuable — the word is the one used of assaying metal. The devil is permitted to strike, and while he strikes he is unwittingly doing the assayer’s work. Job was the first man to live inside that arrangement, and Peter said the same thing to churches in this same province: the tested genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Pet. 1:6–7; cf. Job 1:12).

That single clause is what makes the difference between endurance and mere stoicism, and it is not an abstract comfort. A believer facing something frightening does not principally need to be told that it will end. He needs to know whether it means anything. This says it does: the thing coming at you has been given a purpose it did not choose, and the purpose is not your destruction.

And for ten days you will have tribulation. Ten days is short. In a book where numbers carry meaning, ten is the round figure for a complete but limited stretch — Daniel and his friends were tested for ten days (Dan. 1:12–14). Nobody should press it into a calendar. The point is the shape: the suffering has a stated duration, and the one who states it is not the devil. There is a fence around this, and the fence was not built by the man who is about to be arrested.

Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. The phrase can mean faithful right up to the end of your life, and it can mean faithful even to the point of being killed. Both were true in Smyrna. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath of leaves given at the games — not the royal diadēma. Every athlete in Smyrna knew that the wreath was brown within a week. And the citizens of Smyrna called the ring of buildings on their skyline the crown of the city. Christ takes the local word for beauty that lasts a generation and a sporting trophy that lasts a week, and offers instead a crown that is life.

One honest word for the reader who reads this and is quietly frightened, because many are. The question is not whether you feel you could face a prison. Nobody feels that, and Peter, who was certain he could, could not (Luke 22:33, 57). Grace is not issued in advance for a trial you are not in. It is issued on the day, in the cell, at the fire — which is exactly what Christ promised (Luke 21:14–15). Smyrna was not being asked to generate courage in the weeks before the arrests. It was being told who would be with them when they came.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refrain again — He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches — and then a promise phrased entirely in the negative: The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.

The phrase second death occurs four times in Scripture and all four are in this book. It is defined at 20:14: the lake of fire is the second death, the final and irreversible separation from God of those who have refused him. So the arithmetic of the promise is simple and devastating. There are two deaths available to a human being. The first is what everyone in Smyrna is afraid of and what some of them are about to suffer. The second is the one that actually matters.

Set that against the situation on the ground. The magistrate can compel the first death and has no jurisdiction whatever over the second. The devil can throw them into prison and cannot follow them past the grave. Everything the enemies of this congregation are able to do to it is contained inside the smaller of the two categories. Jesus had said it in one sentence: do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more that they can do (Luke 12:4).

Something is conspicuously not promised, and the honesty of it is part of the comfort. Smyrna is not told it will escape the first death. Several of them will not. Christ does not offer his most faithful church protection from the thing it fears; he offers immunity from the thing it has not thought about. That is a strange kind of consolation until you realise it is the only kind that is actually true, and the only kind that holds when the cell door shuts.

Polycarp was bishop of this church about sixty years after this letter arrived, and he may well have heard it read as a young man. When the proconsul at Smyrna urged him to swear by the genius of Caesar and revile Christ, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years and Christ had never done him wrong, and asked how he could blaspheme his King and Saviour. They burned him in the stadium. The eyewitness letter the church of Smyrna wrote afterwards says that he had prayed all night beforehand and that when the fire was lit he did not need to be nailed to the stake, because he asked them to leave him unfastened: the one who gives strength to endure the fire would give him strength to stay still in it.

The whole letter to Smyrna is four verses long. It contains no criticism, no correction, and no promise of relief. What it contains is a Christ who was dead and is alive, a purpose running through the persecution that the persecutor did not put there, a fence around the suffering, a crown, and an assurance that the worst that can be done to them is the second-worst thing there is. For the poorest and most frightened church on the road, that was enough. It has been enough ever since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — To the Church in Pergamum
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Pergamum, inland on a cone of rock a thousand feet high, was the administrative capital of the province and the seat of the governor — the place where the right of the sword actually resided. Verse 12 accordingly introduces Christ as him who has the sharp two-edged sword. Verse 13 says I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is: the Great Altar of Zeus on its terrace, the serpent-emblemed healing shrine of Asklepios whose god was titled Saviour, and the province’s first temple to a living emperor, all on the same hill. In that city they held fast his name and did not deny the faith even when Antipas — given Christ’s own title from 1:5, my faithful witness — was killed among them.

Verses 14–15 bring the charge. Some there hold the teaching of Balaam, who could not curse Israel and so taught Balak to seduce it instead (Num. 22–24; 25:1–9; 31:16): eating food sacrificed to idols and practising sexual immorality, which in a guild town arrived in the same evening. Verse 15 adds the Nicolaitans — the very group Ephesus was commended for hating in v. 6. The accusation is not that the whole church holds this, but that the church has some there who hold it, unchallenged.

Verse 16 commands the whole congregation to repent, and the pronouns then separate ominously: I will come to you and war against them with the sword of my mouth. A church that will not act against error is not exempted from the action; the action is simply taken by someone else, in the middle of the assembly.

Verse 17 sounds the refrain and gives three promises, each the reverse of what the compromisers wanted: hidden manna instead of guild meat (Ex. 16:33–34; cf. John 6:35), a white stone — a juror’s acquittal pebble, a victor’s banquet token, a guest’s ticket, the readings differ — and a new name known only to the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Strategy

Balaam is in this letter because the sword had failed. Pergamum stood firm against execution and fell to a dinner invitation. What could not be cursed from outside was seduced from inside, and the argument that carried the day was never an argument for wickedness — it was that the ritual is a formality, that everyone does it, that a family has to eat, and that God looks on the heart. The stumbling block is not laid in front of people who want to fall. It is laid in front of people who need the work.

Right Doctrine Is Not the Same as Loyalty

Balaam himself spoke true prophecy, blessed Israel four times against his own financial interest, and foretold the star out of Jacob (Num. 24:17) that this very chapter picks up in v. 28. He died fighting against the people he had blessed (Num. 31:8). A man can say true things about God for years and end on the wrong side, and the drift is rarely announced.

Silence Is a Decision

The command to repent in v. 16 goes to everybody, including the majority who personally held nothing of Balaam’s teaching. Their failure was that nobody said anything. And the weapon Christ names for himself — the word out of his mouth — is the weapon the church should have been using: not force, not expulsion by muscle, but the true thing said out loud.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A dyer or a bronzeworker in Pergamum belongs to a guild, and the guild is also a religious association with a patron god, a temple, and banquets at which the meat has been offered on the altar. Refuse the dinner and you are outside the guild; outside the guild there is no work. Meanwhile the same man has already looked a Roman magistrate in the face and refused to say three words about Caesar. He can face the sword. It is the invitation he cannot face.

Now: Very few readers are asked to burn incense. A great many are asked to say something in a meeting they do not believe, to stay quiet where speaking would cost a promotion, to let an arrangement pass unquestioned, to laugh at the table. The reasoning offered is Balaam’s, unchanged in nineteen centuries, and it is always reasonable.

Against that, the promises of v. 17 are exactly calibrated. A believer who refuses loses contracts, then standing, and finally the way the town speaks of him — he becomes the awkward one who could not be sensible. This letter does not pretend that costs nothing. It says a name is being kept for him that the city could not have given and cannot take away, written on a stone, known to Christ and to him and to nobody else alive.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: 'The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. "'I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pergamum sat inland on a cone of rock a thousand feet above the plain, and it was the administrative capital of the province — the seat of the Roman governor, and therefore the place where the ius gladii, the right of the sword, the authority to execute a Roman citizen, actually resided. Christ introduces himself to this city, and only to this city, as him who has the sharp two-edged sword. The governor of Asia held a sword by delegation and used it on Antipas. There is another sword in this letter, it comes out of a mouth, and its owner did not receive it from anyone.

I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Three things in Pergamum have been proposed as the throne, and there is no need to choose only one, because a first-century Christian climbing that hill would have seen all three. The Great Altar of Zeus stood on a terrace near the summit, forty feet high, its frieze carved with gods destroying giants, and from below it looked like a throne on a mountain. Below that lay the Asklepion, the most famous healing shrine in Asia, whose god’s emblem was a serpent and who was worshipped under the title Saviour. And Pergamum had built the province’s first temple to a living emperor in 29 BC, which made it the birthplace of the imperial cult in Asia. Political power, false salvation, and a serpent, all on one hill.

The verb Christ uses of the church is dwell — katoikeis, the word for settled, permanent residence, not for lodging somewhere temporarily. And at the end of the verse he uses the same root of Satan: where Satan dwells. They live there. He lives there. Nobody is passing through.

Stay with that, because it answers a question honest Christians ask about where they have ended up. Christ does not tell this congregation to move. He does not say that a believer should not be living in a place like that, or that their difficulty would be solved by relocation. He says I know where you dwell — and then commends them for what they have done while dwelling there. The address is not the problem. Faithfulness is measured on the ground a person is actually standing on, and some believers are standing on very hard ground by appointment rather than by mistake.

Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith. Two verbs, one positive and one negative, and in a city with a governor holding a sword they mean something specific. Holding fast the name means still saying it in public. Not denying the faith means that when the question came — and in this city it came formally, with a magistrate and a written record — they did not give the required answer. The test in the Roman world was rarely a demand to renounce Christ in words. It was usually a demand to say three words about Caesar and offer a pinch of incense, after which a man could believe whatever he liked in private. Pergamum would not do it.

Even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you. This is the only place in the Bible where the name occurs, and nothing else is known about him with any certainty. What is known is the title Christ gives him. In 1:5 Christ himself is the faithful witness. Here he hands his own description to a man from Pergamum who died in the same manner. Nobody remembers who the governor was. There is one name from that courtroom that the risen Christ has kept, and it is not the man who held the sword.

Two words remain, and they are among the most consoling in the letter: among you. Not in your city, not in that period. Among you. Whoever these people were, they had watched it happen, and some of them had probably been unable to stop it. Christ names their friend, in a letter, in front of everyone, and gives him his own title. Nothing done to the church at Pergamum happened out of sight.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commendation stops. But I have a few things against you — and the problem is not that Pergamum has denied Christ under pressure, because it has not. The problem is what it has permitted inside the room while standing firm at the door.

The reference is to one of the strangest episodes in the Old Testament, and the reader who has not got it in mind will miss the force of the charge. Balak, king of Moab, hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam tried four times and could not; every time he opened his mouth a blessing came out (Num. 22–24). Curses had failed. So — and Scripture states this explicitly much later, when Moses is accounting for a disaster — Balaam gave Balak different advice: send in the women (Num. 31:16). Israel was invited to the Moabite festivals, ate the sacrifices, committed immorality with the women of Moab, bowed to their gods, and twenty-four thousand died in a plague (Num. 25:1–9).

What could not be cursed from outside was seduced from inside. That is the teaching of Balaam, and it is why Christ raises it in a letter to a church that has just been praised for not denying his name under threat of execution. The sword did not work at Pergamum. So the strategy changed, and the second strategy was working.

The two specifics named — eating food sacrificed to idols and practising sexual immorality — were not two unrelated vices. In a Roman city they usually arrived in the same evening. Trade guilds were also religious associations; the carpenters, the dyers, the bakers each had a patron deity, and membership involved attending banquets held in the temple precincts, where the meat had been offered on the altar and where the later part of the evening commonly involved the women attached to the temple. Refuse the dinner and you are outside the guild. Outside the guild there is no work. The party of accommodation in Pergamum was not arguing for wickedness. It was arguing that a man has to feed his family, that the ritual means nothing to a Christian anyway, and that God looks on the heart.

At that point the letter stops being about the first century. Almost nobody reading it is being asked to burn incense. A great many people are being asked to say something in a meeting they do not believe, to stay quiet where speaking would cost a promotion, to let a client’s arrangements go unquestioned, to laugh at the table. And the argument that carries the day is always Balaam’s: it is only a formality, everyone does it, the alternative is your family’s income, and God knows your heart. The stumbling block is not laid in front of people who want to fall. It is laid in front of people who need the work.

Verse 15 adds the Nicolaitans, and the parallel with verse 6 is exact and pointed. Ephesus hated the works of the Nicolaitans; Pergamum has some who hold their teaching. The same error, forty miles apart, met with rejection in one church and hospitality in the other. Between the two letters Christ has now criticised a church for being loveless and a church for being tolerant, which forecloses the comfortable assumption that one of these is the safe direction to err in.

And the grammar of the accusation should not slip past. He does not say some of you hold this teaching, which would be a charge against individuals. He says you have some there who hold it — the charge is against the church for having them, unchallenged, in the membership. Pergamum’s sin is not that a few people were wrong. It is that nobody said anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore repent. Two words, addressed to the whole congregation, including the majority who have done nothing wrong except let it happen. That is the first thing to see here. The people who held Balaam’s teaching are a faction; the command to repent goes to everyone. A church is answerable for what it tolerates, and silence is a decision.

Then the threat, and its wording is unexpected: If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth. He comes to you; he wars against them. The pronouns separate, and the separation is deliberate and faintly terrifying. Christ will arrive at the congregation and conduct a battle inside it, and the faithful majority will be standing in the room while he does. Refusing to act against error does not exempt a church from the action. It simply means the action is taken by someone else, in the middle of the assembly, without consultation.

The sword is the one from 1:16 and 2:12 — the word of God proceeding from his mouth. That is how he fights. It is not a metaphor for something gentler; a sword is for cutting, and in 19:15 the same sword strikes the nations. But it does tell a church what the instrument of correction is, and therefore what its own instrument should have been. Pergamum was not asked to expel anyone by force or to organise against the faction. It was asked to say the true thing out loud, which is precisely what nobody there was doing.

There is an irony in the letter that a first-century reader in that city would have felt at once. Pergamum is where the sword of Rome lives. The believers there have already faced it and not flinched; Antipas went to his death rather than say the words. The sword they could see did not move them. The danger they had not noticed came from a sword they could not see, and it was pointed the other way — not at their bodies, which were brave, but at the purity of the church, which was unguarded.

Balaam himself is a warning attached to this. He is one of the few figures in Scripture who spoke true prophecy, blessed God’s people four times against his own financial interest, and predicted the star that would come out of Jacob (Num. 24:17) — a line this book will pick up in eleven verses’ time. And he died by the sword, fighting with Midian against the people he had blessed (Num. 31:8). Getting the doctrine right and saying true things about Christ is not the same as being on his side, and a man can do the first for years while drifting into the second.

The word soon should be read the way 1:1 taught us to read it. It does not necessarily mean next month. It means without delay once the decision is taken, and it means the matter is not going to be left indefinitely. God’s patience is real — the next letter will show him giving a false prophetess time to repent — but it is patience with a purpose, not tolerance without a limit. The door that stands open in this verse is the same door that closes in verse 22.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three promises, and every one of them is the reverse of something the compromisers in Pergamum were arguing for. They wanted the guild dinner; Christ offers hidden manna. They wanted the token of admission; Christ offers a white stone. They wanted to keep their standing in the city; Christ offers a new name.

Some of the hidden manna. Manna was the bread that fell in the wilderness for forty years, and a jar of it was kept inside the ark of the covenant as a permanent memorial (Ex. 16:33–34; Heb. 9:4) — hidden, in the sense that it was behind the veil where no one but the high priest could go, once a year. Set that against the issue in the letter and the promise lands exactly. The argument in Pergamum was about meat: eat what the temple provides, or lose your income. Christ answers with a different menu. Israel in the desert was fed by God alone, daily, for four decades, in a place with no fields and no guilds, and nobody starved. And the Lord who says this once said of himself, in a synagogue argument about manna, I am the bread of life (John 6:35, 48–51). What is hidden now is a Person, and the hiddenness is temporary.

A white stone. This one is genuinely uncertain and several proposals have been made by careful readers. A juror in a Greek court dropped a white pebble for acquittal and a black one for condemnation. A victor at the games was given a token that admitted him to the celebration banquet. A guest at a private feast received an inscribed ticket. Anyone freed from slavery received a token of manumission. Any of these would fit; the first and the second fit best, and the letter does not settle it. What all of them share matters more than deciding between them: the stone is small, personal, handed to one individual, and it is the thing that gets him in.

With a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it. A new name in Scripture marks a changed identity conferred by God — Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel, Simon to Peter. But the striking clause is the privacy of it. Nobody else knows it. Whatever else it means, it means that the knowledge Christ has of each of his people is particular and not generic. He is not handing out identical certificates to a crowd.

Consider what that says to the specific people being addressed. A tradesman in Pergamum who refuses the guild dinner loses, in order: his contracts, his standing, and eventually the way the city refers to him. He becomes the awkward one, the man who could not be reasonable. That is a real cost and this letter does not pretend otherwise. What it says is that a name is being kept for him which the city could not have given and cannot take, written on a stone, known to Christ and to him and to nobody else in the world.

And for anyone who has ever felt that God’s love is a general policy rather than something addressed to them personally — that he saves crowds and might not have noticed one particular obscure believer in one particular unglamorous town — this verse is the answer, and it is deliberately intimate. A private name, on a stone, in his hand, for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — To the Church in Thyatira
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Thyatira was the smallest and least distinguished of the seven towns — no great temple, no governor, a valley with no defences, and more trade-guild inscriptions than any of the other six. Lydia, the first convert in Europe, dealt in its purple cloth (Acts 16:14). It receives the longest of the seven letters.

Verse 18 introduces Christ as the Son of God — the only use of that title in Revelation — with eyes like a flame of fire and feet like burnished bronze, in a town of metalworkers. Verse 19 gives the warmest commendation of the seven: love, faith, service and patient endurance, and latter works exceeding the first. Where Ephesus had gone backwards, Thyatira is growing, and love heads the list.

Verses 20–21 bring the charge: they tolerate a woman Christ calls Jezebel — a type, not a name (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4; 21:1–16) — who calls herself a prophetess and teaches Balaam’s programme over again. Nobody is accused of believing her; they are accused of letting her continue. Verse 21 adds that Christ gave her time to repent and she goes on refusing.

Verses 22–23 pronounce judgment, and every clause carries a distinction. The couch of the banquet becomes the sickbed. Those who commit adultery with her are threatened unless they repent — the door still open inside the sentence. Her children, in the Old Testament idiom, are those who have made her teaching their own. And all the churches will learn that he searches kidneys and hearts (Jer. 17:10) and repays each according to his works.

Verses 24–25 turn to the faithful remnant who never learned what some call the deep things of Satan — almost certainly the faction’s own boast about the deep things of God, with one noun replaced. To them: I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.

Verses 26–29 give the promise: authority over the nations, in the words of Psalm 2:8–9, handed on from the Son who received it from his Father; and then the morning star, which the book identifies as Christ himself (22:16; cf. Num. 24:17). Verse 29 closes with the refrain — and from this letter onward the refrain comes after the promise rather than before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment Read Carefully

Verses 22–23 are the hardest sentences in the seven letters, and reading them closely removes most of the horror without removing any of the weight. The threat against those drawn in is explicitly conditional — unless they repent. Her children are distinguished from them in the same breath: the idiom means her spiritual offspring, those who now reproduce the teaching rather than merely having been seduced by it. And the whole passage ends by turning from her and them to each of you.

“According to Your Works” and Justification by Faith

A reader who has grasped salvation by grace alone will stop at v. 23, and the question deserves an answer rather than a hurry. Scripture says both without embarrassment: no one is justified by works of the law (Gal. 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done (Rom. 2:6; 2 Cor. 5:10). Nobody is admitted on the strength of his works. The works are the evidence of whose he is, and the measure of what is given afterwards. A tree is not made alive by its fruit and is identified by nothing else.

Not a Text About Women Teaching

The charge in v. 20 is a self-issued claim to prophetic authority used to promote a doctrine that was destroying people. It is the identical charge brought four verses earlier at Pergamum with no reference to anyone’s sex, and the parallel Christ himself draws is with Balaam, who was a man. What is confronted is the teaching and the pretended authority behind it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A believer in Thyatira who will not attend the guild feast watches his neighbours attend it with a clear conscience, on the authority of a prophetess who says the mature have moved beyond such scruples. He is the awkward one. He is also poorer every year. And he has watched the church say nothing about it for a long time, and has begun to wonder whether God has an opinion.

Now: Two things in this letter are addressed to exhaustion, and both are easy to miss. The first is v. 21: the years in which nothing was done were years the Lord was holding open for a woman to turn (cf. 2 Pet. 3:9). Delay is not always absence, and the silence a believer finds unbearable is sometimes mercy being extended to somebody he has already written off.

The second is v. 24–25, and it is one of the most freeing sentences in the New Testament. To the faithful minority in a compromised church, Christ says: I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come. Not reform it, not purge it, not carry it — hold on. The judgment of Jezebel is his business and he has stated his timetable. There are believers being ground down by a responsibility they were never given, and this verse takes it off them. The requirement is not to fix it. The requirement is to still be holding on when he arrives — and the promise for those who are is not first authority over the nations, staggering as that is, but the morning star himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: 'The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. "'I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thyatira was the least distinguished of the seven towns. It had no great temple, no governor, no wonder of the world; it sat in a valley with no natural defences and made things — wool, linen, leather, bronze, and above all dyed cloth. Lydia, the first convert in Europe, was a dealer in purple from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). More inscriptions recording trade guilds have been found here than in any of the other six cities. And this smallest, dullest, most commercial town receives the longest of the seven letters.

Christ introduces himself as the Son of God — the only occurrence of that exact title in Revelation — who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. Both images come from 1:14–15, and both are chosen for this church. Eyes of fire, because Thyatira’s problem is hidden inside a congregation that looks healthy from outside. Feet of bronze, in a town of metalworkers who would know exactly what refined bronze looked like coming out of the furnace, and would know that you do not argue with it.

Then the commendation, and it is the warmest given to any of the seven: I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first. Read that against Ephesus and the contrast is almost surgical. Ephesus had works, toil, endurance and discernment, and had abandoned its first love. Thyatira is credited with love first in the list, and told that its recent works are greater than its early ones. Ephesus was going backwards. Thyatira is growing.

Four qualities are named and they are paired. Love and faith — the inward dispositions. Service and endurance — the outward expressions, service being the word diakonia, practical help to people who need it. The order is not accidental: love produces service, faith produces endurance. This church was doing more for its poor in the fortieth year than in the tenth.

Which sets up the hardest lesson in the chapter, and it should be said before the criticism arrives so that it is not mistaken for a technicality. A congregation can be growing in love, growing in practical care, more useful this decade than last, warm, generous, and well thought of — and be in serious danger. Warmth is not a substitute for discernment any more than discernment was a substitute for warmth at Ephesus. Two churches, forty miles apart, each excelling exactly where the other failed, and each rebuked.

There is a caution in that for anyone who has decided which sort of church is the dangerous sort. Most Christians have a settled instinct here: some are sure the peril is cold orthodoxy, others are sure it is loose tolerance, and each is quietly confident that the failing they can see in others is the serious one. Chapter 2 rebukes both, in adjacent letters, in the same voice, from the same eyes of fire. Whichever of the two you find it easy to condemn is probably not the letter written to you.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel. The name is almost certainly not hers. Christ is naming a type, the way we might call a politician a Judas, and every hearer in Thyatira would have caught it instantly. Jezebel was the Phoenician princess Ahab married, who imported Baal worship into Israel, kept four hundred and fifty prophets at her own table, hunted the prophets of the LORD to death, and arranged a judicial murder to get a man’s vineyard (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4, 19; 21:1–16). She was not a marginal figure. She was the queen, and she operated from inside the institution.

Two things are said about the woman in Thyatira, and only one of them is the problem. She calls herself a prophetess — the claim is self-issued, and no one has tested it, which is precisely what Ephesus did do and was commended for (v. 2). And she is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. That is Balaam’s programme again, verbatim from verse 14, now with a prophetic authority claimed behind it.

It should be said plainly, because the passage has been used this way, that the objection is not to a woman teaching as such. The charge here is a false claim to prophetic authority in the service of a doctrine that was destroying people, and it would be the identical charge against a man — it was, four verses earlier, at Pergamum, where the same teaching is condemned with no reference to anyone’s sex at all. The parallel Christ draws is with Balaam, who was a man. What is being confronted is the teaching and the pretended authority.

The verb aimed at the church is tolerate, and it carries the sense of letting something be, leaving it alone. Nobody in Thyatira is accused of believing what she taught. They are accused of letting her go on teaching it. And the reason is not hard to reconstruct in a guild town: her doctrine solved a real problem. If the sacrificed meat is nothing and the temple evening is a formality, then a dyer can keep his membership and his contracts. She was not offering vice. She was offering relief, with a spiritual justification attached, and it is very difficult to confront somebody who is telling frightened people what they urgently want to be true.

Then verse 21, which is one of the most searching sentences in the chapter: I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality. The delay was not indifference. The years in which the church did nothing and the false teaching flourished were years the Lord was holding open. What looked to the faithful remnant like God ignoring an outrage was God waiting for a woman to turn.

Hold on to that when a wrong goes unpunished for a long time and heaven appears to have no opinion. Peter wrote to churches in these same provinces that the Lord is not slow as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Pet. 3:9). Delay is not always absence. Sometimes the silence a believer finds unbearable is mercy being extended to somebody he has already written off. Sometimes it is being extended to him.

But the verb in the second half is present and continuous: she refuses. This is not a woman who has not yet made up her mind. She has been given room, she knows what it is for, and she is going on saying no. Mercy that is refused for long enough does not become permanent tolerance. It runs out, and the next verse is what that looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the hardest two verses in the seven letters, and softening them would be dishonest. But reading them carefully takes most of the horror out of them, because almost every clause contains a distinction that a quick reading loses.

Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed. The Greek is a deliberate irony that the English cannot fully carry: the word for the bed is the same word used for the couch on which the guild banquets were eaten and the sin committed. The bed she chose becomes the bed she cannot leave. And the verb is throw, the same verb used of the devil throwing believers into prison at Smyrna in verse 10. Different hand, different purpose, and the reader is meant to feel the symmetry.

And those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works. There it is — the door, standing open in the middle of the sentence of judgment. The threat is conditional for everyone except the woman who has already spent her allotted time refusing. Even at this point, with the verdict being pronounced, anyone who will turn may turn. Judgment in Scripture almost always arrives with that clause attached, and it is not decoration.

Then: and I will strike her children dead. This is the sentence that makes readers flinch, and it should not be waved away. Two things need saying. First, her children in the Old Testament idiom that Christ is using here means her spiritual offspring — those who have taken her teaching so far into themselves that they now reproduce it. Verse 22 has just distinguished two groups: those who commit adultery with her, who may still repent, and the children, who are hers. The wording marks a difference between people who have been drawn in and people who have become her. Second, this is what Scripture consistently says the end of persistent, chosen rebellion is, and it says it plainly rather than leaving the reader to discover it later. Christ is not more severe here than the New Testament is elsewhere; he is simply less indirect.

And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart. The Greek is literally kidneys and hearts, and it is a straight quotation of the Old Testament’s standard claim about God alone: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind (Jer. 17:10; cf. Ps. 7:9). Hebrew placed the deepest, most hidden affections in the kidneys, the organs furthest inside a body. The claim is not that Christ is well informed. It is that he sees the part of a person that the person himself cannot get at — and this is said in a letter to a church that could not tell a prophetess from a fraud.

And I will give to each of you according to your works. A reader who has grasped that salvation is by grace through faith alone will stop at that sentence, and the question deserves a straight answer rather than a hurried one. Scripture says both things without embarrassment: no one is justified by works of the law (Gal. 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done (Rom. 2:6; 2 Cor. 5:10). They are not in tension once the question each is answering is clear. Nobody is admitted on the strength of his works; the works are the evidence of whose he is, and they are the measure of what is given afterwards. A tree is not made alive by its fruit and is identified by nothing else.

The pronoun shifts at the end, and it changes who is being addressed. Verses 20 to 23 have been about her and them. The last clause turns and says each of you. The letter has been discussing a faction, and it ends the discussion by putting the whole congregation, one by one, in front of the eyes of fire.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone changes completely. But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching… — and for the remainder of the letter Christ is speaking to the faithful. They exist. They have not been swept up. In a church whose besetting fault was tolerance, there were people who had quietly refused, and Christ addresses them directly and separately, which is itself a kindness. He knows exactly who in that congregation had said no.

Who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan. The phrasing — what some call — suggests Christ is repeating the faction’s own slogan back at them with one word changed. They were very likely advertising the deep things of God: a mature, advanced spirituality for people who had got beyond scruples, an inner freedom that let a believer walk through the guild feast untouched because he understood what the ordinary members did not. Every generation produces some version of that offer, and it always flatters. Christ substitutes one noun and the whole thing collapses.

Then a sentence that ought to be read slowly by anyone who is tired: to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. He does not give the faithful remnant a programme. He does not tell them to launch a campaign, purge the membership, or fix the church. He has already said what he will do about Jezebel and he will do it himself. To the people who have been holding on in a compromised congregation, the risen Christ says: nothing further is required of you.

That is an extraordinary pastoral moment, and it is aimed at a recognisable kind of exhaustion. There are believers in difficult churches who carry the whole thing on their shoulders, who feel personally answerable for every error nobody else is confronting, and who are being slowly ground down by a responsibility they were never actually given. The letter puts the weight where it belongs. He is the one with the eyes of fire; he is the one who searches minds and hearts; the judgment of Jezebel is his business and he has stated his timetable. The remnant is asked for one thing.

Only hold fast what you have until I come. That is the one thing. Not advance, not achieve, not reform — hold. The verb is the same one used of Pergamum holding fast his name in verse 13, and it is a word for gripping something in a wind. What they already have is enough; the whole task is not to let go of it.

And the time limit is stated: until I come. Holding on is not asked of anyone indefinitely, and this is the first mention of his coming in the seven letters. There is a terminus. A believer is not being asked to grip in the dark for ever with no prospect of relief; he is being asked to grip until a specific person arrives, and that person has set out.

Anyone worn down in a hard congregation, or in a hard household, or in a hard stretch of years, can take the instruction exactly as it stands. The requirement is not to fix it. The requirement is to still be holding on when he gets there.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise to Thyatira is the longest of the seven and the strangest, and it is given to the smallest church in the least important town on the road. To him I will give authority over the nations.

The wording of verses 26 and 27 is a direct quotation of Psalm 2, the great coronation psalm in which the nations rage and plot and God installs his King on Zion and says to him: Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage… you shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel (Ps. 2:8–9). That psalm is about the Messiah. Christ quotes it, and then does something startling with it — he hands it over. The authority the Father gave him, he gives to the ones who conquer. He says so explicitly at the end of verse 27: even as I myself have received authority from my Father.

Note where the image comes from and who is hearing it. Thyatira was a town of makers, and its potters knew that unfired clay can be reshaped but a fired pot can only be broken. And the people receiving this promise are the ones who have just been told that their whole assignment is to hold on. They have no authority over anything. Some of them have lost their guild membership and cannot get work in a town where everything is guild work. To these people, Christ promises the authority of Psalm 2.

There is a condition, and it is repeated twice for emphasis: the one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end. Conquering, in this book, is not a single dramatic act; it is defined by duration. And my works stands over against Jezebel’s works in verse 22. The two sets of works are the two ways of getting through life in a guild town, and the letter has now named both.

And I will give him the morning star. Every other promise in the seven letters is a thing — a tree, a crown, a stone, a name, a pillar, a throne. This one is a person, and the book says so in its final chapter: I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (22:16). Behind it stands Balaam’s own prophecy, which is a fine irony in a letter about Balaam’s teaching: a star shall come out of Jacob (Num. 24:17). The morning star is the one that rises last, when the sky is at its darkest, and it does not announce more night. It means the sun is coming.

So the last word to Thyatira is not authority after all. Authority is promised, and then something better is added on top of it, and the something better is himself. To a congregation being urged to hold on until he comes, the final promise is that when he comes he will give them himself. Every other reward in these letters is something from his hand. This one is the hand.

He is the bright morning star. He rose while it was still dark, and he has not set since, and every believer who has ever held on in a difficult church, in an unremarkable town, doing work nobody recorded, was looking at the same light. The night in Thyatira did not last. The star did.

Then, for the fourth time, the refrain: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. In the first three letters it came before the promise; from Thyatira onwards it comes after. The change is small and probably deliberate. In the last four letters the promise is the last thing in the reader’s ear, and the call to hear stands over the whole of it. Whoever has an ear — and that is the point of the plural churches — this was written to be overheard.
