Isaiah heard this song seven hundred years earlier, and heard it in the year King Uzziah died — that is, in the year the political certainty of his lifetime came to an end (Isa. 6:1–3). It is the same three words, and the fact that they have not changed in seven centuries, or in the centuries since, is part of the point. Empires have come and gone in the interval. The song has not been revised.

Hebrew has no -er and -est; to intensify a word you repeat it. Twice means emphasis. Three times is the superlative, and there is only one attribute of God that Scripture ever trebles. Nobody sings loving, loving, loving or mighty, mighty, mighty. God is love and God is almighty and both are said plainly, but the word said three times before the throne, day and night, without ceasing, is holy.

Holy in Hebrew means separate, cut off, other. It is not first a moral word but a word about distance — God is not a larger version of us, not the best example of anything on our scale. He is in a category with one member. The moral meaning follows from that: because he is wholly other, he is wholly pure. R. C. Sproul spent a ministry on this one word, and rightly: get it wrong and every other doctrine sags, because sin stops being an outrage and grace stops being a miracle.

Then the threefold name again — and this time the order has changed. At 1:4 and 1:8 it was who is and who was and who is to come, beginning with the present. Here it is who was and is and is to come, beginning with the past. From the throne room, where eternity is the vantage point rather than a struggling church in Asia, the sequence runs in ordinary order. And the middle term is the one being sung over: he is.

Now the question a thoughtful reader will actually be carrying, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a nervous one. If God requires unceasing praise, is he vain? Would a man who demanded this of his household be tolerable?

Two things answer it. First, praise is not something God lacks and needs topping up. He was not lonely or unadmired before there was a universe; Father, Son and Spirit have delighted in one another from eternity, and nothing was made to fill a gap. Second, and more to the point, praise is what happens when anything true is seen clearly. Nobody watching a sunrise over water has to be commanded to say something; the praise is not a tax levied on the viewer but the completion of the seeing. To ask people who are looking at God to stop praising him would be to ask them to look at him and not notice. What is happening in this room is not flattery. It is accuracy.

Which also settles the fear that heaven might be tedious — a worry more believers carry than admit. Boredom is what happens when a thing is exhausted, when you have seen all there is and the eye has nowhere further to go. The creatures nearest the throne are covered in eyes, have been looking without pause since before the world was made, and have not yet come to the end of the first word. Holy. Holy. Holy. It is not that they must keep saying it. It is that they cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a movement, and it is the most eloquent gesture in the book. Whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him … and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne.

The word whenever makes it a pattern rather than a single event. Every time the creatures begin, the elders go down. And two things happen: they fall, and they throw. Falling is what everyone does in the presence of God — Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, John himself in chapter 1. Throwing the crown is different. That is a decision about what to do with a reward.

These crowns were given. Nobody in that room manufactured one. They are the victor’s wreaths promised to the conquerors of Smyrna and Philadelphia, handed over by Christ himself — and the elders will not keep them on in front of the throne. In the Roman world a client king laid his crown at the emperor’s feet to acknowledge where his authority came from; Tacitus describes Tiridates of Armenia doing exactly that before Nero. Heaven does the same thing with far better cause.

There is a very practical question in that gesture for anybody who has ever done anything well. What are you holding that was given to you and is being worn as though it were earned? A capacity, a competence, an upbringing, a marriage, a body that still works, thirty years of faithful service in a church. None of it was self-generated. The elders’ instinct is the only sane one, and it can be practised now: what is worn in this life is thrown down in the next, and the sooner a person starts throwing, the less it will cost him at the end.

Then the words themselves: Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power.

A first-century hearer would have flinched at that phrase. Dominus et Deus noster — our Lord and God — was precisely the title Domitian required in petitions addressed to him, and Suetonius records that he had it used as a matter of course. The congregations hearing this letter were under pressure to say those words to a man in Rome. John gives them the same words to say, and a different throne.

And the ground of the worthiness is stated: for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created. Creation is the reason. Not because you are strong and not because you will win, but because everything that exists does so at his pleasure and would stop existing if he stopped willing it. Take the order seriously: by your will they existed comes before and were created. The intention preceded the act. Nothing in the universe is an accident or an afterthought, including the small congregation in Thyatira and the man reading this sentence.

That is where chapter 4 stops, and it is deliberately incomplete. The song here is about creation, and creation alone is not enough to save anybody; the world he made is the world in rebellion against him. In the next chapter a scroll will appear that nobody in heaven or earth is able to open, and John will weep. The answer to that will be a new song, and the new song will not be about creation.

But before the scroll, before the seals, before the horsemen and the martyrs and the long war — there is a throne, and it is occupied, and the one seated on it is holy, holy, holy. He was before anything was. He is, while everything shakes. He is coming, and the storm going out from his throne is fenced by a rainbow. Worthy is he to receive glory and honour and power, for he made all things, and they exist because he wanted them to.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.”<sup>2</sup>At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.<sup>3</sup>And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.<sup>4</sup>Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.<sup>5</sup>From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,<sup>6</sup>and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind:<sup>7</sup>the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.<sup>8</sup>And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”<sup>9</sup>And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,<sup>10</sup>the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying,<sup>11</sup>“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is perhaps the most emotionally dramatic chapter in the entire Bible. It begins with a crisis — a sealed scroll that no one can open — passes through grief — John weeps uncontrollably — and arrives at an explosion of worship that fills all of heaven and earth. The transition from weeping to worship is accomplished by a single announcement: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and he can open the scroll. And when John looks for the conquering Lion, he sees — a Lamb, standing as though slaughtered.

The scroll sealed with seven seals is the interpretive key to the chapter. A scroll sealed with seven seals in the ancient world was typically a legal document of great importance: a will, a deed of purchase, or a covenant document. Most scholars understand it as the scroll of history — God’s redemptive plan for the world, the title deed to creation, the covenant document of the new age. Seven seals indicates absolute sealing: only the one who is truly worthy can break them and open what they guard. The entire drama of Revelation — the seals, the trumpets, the bowls — is the Lamb opening this scroll.

The Lion who is the Lamb — the great reversal at the heart of chapter 5 — is the christological center of Revelation and, in a sense, of the entire New Testament. John is told to look for a conquering Lion. He looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb. The conquest was accomplished through the cross. The power that governs history is the power of self-giving love. The one who has the authority to open the seals of history is the one who was willing to be the sacrifice that history required. This is the theological answer to every form of worldly power: the crucified one reigns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 put a scroll in the right hand of the one on the throne, written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Writing on both sides meant the contents were complete; seven seals was the number required for a Roman will, openable only by the rightful heir. A mighty angel heralds one question across creation — not who is strong enough but who is worthy?

Verses 3–4 answer it: nobody, in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Not the elders, not the living creatures, not Abraham or Moses or David. And John breaks down — I began to weep loudly — the only tears anyone sheds in the throne room of this book, and they are not rebuked. An unopened scroll means a world with no resolution: the martyrs never answered, Rome for ever, history running down like a clock nobody winds.

Verse 5 stops the weeping with an announcement rather than an argument: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Gen. 49:9–10; Isa. 11:1–10). The verb is the past tense of the word that ends every one of the seven letters. Whatever the churches are being asked to do, he has already done.

Verses 6–7 are the hinge of the book. John is told a Lion and sees a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain — arnion, the diminutive, a lambkin, which becomes John’s main name for Christ twenty-eight times over. The participle is perfect: a past slaughter whose marks are still present. Seven horns are complete power, seven eyes complete knowledge (Zech. 4:10). Then, without ceremony, he went and took the scroll.

Verses 8–10: the creatures and elders fall before the Lamb — worship no creature in this book may receive (19:10; 22:8–9) — holding harps and golden bowls of incense which are the prayers of the saints (cf. Ps. 141:2). The new song grounds his worthiness in his death: you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, made them a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.

Verses 11–12 widen the circle to myriads of myriads of angels (cf. Dan. 7:10) with a sevenfold ascription: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing. Verses 13–14 widen it to every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, addressing one doxology to the throne and the Lamb together; the living creatures say Amen, and the elders fall down and worship in silence.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion and the Lamb: the Key to the Whole Book

John hears a Lion and sees a Lamb, and that single substitution governs everything after it. Revelation will go on speaking of conquest, warfare, thrones and armies for seventeen chapters, and this verse has defined what those words mean when Christ is their subject. He conquers by dying. A reader who takes the military vocabulary at face value and forgets 5:6 will misread every battle in the book — and, worse, will look for the wrong kind of victory in his own life.

The Wounds Are Permanent

Esphagmenon is a perfect participle from a verb used for cutting a sacrificial animal’s throat: a past act whose result stands. The Lamb is standing, which is resurrection, and is at the same time visibly a slaughtered animal. When Thomas needed proof the risen Christ produced not a restored body but a scarred one (John 20:27). Heaven is not a place where the crucifixion has been tidied away; the marks are the credential the whole company falls down before.

Worship the Lamb Receives

In this book an angel twice refuses worship outright and tells John to give it to God (19:10; 22:8–9). Here the Lamb receives the identical worship, in the presence of the Father, and by v. 13 a single doxology with a single verb is addressed to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. Revelation never argues the deity of Christ. It simply shows what heaven does.

A Song the Angels Cannot Fully Sing

The new song of v. 9 belongs to those ransomed by his blood. The myriads of angels in v. 12 sing about a redemption they have watched and not received — Peter says they long to look into these things (1 Pet. 1:12). The forgiven sinner in the back row of an ordinary congregation has a line in this song that Gabriel cannot sing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation in Asia hears verse 4 read aloud and knows exactly what the man is crying about. They have buried people. They have watched a magistrate take a bribe. They have prayed for years and read no answer in the newspaper. The unopened scroll is their own experience of the world, stated by somebody in heaven who found it unbearable too.

Now: John’s grief is not treated as a failure of faith, and the permission that gives a reader matters. He is standing in front of the throne he saw in chapter 4 and he still weeps, because a throne on its own does not answer the question of whether history is going anywhere. Scripture records the tears without embarrassment and without rebuke, and then answers them — not with an argument that things are not so bad, but with a person walking into the room. That is the shape of every real Christian comfort.

And take verse 8 as concretely as it is meant. Every desperate prayer said the night before a hearing; every prayer of a slave that nobody in the household knew about; every muttered, distracted, badly-worded prayer said at a kitchen table before work — the ones that felt like they hit the ceiling and slid down the wall. None of them evaporated. They were collected. They are in golden bowls in the throne room, held by the highest beings in creation, at the moment the scroll is opened. And at 8:3–5 those same prayers are thrown back onto the earth as thunder, lightning and an earthquake. Nothing prayed in faith is wasted, and some of it turns out to have been explosive.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The camera has not moved. John is still in the throne room of chapter 4, still looking at the one seated on the throne — and now he notices something in his hand.

Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Two details, and both are unusual. Ancient scrolls were normally written on one side only, because the papyrus fibres ran the wrong way on the reverse and the pen caught. A document written on both sides — an opisthograph — meant one thing: the contents were complete. There was no room for anything further. Nothing can be added to this and nothing left out.

And it is sealed seven times. Under Roman law a will was sealed with seven seals, one for each of the seven witnesses required, and it could be opened only by the rightful heir and only in the presence of those witnesses. A sealed document was also a standard prophetic image: Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end (Dan. 12:4, 9), and Ezekiel was handed a scroll written on the front and the back with words of lamentation and mourning and woe (Ezek. 2:9–10). John’s vision is built out of both.

What exactly is in the scroll is not stated, and readers have answered it in several ways. Some take it as the title deed to creation, the world’s ownership document waiting for the heir to claim it. Some take it as God’s decreed purpose for history, the whole future in a sealed envelope. Some take it as the covenant will, the inheritance of the saints. The text itself only shows what happens when it is opened, and what happens is the sweep of history from the cross to the end. The safest thing to say is the thing that matters most: this is God’s purpose for the world, it is complete, it is written, and at this moment it is shut.

That is the situation the chapter begins in, and it should be felt before it is explained. The plan of God for the world exists. It is finished, in writing, in his hand. And it is not happening, because nobody has opened it.

Then the challenge goes out: And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?” The verb for proclaiming is the herald’s word, and the voice is loud enough to reach, as the next verse shows, heaven and earth and under the earth. This is a summons to the entire creation, and it asks one question.

Notice which question. Not who is strong enough, and not who is clever enough. Who is worthy? The issue is not capability but standing. Anyone can break a seal; a seal is wax. What the moment requires is somebody with the right to break it — and the whole tension of the chapter, and arguably of the book, is that the future of the world waits not on power but on the moral qualification of a person.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it. The three-tier phrase is the ancient way of saying everywhere — the living, the dead, and the powers above. It is a complete search of the universe, and it returns nothing.

Consider who was in the room while that search was conducted. Twenty-four elders. Four living creatures who have never taken their eyes off God. Presently, myriads of myriads of angels. Not one of them was worthy. And on earth, the whole roll of human greatness — every philosopher, reformer, general and king — and not one. And under the earth, the dead, including every saint who had died in faith. Abraham was not worthy. Moses was not worthy. David, who wrote half the songs sung in that room, was not worthy.

And I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.

These are the only tears in heaven. Nowhere else in this book does anyone in the throne room weep, and two chapters from the end God himself will wipe every tear from every eye (21:4). The Greek is emphatic — John did not become quietly emotional; he broke down and sobbed, and the tense suggests he kept on doing it until somebody stopped him.

Why so extreme a reaction to an unopened document? Because John has grasped what the closed scroll means. If nobody opens it, the plan stays shut. The martyrs under the altar are never answered. Rome goes on for ever. The seven churches keep meeting in borrowed rooms until they die out one by one, and nothing in the sealed purposes of God ever comes to anything. An unopened scroll is a world with no resolution — injustice with no verdict, suffering with no meaning, and history simply running down like a clock nobody winds.

That grief is not exotic, and any honest believer has felt a version of it. It is what settles on a person reading the news for the fortieth year and noticing that the same things keep happening. It is what a woman feels standing in a cemetery in a country where nobody was ever tried for what was done. It is the specific despair of suspecting that the world is not going anywhere — that there is no scroll, or that if there is one, it will never be opened.

Note what John does not do. He does not tell himself that it will probably work out. He does not console himself with the throne he has just seen, though the throne is still there in front of him. He weeps, in heaven, in the presence of God, and Scripture records it without embarrassment and without rebuking him. There is no verse in this book telling the reader that grief over a world out of joint is a failure of faith.

And the weeping is answered, but not by an argument. Nobody in the following verse tells John he was overreacting.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

Two titles, and both come out of the Old Testament’s deepest promises about a coming king. The Lion of the tribe of Judah goes back to the blessing of Jacob on his deathbed: Judah is a lion’s cub… the scepter shall not depart from Judah… until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Gen. 49:9–10). The Root of David comes from Isaiah’s promise of a shoot from the stump of Jesse, on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest, who would judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isa. 11:1–4, 10). Between them these two titles carry the whole hope of Israel: the royal lion, and the living root of a dynasty that had been cut down to a stump.

Has conquered. The verb is enikēsen — the same word, in the past tense, that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the one who conquers. Whatever the churches of Asia are being asked to do, he has already done it, and the doing is finished. That is why the whole address is in the aorist: not he is conquering, not he will conquer, but he conquered, and the matter is closed.

And observe the logic of the sentence, because it is easy to slide past. He can open the scroll because he has conquered. The right to unroll the purposes of God was not his by rank. It was won. Somewhere in history a battle was fought, and the outcome of it is the reason anything at all is about to happen in this book.

Here the reader is at the exact hinge of Revelation, and everything depends on reading the next two verses in the right order. What John is told is: a Lion. What John then sees is something else entirely. Hold the Lion in mind for one more sentence, because the elder has just announced, in the most muscular language the Old Testament has, that the conqueror has arrived and the scroll is as good as open.

And one more thing in the elder’s first two words. Weep no more. Not you were wrong to weep. Not compose yourself. The tears are not criticised, they are ended — and they are ended by an announcement about a person, not by advice. That is the shape of every real Christian comfort. Nobody is talked out of grief by being told that things are not so bad. Grief stops when somebody walks into the room.

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain.

He was told a Lion. He sees a Lamb. That single substitution is the interpretive key to the whole book, and everything that follows must be read through it. Revelation will go on speaking the language of conquest, warfare, thrones and armies for seventeen more chapters, and this verse has just defined what every one of those words means. The Lion conquers as a Lamb. The victory the elder announced was won by dying.

The word John uses is arnion, and it matters. It is not the dignified sacrificial term amnos used of Christ elsewhere (John 1:29; Acts 8:32); arnion is the diminutive — a little lamb, a lambkin. John uses it twenty-eight times in this book and it becomes his main name for Christ. In the most violent, cosmic, thunderous book in the Bible, the name of the conqueror is the smallest and most defenceless word available.

Standing, as though it had been slain. Two impossible things in one clause. The Greek behind slain is esphagmenon, from a verb used for cutting a sacrificial animal’s throat — butchered, not merely killed — and it is a perfect participle, which in Greek means a past action whose result is still in force. The wounds are not a memory. They are present tense. This Lamb is standing, which is resurrection and life, and is at the same time visibly, permanently, a slaughtered animal.

Stay with that, because it is the centre of the Christian faith rendered as a picture. The one thing that will never be erased from the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. When Thomas needed proof, the risen Christ did not produce a restored body but a scarred one (John 20:27). Heaven’s throne room is not a place where the crucifixion has been tidied away and forgotten. It is a place where the marks are the credential, and the whole company falls down in front of them.

With seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. A horn in the Old Testament is strength — seven of them is complete power. Seven eyes, identified as the sevenfold Spirit, is complete knowledge; the phrase is quarried from Zechariah, where the seven eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth (Zech. 4:10). So the little Lamb is omnipotent and omniscient, and the picture is deliberately impossible to draw. It is not meant to be sketched. It is meant to be believed.

And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne. The sentence is flat, almost domestic, and the room has been holding its breath for six verses. Nobody stops him. There is no challenge, no ceremony, no coronation first. He walks up and takes it, and the reaching out of that hand is the moment the future of the world is unlocked.

There is no one else in the universe who could have done it. Heaven was searched, and earth, and the place of the dead, and every candidate failed on the same question — not strength, but worth. And then a Lamb with its throat cut walks out from among the elders and takes the scroll out of the hand of God, and every creature in the room goes down on its face. He conquered. He was slaughtered, and he is standing, and the wounds are still open, and history has begun to move again.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response to the taking of the scroll is immediate and total. The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. The same posture given to the one on the throne in chapter 4 is given here to the Lamb, without a word of explanation and without anyone objecting — and in this book angels twice refuse worship outright (19:10; 22:8–9). No creature may receive it. The Lamb receives it in the presence of God the Father, and the room approves.

They are holding two things. Each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. The harp is for the song about to be sung. The bowls need dwelling on.

Incense rose twice a day in the temple, on the golden altar in front of the veil, and the picture behind it is stated in the Psalms: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Ps. 141:2). What John sees is that image made literal. The prayers of ordinary Christians are in golden bowls in the throne room of the universe, held by the highest beings in creation, at the moment the scroll is opened.

Take that as concretely as it is meant. Every desperate prayer prayed by a believer in Smyrna the night before a hearing. Every prayer of a slave in Laodicea that nobody else in the household knew about. Every muttered, distracted, badly-worded prayer said by anyone reading this at the kitchen table before work — the ones that felt like they hit the ceiling and slid down the wall. None of them evaporated. They were collected. They are in golden bowls, and the bowls are full, and an elder is holding them in front of the throne.

And there is more in the picture. At 8:3–5 those same prayers, mixed with incense, are thrown back onto the earth and become thunder and lightning and an earthquake. Prayers that seemed to accomplish nothing come down again as the opening act of God’s judgment on the world that ignored them. Nothing prayed in faith is wasted, and some of it turns out to have been explosive.

And they sang a new song. The Old Testament calls for a new song whenever God does something unprecedented (Ps. 96:1; 98:1; Isa. 42:10). Chapter 4 ended with a song about creation. This one has a different subject: Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God. There is the answer to the herald’s question in verse 2, and the ground of the worthiness is not his power. It is his death.

Ransomed is the slave-market word — to buy a person out of ownership by paying the price. The price is named in the same clause: by your blood. And the scope is named four ways over, from every tribe and language and people and nation, a fourfold phrase John will use seven times in this book, each time in a slightly different order, as if to stop anyone turning it into a fixed list. Nobody is outside the reach of it. And nobody is ransomed as a nation or a category — the purchase is of people, one at a time, out of every group there is.

And you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth. The same phrase as 1:6, and both are lifted from Sinai (Ex. 19:6). Two small things in it should not be missed. The first is the tense: you have made — already done, not pending. The second is the location: they shall reign on the earth. Whatever a reader concludes about the timing of that reign — and the question is taken up where the text raises it, at chapter 20 — the destination of the redeemed in this book is not an escape from the material world into a spiritual one. It is this earth, renewed, with the ransomed reigning on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The circle widens. Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands.

A myriad is ten thousand, the largest number Greek had a single word for. Myriads of myriads is therefore not a count; it is the language running out. Daniel used exactly the same expression of the throne of the Ancient of Days — a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him (Dan. 7:10) — and John has been quarrying Daniel 7 since chapter 1. The point is not arithmetic. It is that the ring of worshippers extends beyond the range of counting, and the singing has been going on out there the whole time John was weeping.

Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing! Seven attributes, and in this book seven means the complete set. Everything there is to give is given, and it is given to a slaughtered lamb.

Set the two songs side by side, because the difference between them is the gospel. In chapter 4 the elders sang Worthy are you, our Lord and God, and the ground was creation: you made all things. Here the angels sing Worthy is the Lamb, and the ground is the cross: you were slain. Two songs, one throne, and the second could not have been sung by anyone before Calvary.

And there is something the angels are doing here that they cannot do in the fullest sense. Verse 9’s song is sung by those ransomed by his blood; the angels in verse 12 sing about a redemption they have watched but not received. Peter says they long to look into these things (1 Pet. 1:12). Whatever the honour of an unfallen angel, it does not include being bought. The forgiven sinner in the back row of an ordinary congregation has a line in this song that Gabriel cannot sing.

Note also the order of the seven. Power comes first and blessing last, and in between are wealth, wisdom, might, honour and glory — every currency the Roman world traded in, and every one of them claimed by or for the emperor. A congregation that had been shut out of the guilds, fined, boycotted and in some places killed is being told where all seven actually belong.

Worthy is the Lamb. Not worthy to be pitied, not worthy to be remembered, but worthy to receive everything there is — and the reason given by the whole of heaven is not that he is strong, though he holds seven horns, and not that he sees everything, though he has seven eyes. The reason is that he was slaughtered. Ten thousand times ten thousand voices, and the argument they make is a wound.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The circle widens one last time, and this time it takes in everything that exists. And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them.

Those are the same three regions searched in verse 3, with the sea added. There, the search found nobody worthy; here, the whole of it is singing. The chapter has come full circle. What began with a silence that made a man weep ends with every created thing — the living, the dead, the powers above, and whatever is in the deep — making one sound.

To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever! One doxology, two recipients, no distinction between them. Chapter 4 worshipped the one on the throne. Chapter 5 worshipped the Lamb. Now the two are addressed together in a single sentence with a single verb, and nobody in the room regards that as a problem. The doctrine of the Trinity is not argued anywhere in Revelation. It is simply what worship in heaven looks like.

And four attributes here rather than seven, but the fourth of them is new to the chapter: blessing, which is not something a creature can add to God. To bless God is to speak well of him, to say back to him what he is. That is the last thing all creation does in this vision, and it is the only thing it can do that God has not already got.

And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” The beings nearest the throne, who have been singing holy, holy, holy without pause since before the world was made, do not add anything. They agree. And the elders fell down and worshiped — the last movement in the chapter is a silence, twenty-four figures on their faces with their crowns already on the floor, and John does not record a single further word.

Look back at where this chapter started. A sealed scroll, a challenge nobody could answer, and a man weeping loudly in the middle of heaven because it looked as though the world would never be put right. Fourteen verses later the same man is listening to every creature in existence say the same thing at once. Nothing changed in between except that a Lamb walked forward and took a scroll.

The seven seals are about to be broken, and the four horsemen are behind the first four of them. Conquest, war, famine and death are coming, and after them the souls under the altar and the sky rolling up like a scroll. Every one of those seals is opened by the hand that was pierced. Whatever rides out of this scroll rides at the word of the Lamb who was slain, and it goes no further than he permits.

Worthy is the Lamb. He was searched for through heaven and earth and the grave and not found, because he was not looking like a lion; he was standing among the elders with his throat cut and his hands open. He took the scroll. He is opening it still. And when the last seal is broken and the last trumpet has sounded and the last enemy is gone, the song that all creation is singing here will not have changed a word.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals.<sup>2</sup>And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”<sup>3</sup>And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it,<sup>4</sup>and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.<sup>5</sup>And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”<sup>6</sup>And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.<sup>7</sup>And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.<sup>8</sup>And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And they sang a new song, saying, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation,<sup>10</sup>and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”<sup>11</sup>Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,<sup>12</sup>saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”<sup>13</sup>And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!”<sup>14</sup>And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
The Lamb begins to open the seven seals, and with each seal a new dimension of history is revealed. The first four seals release the famous Four Horsemen — one of the most powerful images in Western literature. The fifth seal lifts the veil on the souls of the martyrs beneath the heavenly altar and their agonizing cry: “How long, O Lord?” The sixth seal unleashes cosmic convulsion on a terrified earth. The seventh seal — which will bring complete silence in heaven — is withheld until chapter 8.

Interpretive flag — Sequential or Recapitulatory? This is the second major structural decision point of Revelation. The sequential reading (predominant in dispensational premillennialism) understands the seals, trumpets, and bowls as three successive series of events: the seals run their course, then the trumpets begin, then the bowls pour out — covering the seven-year tribulation in ascending severity. The recapitulatory reading (predominant in amillennial/idealist interpretation) understands the three series as parallel sweeps, each covering the same period (the church age and/or the final tribulation) from different vantage points and with increasing intensity. Several features of the text favor recapitulation: (1) the sixth seal already appears to describe the final judgment (vv. 12–17), yet the narrative continues; (2) the sixth trumpet and sixth bowl also appear to describe the same climactic events; (3) the interludes (chapters 7, 10–11) break the sequential pattern; (4) the phrase “the great day of their wrath has come” (v. 17) sounds like a finale, yet much remains. This commentary reads the seals as the first of three parallel sweeps, while noting the sequential reading respectfully.

The Four Horsemen are among the most theologically misread images in Revelation. They are not four distinct events in a future tribulation timeline. They are the recurring instruments of divine governance that have marked history since the fall: war, internecine conflict, famine, and death. They describe the ongoing reality of a fallen world under the Lord’s providential judgment — not unprecedented novelties but the intensified concentration of what the church has always known. The question the martyrs ask — “How long?” — is the question the church has been asking since Abel’s blood first cried from the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature calls Come! with a voice like thunder, and a white horse rides out whose rider has a bow and a crown that was given to him. Whether that rider is Christ, the gospel’s advance, or conquest itself is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse. Verses 3–4: a bright red horse, whose rider is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people should slay one another — mutual killing, the neighbour with the knife — and is given a great sword.

Verses 5–6: a black horse, its rider holding scales, and a voice from the midst of the living creatures quoting the price list. A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was one man’s daily ration. A labourer in full work can feed himself and nobody else. Do not harm the oil and wine sets a limit on the famine and also describes its injustice: bread is rationed while the luxury trade goes on undisturbed.

Verses 7–8: a pale horse — chlōros, the green of a corpse — and the only rider who is named. Death rides, and Hades follows to collect. They are given authority over a fourth of the earth, with the four instruments of Ezekiel 14:21. The fraction matters: the trumpets will touch a third, and only at the end does anything become total.

Verses 9–11 break the pattern: no horse, no rider. Under the altar, where the blood of every sacrifice was poured out (Lev. 4:7), are the souls of those slain — esphagmenōn, the word used of the Lamb at 5:6 and of no one else in the book. They cry how long? like a third of the psalter. Verse 11 answers with a white robe each, permission to rest, and a reason for the delay that is very hard: until the number of their brothers who are to die in the same way is complete.

Verses 12–14: the sixth seal removes every fixed point in the universe — earthquake, sun black as sackcloth (goat hair, so the comparison is exact), moon like blood (Joel 2:31), stars falling like the winter figs a gale brings down, the sky rolled up (Isa. 34:4), every mountain and island moved. Verses 15–17: seven classes of people, from kings down to slaves, hide in caves and beg the mountains to fall on them — choosing burial over being looked at — and the chapter ends on an unanswered question: who can stand?
verseByVerse.theology:
Recapitulation or Sequence? Where Godly Readers Differ

The seals are the first of three sevens, and how a reader relates them decides the shape of the book. On the recapitulation reading (Augustine, Hendriksen, Beale, the amillennial tradition) the seals, trumpets and bowls are three parallel passes over the same stretch of history, each running from the cross to the last day; what favours it is that all three series arrive at the end (6:14; 11:15; 16:17), and three arrivals are hard to fit on one line. On the sequential reading (the futurist and dispensational tradition, worked out by Walvoord and MacArthur) they follow one another within a defined future tribulation; what favours it is the plain progression — the seventh seal opens onto the trumpets (8:1–2), the fractions escalate from a fourth to a third to everything, and the text never says it is going back.

A third view holds that they overlap and advance at once, spiralling rather than repeating. This commentary reads them as recapitulating and flags the alternative where it matters.

Four Passive Verbs

A crown was given; the rider was permitted; he was given a great sword; they were given authority over a fourth. Nothing in this chapter takes itself, and every seal is broken by the Lamb. Scripture holds two things together here and releases neither: God is never the author of evil, and no man with a sword can plead that heaven made him use it.

And nothing happens outside God’s governance. Joseph put both in one sentence: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20).

The Wrath of the Lamb

The phrase in v. 16 should not fit. Lambs have no wrath, and that is the point — it is the exact counterpart of 5:5–6, where John was told a Lion and shown a Lamb. This is not a mild Christ who has finally lost patience; it is the same Lamb with the same wounds, and the wrath is the other face of the love that bore them. Nothing is more terrible than mercy refused for long enough.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The congregations first hearing this had met the red horse and the pale one personally. They were not given an explanation of why their friends had died. They were given the identity of the hand on the seal, a fraction rather than a totality, and a company under the altar who were asking the same question they were.

Now: Verse 10 lifts a burden many believers carry needlessly. Anyone genuinely wronged — assaulted, defrauded, lied about, bereaved by somebody never charged — often carries two things: the injury, and guilt at still minding about it. The holiest company in Scripture, in the immediate presence of God, are asking out loud how long justice is going to take, and nobody tells them to stop. Their prayer is not for permission to act; vengeance is handed over to the only one entitled to it (Rom. 12:19), which is what that command is actually for. And it does not compete with praying for one’s persecutors: the one who repents is forgiven, the one who does not is judged, and asking for both is the gospel with nothing left out.

Verse 11 is harder and should not be softened. The reason for the delay is that more are still to die. But two things stand beside it. God has a number — a roll, not a casualty estimate; nobody in it is an accident and nobody outside it is taken by mistake. And every year judgment is postponed is a year in which an enemy of God can be brought in. The man who wrote most of the New Testament’s letters about grace was holding the coats at the first martyrdom (Acts 7:58; 8:1). The patience the martyrs are asked to accept is the patience that produced Paul.

And the question the chapter ends on — who can stand? — is a real one, answered in the next chapter by a multitude nobody can number, standing. The difference between the seven classes behind the rocks and the multitude before the throne is not courage or achievement. It is 7:14: they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. The wrath they are spared is the Lamb’s, and so is the blood that spares them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scroll is opened, and history begins to move. Before the first horse rides, three things about the mechanics of this chapter need saying, because they govern how everything after it is read.

First, who is doing it. Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals. Not an angel, not fate, not an enemy. Every horror in this chapter is released by the hand that was pierced, and the reader who has just watched chapter 5 knows exactly whose hand that is. Second, the summons. One of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne — calls Come! with a voice like thunder, and the horseman comes. Heaven speaks first; earth responds. Third, the grammar. Watch for the passive verbs through the next seven verses: a crown was given, the rider was permitted, he was given a great sword, they were given authority. Four times. Nothing here takes itself.

Now the structural question, since the seals are the first of three sevens and the way a reader relates them decides the shape of the whole book. Godly readers differ, and the differences should be stated rather than smoothed over.

On the recapitulation reading — held by Augustine, Hendriksen, Beale and the amillennial tradition generally — the seals, trumpets and bowls are not consecutive but parallel: three passes over the same stretch of history, each running from the cross to the last day, each more intense than the last. What favours it is that all three series end at the same place. The sixth seal brings the sky rolling up and the kings hiding (6:12–17); the seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord (11:15); the seventh bowl is followed by a voice saying It is done (16:17). Three separate arrivals at the end are hard to fit on one line.

On the sequential reading — held by the futurist and dispensational tradition, and set out at length by Walvoord and MacArthur — the three sevens follow one another in order, and the whole sequence describes a defined future period of tribulation. What favours it is the plain progression: the seventh seal opens onto the seven trumpets (8:1–2), and the seventh trumpet leads towards the bowls; the fractions escalate from a fourth (6:8) to a third (8:7–12) to everything (16:3); and the text nowhere says it is going back to the beginning.

A third position, held by many, is that both are partly right: the series overlap and advance at the same time, spiralling rather than either repeating or marching. This commentary reads the visions as recapitulating, and will say so where it matters, and will flag the alternative each time. What is not in dispute is the point of the chapter either way: whatever these riders are, and whenever they ride, the Lamb sends them.

Then the first horseman. And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer. Who is he? This is one of the genuine disputes of the book, and it will not be settled by assertion.

Many take him to be Christ, or the victorious progress of the gospel. In favour: white is the colour of holiness everywhere else in Revelation — white robes, white stones, a white throne — and at 19:11 Christ himself rides a white horse; conquering, and to conquer uses the same verb applied to him at 5:5; and the gospel does go out first, before the tribulations that follow it (cf. Mark 13:10).

Many others take him to be conquest itself, the spirit of military aggression, or an antichrist figure who imitates Christ. In favour: his crown is a stephanos, the athlete’s wreath, while the rider of 19:12 wears many diadēmata, royal crowns; his crown was given to him, whereas Christ’s authority is his own; he carries a bow, and Christ’s weapon in this book is always the sword from his mouth; and the other three riders are unambiguous disasters, which makes it odd for the first of a matched set to be the Saviour.

The second reading is the stronger, and this commentary follows it. But the first is held by careful readers and should not be dismissed, and either way the four ride together as one picture: the ordinary, recurring furniture of a fallen world. Conquest, then war, then famine, then death — in that order, because that is the order in which they actually arrive. Every war in history has run that sequence, and the four have been riding since the first century without a break.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And out came another horse, bright red. The Greek is pyrros, the colour of fire, and its association is unmistakable in a chapter about slaughter. The first rider went out to conquer. What follows conquest is not peace.

Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth. Two things in that clause. The rider does not bring war; he takes peace away, which assumes that peace was there and was a gift. Ordinary quiet — a town where the shops open, a night without sirens, children walking to school — is not the natural state of things that occasionally breaks down. It is a mercy being extended, and it can be withdrawn.

And he was permitted. The verb is a divine passive, the third of the chapter’s four, and it is the hinge of the whole vision. Nothing here is out of control. That is a hard comfort rather than an easy one, and it should be given as it stands: Scripture does not say that God is doing his best against forces he cannot restrain. It says that even the horse of war rides on a permission, and therefore on a leash.

Then the specific horror: so that people should slay one another. Not so that armies should destroy nations. The Greek is reciprocal — one another, each other, mutual killing. This is civil war, the neighbour with the knife, the country that turns on itself. And the twentieth century, which killed more people than any century before it, did most of its killing exactly that way: not chiefly invaders against defenders but citizens against their own, in Rwanda, in Cambodia, in the Soviet countryside, in the Balkans.

And he was given a great sword. The word is machaira, the short blade a Roman soldier actually carried and the word used for the sword of the state’s authority in Romans 13:4. It is not the long ceremonial weapon of a general. It is the instrument of ordinary official violence, and here it has been handed to a horseman whose only business is that men should kill each other.

Which raises the question a thoughtful reader is already asking, and it should not be dodged. If God permits this, is he responsible for it? Scripture holds two things together without flinching and refuses to release either. God is never the author of evil, and no man who takes up a sword can plead that heaven made him do it. And nothing happens outside God’s governance, including this. Joseph said both in one sentence about the worst thing his brothers ever did: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The brothers were guilty. God was not idle. Both clauses stand.

And the practical difference that makes is not small. A believer watching the news from a war can hold one of two things. Either the world has slipped its moorings and God is somewhere off-stage hoping for the best — in which case there is nothing to pray for and no reason to expect an end. Or the red horse rides on a permission granted in the throne room, in front of a rainbow, by a Lamb with the marks still on him. The second is far harder to look at and is the only one with any hope in it.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. War has ridden through; now comes what always follows an army. Fields trampled, men conscripted off the land, granaries emptied, roads unsafe for carts. Famine is not usually a separate disaster. It is the second half of a war.

The scales are the point. Grain sold by weight rather than by the sackful is grain being rationed, and the prophets used exactly this image: when I break your supply of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven and shall dole out your bread by weight (Lev. 26:26; cf. Ezek. 4:16). A man watching his food weighed out in front of him knows precisely how bad things have become.

Then the voice from the middle of the four living creatures gives the market prices, and the figures are exact enough to be checked. A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius. A denarius was a labourer’s wage for a full day (Matt. 20:2). A quart of wheat — roughly a litre — was about one man’s daily ration. In normal times that denarius bought eight to twelve times as much.

So do the arithmetic the way a first-century hearer would have done it instantly. A man works from dawn to dusk and earns enough to feed himself, and nothing for his wife or his children. If he switches to barley — coarse, cheap, what you fed animals — he gets three days’ worth, and the family eats badly and is still hungry. This is not a picture of mass starvation with bodies in the street. It is something more familiar and more grinding: a working man in full employment who cannot feed his household, and who knows there is nothing further he can do about it.

And do not harm the oil and wine! The line is often read as a mercy — a limit set on the famine. There is truth in that, since limits are set everywhere in this chapter. But olive trees and vines have deep roots and survive a drought that destroys a grain crop, and both were luxury goods in the Roman economy, the produce of estates rather than smallholdings. What the prohibition describes is the specific injustice of every food crisis in history: the price of bread trebles and the luxury trade goes on undisturbed. The rich man’s cellar is untouched while a labourer counts out grain by weight in the street outside.

Name that plainly, because it is the shape the world still takes. Famines are rarely a simple absence of food; they are ordinarily a failure of access, and the people who die are the people who cannot pay. Christ, opening the third seal, does not describe it in the abstract. He quotes the price list.

And this seal, like the others, comes out from the throne. The voice setting the limits speaks from the midst of the four living creatures — that is, from the immediate presence of God. The famine is not a gap in his attention. The boundary around it was drawn in the throne room, and so was the invoice.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! The word is chlōros, the root of chlorophyll — the yellowish-green of vegetation, and, used of a body, the colour of a corpse. Elsewhere in the New Testament it means the green of grass. Here it means the green of a face.

And this rider is the only one of the four who is named. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. The first three were anonymous forces; this one has a name, and behind him walks a second figure. Hades is the realm of the dead, the place that receives what Death takes. The image is of a reaper and a cart: one kills, and the other collects.

Which is exactly where a reader of this book has heard both words before, and John expects him to remember. In the first chapter the risen Christ said: I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). The two figures riding out at the fourth seal are the two whose keys are on the belt of the one who opened the seal. They ride, and the man who holds their keys is the man who let them out. And at 20:14 the same two are thrown into the lake of fire.

And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth. The fourth divine passive of the chapter, and this time an explicit fraction. A fourth. Not half, not all.

Stay with that limit, because it is easy to read past a number in a list of horrors. Every rider so far has been permitted, and now the permission is quantified. Death is given a portion and not the whole. Later in the book the trumpets will touch a third (8:7–12), and only at the very end does anything become total. The judgments in Revelation escalate, and they escalate because they are being measured out by somebody, in stages, with a purpose — and the purpose is stated later in plain words: they did not repent (9:20–21). These are not the death-throes of a world God has abandoned. They are warnings loud enough to be heard.

The four instruments named are quoted almost directly from Ezekiel, where God speaks of sending my four disastrous acts of judgment, sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence against Jerusalem (Ezek. 14:21). John is not inventing a scenario. He is using the standing vocabulary of covenant judgment that every reader of the prophets already knew.

So the four horsemen are complete. Stand back and look at what has actually been shown. Not a coded map of the twenty-first century. Not a set of clues about a particular decade. The ordinary, terrible furniture of human history — empires that conquer, nations that turn on themselves, hunger that follows the armies, and death that gathers what is left — and every one of the four riding out at the word of the Lamb, on a permission, within a fraction, in front of a throne.

That is not a comfortable doctrine and it was never meant to be. It is, however, the only alternative to the thought that these things ride at nobody’s word at all. The churches in Asia were about to meet the red horse and the pale one personally. What they were given was not an explanation of why. It was the identity of the hand on the seal.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth seal breaks the pattern. There is no horse, no rider, no thundered Come! The camera turns away from the earth altogether, and what John sees is a congregation.

I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. The verb for slain is esphagmenōn — the same word, in the same form, used of the Lamb at 5:6. John does not use it of anyone else in the book. What was done to Christ has been done to them, and Scripture says so with a single deliberate word.

Why under the altar? In the temple, the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offering (Lev. 4:7), and Leviticus says the life of a creature is in the blood (Lev. 17:11). So the place where the life of every sacrifice collected was the foot of the altar. These people are lying exactly where the blood of the offerings went. Their deaths were not waste; they were an offering, and heaven has put them where an offering belongs. Paul used the same image of his own approaching death: I am already being poured out as a drink offering (2 Tim. 4:6).

The verse also settles, in passing, a question ordinary Christians ask constantly at funerals: where are they now? Between death and resurrection, believers are conscious, recognisable, in the presence of God, capable of speech — and not yet finished, because the body is still in the ground and the resurrection has not happened. Paul says the same: to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Phil. 1:23). Not asleep in the sense of unconscious. Not yet complete. With him.

Then they speak, and what they say is startling: O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?

This is the cry of the psalms of complaint, word for word in substance — How long, O LORD? Will you forget me for ever? (Ps. 13:1); How long will the wicked exult? (Ps. 94:3). Something like a third of the psalter is made of it. Sovereign Lord is despotēs, the word for an absolute master over a household — a title chosen because their complaint is precisely that he has the power to act and has not.

And now the question a careful Christian will raise, and it deserves a real answer rather than a nervous one. Should believers pray for vengeance? Did not Christ say to love enemies and pray for persecutors (Matt. 5:44), and did not Stephen die asking that the sin not be held against them (Acts 7:60)?

Four things settle it.

First, they are not asking to do anything; they are asking God to do it. Vengeance belongs to him and nobody else, which is the whole point of never avenge yourselves… leave it to the wrath of God (Rom. 12:19–20) — and that command is a command to hand the matter over, not to pretend the matter does not exist.

Second, they do not name individuals or ask for a particular punishment. They ask the judge to judge. Third, what they are asking for is not private satisfaction but justice, which is a thing God has promised and a thing the world urgently needs. A universe in which murder is finally shrugged at is not a kind universe. Fourth, the two prayers are not actually rivals: Christ prayed for his executioners’ forgiveness and also promised that every hidden thing would be brought into the open (Luke 12:2–3). The one who repents is forgiven. The one who does not is judged. Praying for both is not confusion; it is the whole gospel with nothing left out.

Which frees a believer from something needless. Anyone who has been genuinely wronged — assaulted, defrauded, lied about, bereaved by somebody who was never charged — often carries a double burden: the injury itself, and the guilt of still minding about it. This verse takes the second one away. The holiest company in Scripture, standing in the immediate presence of God, wearing the marks of martyrdom, are asking out loud how long justice is going to take. Nobody tells them to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer comes in two parts, and neither is what the question asked for. They asked how long? and they are given a garment and a word.

Then they were each given a white robe. Before anything is explained, something is handed over. The white robe is the promise made to Sardis (3:4–5) and worn by the elders (4:4) and by the great multitude (7:9), and 7:14 will say where the whiteness comes from — washed in the blood of the Lamb, which is a deliberately impossible image and settles that the robe is not a reward for dying well. It is the verdict of the court delivered in advance. Whatever the world’s courts said about these people, and several of them were executed as criminals under due process, heaven has dressed them in the colour of innocence.

Note the word each. Not a general amnesty issued to a category; a robe apiece, handed to individuals. This is the same God who counts a few names in Sardis one at a time.

Then the word: and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.

Three things are in that sentence, and the third is very hard.

The first is rest. The verb means to cease from labour, to stop. It is not a command to be patient in the sense of gritting the teeth; it is permission to stop working. Their part is finished. Whatever is still to be done about the injustice done to them is not their assignment any more.

The second is a little longer. There is an end, and God has an opinion about the length of the wait. He does not say indefinitely. He calls it short — which, said to people already dead and already in his presence, is a measurement taken from a place where the arithmetic looks different from the way it looks in a cell.

The third is the reason, and it will stop a reader who is paying attention: until the number… should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been. The delay in judgment is not administrative. God is waiting because there are more still to come, and they will die in the same way. The answer to how long until you avenge our blood is: until the rest of your brothers have shed theirs.

Nothing softens that, and it should not be softened. But two things sit alongside it. The first is that God has a number, and the number is known to him, and it is not a casualty estimate but a roll. Nobody in it is an accident, and nobody outside it will be taken by mistake. The second is what that delay is doing on the other side of the ledger: every year the judgment is postponed is a year in which somebody who is currently an enemy of God can be brought in — and the man writing the New Testament’s letters about grace had held the coats at the first martyrdom (Acts 7:58; 8:1). Paul was in the number of the persecutors before he was in the number of the persecuted. The patience the martyrs are being asked to accept is the patience that produced Paul.

So the fifth seal does not answer the question of timing at all, and it is honest enough not to pretend it has. It gives three things instead: a verdict delivered early, an end that is fixed, and a reason for the wait that is not indifference. For a congregation in Smyrna expecting arrests, that was the whole of the comfort available — and it turned out to be enough for sixty generations.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth seal is opened and the world comes apart. Six things go, in order, from the ground upward: the earth quakes, the sun goes black, the moon turns to blood, the stars fall, the sky rolls up, and every mountain and island is moved out of place. The whole stage is struck.

Every image is quoted. The sun became black as sackcloth — sackcloth was woven from black goat hair, so the comparison is exact and not merely poetic; Joel said the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Joel 2:31), and Peter quoted it at Pentecost (Acts 2:20). The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up comes straight from Isaiah 34:4. Every mountain and island was removed echoes the prophets’ standard picture of God arriving.

Which raises a fair question about how literally to take it, and the honest answer requires looking at how the prophets used this language. Isaiah announced that the stars would not give their light and the sun would be dark at its rising — and the subject of that passage is the fall of Babylon to the Medes (Isa. 13:1, 10). Ezekiel said God would cover the heavens and darken their stars, and the subject was Egypt (Ezek. 32:7–8). Isaiah 34:4, the source of the rolled-up scroll, is about Edom. In every case the cosmos-collapsing vocabulary describes a historical political catastrophe, and it means what it feels like when an empire that seemed permanent ends.

So two readings are available and both are held by serious people. Some take the sixth seal as the literal end of the physical universe, arriving here at the close of a sequence. Others take it, on the prophets’ own precedent, as the recurring end of worlds — the day the empire falls, the day the certainties collapse — reaching its final instance at the last day. The recapitulation reading favours the second; the sequential reading the first. What both agree on is what the language is for. When everything a person has treated as fixed is removed, it feels exactly like the sky being rolled up.

The one detail that is unmistakably John’s own is the fig tree. The stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. Late figs that never ripened hang on through the winter, hard and green and useless, and the first real storm brings them down in a shower. It is a small, domestic, almost homely image dropped into the middle of a cosmic catastrophe — and it reduces the stars to windfall. The lights that sailors steered by and astrologers consulted and emperors were named after come down like unripe fruit off a tree in a gale, and the tree does not notice.

That is the actual argument of these three verses, and it is aimed at people under pressure from something that looks immovable. Everything humanity has ever used as a fixed reference point is in this list. The ground, which does not move. The sun, which always rises. The stars, which are how you find your way home when nothing else is visible. Mountains, which are the standing definition of permanence. Every one of them, in four verses, gone.

And the throne is not in the list. Chapter 4 established where the one fixed point is, and chapter 6 now removes every rival. When the sky is rolled up like a scroll there will be one thing left standing in the universe, and it will be the thing that was described first.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last three verses of the chapter turn from the cosmos to faces, and they are the most searching in it.

Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains. Seven categories, which in this book means the complete list. Five of them are the top of the pyramid — kings, magnates, military commanders, the wealthy, the strong — and then the sentence widens to take in everybody, and finishes with the two words that in the Roman world divided the whole human race: slave and free.

The order is deliberate and it starts at the top. Every category that ordinarily protects a person is named first and named uselessly. A king has an army. A general has the army itself. A rich man can buy his way out of most things and a powerful one can arrange them. On this day the list of people who cannot help themselves runs from the throne down to the labour gang, and the emperor and the man he owns end up behind the same rock.

And what they say is the terrible part: Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. They are asking mountains to crush them. Given the choice between being buried alive and being looked at, they choose the burial. Hosea recorded the same cry over Israel (Hos. 10:8), and Jesus quoted it to the women weeping on the way to the cross (Luke 23:30).

Sit with what they are hiding from, because it is not fire and it is not an army. It is the face. Moses asked to see that face and was told no man could see it and live (Ex. 33:20). The great blessing of Israel was that the LORD would make his face shine upon you (Num. 6:25). The whole hope of this book is that his servants will see his face (22:4). The same face, and here men are begging geology to spare them from it.

Then the phrase that ought to stop every reader: the wrath of the Lamb. Put the two words side by side and they should not fit. Lambs do not have wrath. That is the point, and it is the exact counterpart of 5:5–6: there John was told a Lion and shown a Lamb, and here the Lamb turns out to be what men flee from.
