This is not a mild Christ who has finally lost his temper. It is the same Lamb, with the same wounds, and the wrath is the other face of the love that bore them. Nothing is more terrible than mercy that has been refused for long enough, and the only thing left to meet is the one who offered it.

For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? The question is the last word of the chapter and it is left hanging deliberately. It is not rhetorical despair; it is a real question, and the whole of the next chapter is the answer. Before the seventh seal is opened, John will be shown a hundred and forty-four thousand sealed on the forehead and a multitude nobody can count, standing — standing — before the throne and before the Lamb.

So the honest question this chapter leaves with a reader is not whether the world is going to be shaken. It says plainly that it is, and that the shaking has been going on since the first horse rode out. The question is where a person will be standing when the last of the fixed points goes, and there are only two options in the text: behind a rock, or in front of the throne in a white robe.

And the difference between them is not courage or achievement. Every one of the seven classes hiding in the caves failed for the same reason, and every one of the multitude in the next chapter succeeded for the same reason, and it is the reason given in 7:14. They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. The wrath they are spared is the Lamb’s, and so is the blood that spares them.

7.title: The Sealed and the Standing: God's People in the Storm
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the first great interlude of Revelation — a pause between the sixth and seventh seals that answers the question that ended chapter 6: “Who can stand?” The answer comes in two scenes that together present the whole people of God from two perspectives. The 144,000 sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 1–8): the church as it endures on earth, the complete and protected people of God in the midst of judgment. The great multitude from every nation (vv. 9–17): the church as it will appear before the throne, the redeemed in their innumerable fullness, already standing where the kings of the earth could not.

The 144,000 has generated more interpretive controversy than almost any other passage in Revelation. A strictly literal reading — exactly 144,000 ethnic Jewish males from the twelve tribes of Israel — faces several difficulties: (1) Dan is missing from the list and Manasseh (Joseph’s son) substituted, while Levi (not a territorial tribe) is included, making this no straightforward census; (2) the twelve tribes as distinct ethnic communities had not existed since the Assyrian deportation of the northern tribes in 722 BC; (3) the number 12 × 12 × 1,000 is conspicuously mathematical — in a book where seven means completeness, twelve means the people of God, and 1,000 means an immense completeness, 144,000 is the fullness of the fullness of God’s people. The majority Reformed/amillennial reading understands the 144,000 as the complete church of both testaments, the spiritual Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Galatians 3:29; 6:16; Philippians 3:3), sealed for protection through the tribulation. The dispensational reading understands them as 144,000 literal Jewish evangelists who will be saved and minister during the tribulation.

The great multitude of verses 9–17 is almost certainly the same group seen from a different vantage point — not a second group that supplements the 144,000 but the 144,000 as they appear before the throne, their number now seen to be “a great multitude that no one could number.” The innumerable quality is not a contradiction of the 144,000 but its complement: both “complete” and “uncountable” describe the fullness of the redeemed. The scene before the throne anticipates the final state, giving the church a vision of its own destiny as it endures the trials of the present.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 6 ended with the sky rolled up and a question hanging: who can stand? The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1, and everything here sits in that gap, answering the question before the last seal breaks.

Verse 1: four angels at the four corners of the earth hold back the four winds, so that no wind blows on earth or sea or against any tree. The stillness before a storm — destruction under restraint. Verse 2: a fifth angel ascends from the rising of the sun with the seal of the living God, and outranks the four. Verse 3 gives his order: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads. Judgment is not cancelled; it is delayed until God’s people are marked (cf. 2 Pet. 3:9).

The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9:4, where a man with a writing case marks the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over what is being done in Jerusalem, and the executioners are told to touch nobody who carries the mark. A seal marked ownership, gave protection, and guaranteed authenticity; all three apply.

Verse 4 gives the number: 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Verses 5–8 list the twelve, twelve thousand each — Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin. The list matches no tribal register in the Old Testament: Judah heads it rather than Reuben the firstborn; Dan is missing; Levi, which had no territorial allotment, is counted; and Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, his own father. Who the 144,000 are is set out at the verse, with the evidence on both sides.
verseByVerse.theology:
The 144,000: Where Godly Readers Differ

The literal reading takes the number and the names at face value: a preserved remnant of ethnic Israel, sealed through a future tribulation. This is the standard dispensational understanding (Walvoord, Ryrie, MacArthur), and what favours it is real — the text says from every tribe of the sons of Israel and then names them, which is a great deal of trouble for a symbol; a precise figure is given; and Paul says plainly that God has not rejected his people (Rom. 11:1, 25–26).

The symbolic reading takes it as the whole people of God, numbered and complete: twelve times twelve times a thousand, Israel multiplied by the apostles multiplied by vastness, which is how numbers work in a book where seven means fullness. What favours it is the four irregularities in the list itself, and above all the movement of vv. 4 and 9 — John hears a number from the tribes of Israel and then looks and sees a multitude nobody can count from every nation. That is exactly the structure of 5:5–6, where he was told a Lion and saw a Lamb, and there the two were one person described twice.

This commentary follows the symbolic reading. But the point agreed on every side is the one that matters: God knows the number. There is no rounding and no estimate here, and the counting was finished before the winds were released.

What the Seal Does Not Do

The winds are eventually released, and the very next scene shows this company coming out of the great tribulation — which means they went through it, and the martyrs of 6:9 are part of the same story. The seal is not a shield against suffering; it is a mark of ownership that suffering cannot remove. What is guaranteed is not an easy passage but a safe arrival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ezekiel’s mark went on the foreheads of the people who were grieved by what was happening around them — not the strong, not the successful, but the ones who sighed and groaned. That is who gets sealed before the winds are let go, and a congregation in Asia hearing it read would have recognised itself immediately.

Now: This passage is the one a stranger is most likely to raise at the door, and the teaching that only 144,000 people go to heaven cannot be got out of this chapter. The very next verse puts a multitude that no one could number in front of the throne, in the same vision, in white robes. Whether the 144,000 are that multitude under another figure or a distinct group within it, the text does not cap the number of the redeemed — it names a number and then immediately shows a crowd too large to count.

And to a Christian who reads a list like this and wonders whether he is in it: the chapter never asks anyone to work out his tribe. What it says about the sealed is that they are the servants of our God, and what it says about the multitude is that they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Those are the two descriptions given, and neither of them is a bloodline.

One further thing, and the book turns on it later. The mark goes on the forehead. In chapter 13 another power will demand a mark on the right hand or the forehead, without which no one can buy or sell. Everyone alive is marked by somebody; the only question is whose name is on you. And the sealing happens here, six chapters before the counterfeit is even offered.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 6 ended with the sky rolled up and seven classes of people hiding in caves, and with a question left hanging in the air: who can stand? The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1. Everything in this chapter sits in the gap between the sixth and the seventh, and its whole business is to answer that question before the last seal breaks.

After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Four angels, four corners, four winds — four is the number of the created world in this book, its compass points and its extent. The picture is of destruction under restraint. Something is coming that would strip the earth, and four angels have hold of it, and the whole world has gone still.

Anyone who has stood outside before a storm knows that stillness. The air stops. The leaves do not move. Nothing has happened yet, and everything is about to. That is the atmosphere of the first three verses, and the reader is meant to feel it: the winds have not been cancelled. They are being held.

Then a fifth angel: Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God. He comes from the east, which is the direction of dawn and, in Ezekiel, the direction from which the glory of God returns to his temple (Ezek. 43:2). And he outranks the four, because he gives them orders: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.

That is the shape of the whole chapter in one sentence. The judgment is not cancelled — it is delayed, and it is delayed for one reason: God’s people are not marked yet. The winds of the world are held on a leash until the last of the servants has been sealed. Every year of history since is an instance of the same arrangement, and the reason is stated elsewhere in one line: the Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Pet. 3:9).

A seal in the ancient world did three things. It marked ownership, like a brand or a signet pressed into wax. It gave protection, because tampering with a sealed item was an offence against the owner. And it guaranteed authenticity. All three are in play here.

The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9, and John expects the reader to know it. Before judgment fell on Jerusalem, a man with a writing case was sent through the city to put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it (Ezek. 9:4), and the executioners were told to touch nobody who carried it. Note who was marked: not the strong or the successful, but the people who were grieved by what was happening around them.

And note what the seal does and does not do, because this is where the verse is most often misread. The four winds are eventually released. The sealed are not exempted from trouble; the very next scene shows this same company coming out of the great tribulation, which means they went through it, and some of them were killed, since the martyrs under the altar in 6:9 are part of the same story. The seal is not a shield against suffering. It is a mark of ownership that suffering cannot remove. What is guaranteed is not an easy passage but a safe arrival.

One more thing, and the whole book turns on it later. The mark goes on their foreheads. In chapter 13 another power will demand a mark on the right hand or the forehead, and nobody will be able to buy or sell without it (13:16–17). Everyone alive is marked by somebody. The only question in this book is whose name is on you, and the sealing happens first — six chapters before the counterfeit is even offered.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Then twelve tribes, twelve thousand each, named one after another with a deliberateness that slows the reading right down.

Who are they? This is one of the most argued questions in the book, and both main answers are held by people who love Scripture and read it carefully. It deserves the evidence rather than an assertion.

The literal reading takes the number and the tribal names at face value: a specific remnant of ethnic Israel, sealed and preserved through a future tribulation. This is the standard dispensational understanding, worked out in detail by Walvoord, Ryrie and MacArthur. What favours it is considerable. The text says from every tribe of the sons of Israel and then lists the tribes by name, which is a great deal of trouble to go to for a symbol. A precise number is given and repeated. And Paul says plainly that God has not rejected his people and that a future lies ahead for them (Rom. 11:1, 25–26), so a preserved Jewish remnant is not an idea foreign to the New Testament.

The symbolic reading takes the 144,000 as the whole people of God, complete and numbered, under a figure. What favours it is the arithmetic and the list itself. Twelve times twelve times a thousand is the number of Israel multiplied by the number of the apostles multiplied by a figure of vast completeness — and in a book where seven means fullness and ten thousand means uncountable, that is how numbers work.

And the list is strange in four ways at once, which is the strongest evidence of all. Judah is first, though Reuben was the firstborn — because the Lion of the tribe of Judah has just been introduced two chapters earlier. Dan is missing altogether, and Dan was the tribe that set up an idol and became a byword for apostasy (Judg. 18:30–31; 1 Kings 12:29–30). Levi is counted as a tribe, though Levi never had a territorial allotment and was normally left out of such lists. And Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, which double-counts, since Manasseh was Joseph’s son. The result is a list that matches no tribal register in the Old Testament. It is twelve names arranged theologically rather than genealogically.

There is one further consideration, and it is the one that persuades many. Look at what happens in verse 9. John hears a number — 144,000, from the tribes of Israel — and then looks, and sees a multitude that no one could number, from every nation. That is precisely the movement of 5:5–6, where he was told a Lion and saw a Lamb, and there the two were the same person described two ways. If John is doing the same thing here, then the numbered army of Israel and the uncountable multitude of the nations are one company seen from two sides: as God counts them, exact and complete with nobody missing; as they actually appear, beyond counting and drawn from everywhere.

This commentary follows the symbolic reading. But the point that matters most is agreed on every side, and a reader should not lose it in the argument: God knows the number. There is no rounding here and no estimate. Whatever the 144,000 turns out to be, it is a figure that has been counted, and the counting was done before the winds were released.

One practical word, because this passage is the one a stranger is most likely to raise on a doorstep. The teaching that only 144,000 people go to heaven while the rest of the saved live for ever on earth cannot be got out of this chapter. The very next verse puts a multitude that no one could number in front of the throne, in the same vision, in white robes. Whether the 144,000 are that multitude under another figure or a distinct group within it, the one thing the text does not do is cap the number of the redeemed. It does the opposite: it names a number and then immediately shows a crowd too large to count.

And a word to a Christian who has ever wondered, reading a list like this, whether he is in it. The chapter never asks anyone to work out his tribe. What it says about the sealed is that they are the servants of our God, and what it says about the multitude is that they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Those are the two descriptions given, and neither of them is a bloodline.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — A Great Multitude from Every Nation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–10: John looks and sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages — the fourfold phrase of 5:9, so that this chapter is the receipt for that purchase. They are standing, which answers 6:17 directly, in white robes and holding palm branches (Lev. 23:40–43; John 12:13), and they cry Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! Not a syllable of the song is about what they did.

Verses 11–12: all the angels stand in the outer ring — the redeemed are nearer the throne than the angelic host — and fall on their faces with a sevenfold doxology bracketed by Amen. It matches the ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving replacing wealth. Heaven falls down because a crowd of forgiven human beings has just sung.

Verses 13–14: an elder asks who they are and where they have come from, and John answers Sir, you know (cf. Ezek. 37:3). The answer has two halves: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation — a present, continuous participle, a stream still emerging — and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Blood does not whiten cloth; the image is deliberately impossible.

Verse 15: therefore they are before the throne, serving him day and night in his temple in priestly service (latreuō), and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence — literally, will spread his tent over them (cf. Ex. 40:34; John 1:14; Rev. 21:3). Verses 16–17 close with five promises quoted from Isaiah 49:10: no hunger, no thirst, no sun, no scorching heat; the Lamb in the midst of the throne as their shepherd, guiding them to springs of living water; and God wiping away every tear from their eyes.
verseByVerse.theology:
“The Great Tribulation”

Two things in v. 14 are argued over. The participle is present and continuous — the ones coming out — so people are still emerging while John watches. And the article, the great tribulation, is read by the dispensational tradition as the technical name for a defined seven-year period still future. The amillennial reading points out that John has already called himself their partner in the tribulation in his own present circumstances (1:9), and that Jesus said flatly in the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33). What neither reading permits is a promise of smooth passage: under both, these people went through something severe enough to be called great.

Washed in Blood

The sentence is flagrantly impossible, and every hearer who had ever killed an animal knew it. There is one substance in the universe that reverses its own nature at this one job. And the verb is active — they washed — so something is genuinely required of a person; but the sentence carries its own safeguard, because what they washed in was his blood. The action is entirely theirs; the detergent is entirely his.

That also answers the elder’s second question, which is the more important one. He asked not only who but from where. They came out of every nation, and out of the great tribulation, and some from under the executioner’s sword — and none of that is the answer. They came from the blood of the Lamb. There is no second road, and nobody in that crowd has a better story about the journey than the person beside him.

The Lamb Who Is the Shepherd

Lambs are shepherded; they do not shepherd. This is the third great reversal of the book — the Lion who is a Lamb (5:5), the Lamb who has wrath (6:16), the Lamb who is the Shepherd — and each works the same way: the image that ought to be weak turns out to be the strong one. Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34:11–16 and John 10:11 all arrive at once, and the shepherd leading this flock is the one who was himself led to the slaughter (Isa. 53:7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The five promises of vv. 16–17 are not vague comfort about a better place. They answer, item by item, what had actually made these people’s lives hard. The black horse rode out with a pair of scales and a labourer’s whole day bought one man’s ration of wheat. Believers under boycott in Smyrna were poor in the beggar’s sense. A slave in a field in Asia Minor in August knew exactly what scorching heat does to a man who cannot stop. The empty stomach, the dry throat, the sun on the back of the neck at the fourteenth hour: named, and answered.

Now: Verse 10 is a test that can be run quietly at any moment. This multitude has come out of the great tribulation; some of them died under torture; every one of them held on when it would have been easier not to. And when they open their mouths in front of the throne, they do not sing we endured. They sing that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and there is no second clause. If everything you are were explained out loud in front of that throne, whose name would the account turn on?

And take the last line of the chapter exactly as written, not one degree weaker. God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. It assumes there were tears — the promise is not that nothing bad happened but that something is done about it afterwards. It assumes he knows which ones and whose: every tear, not the general average of human sorrow. And it says he does it himself — not an angel with a cloth, not time healing it, but God, personally, close enough to touch a face. Anyone who has sat with someone dying, or stood at a small grave, or simply gone on getting up in the morning after the worst thing, is being addressed here by name.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages.

Set that beside what John has just heard. A moment ago there was a precise figure and a list of twelve names. Now there is a crowd nobody can count, from every nation there is. And no one could number is a deliberate phrase, because it takes the reader back to a promise made to a childless old man standing outside his tent at night: look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them… so shall your offspring be (Gen. 15:5). That promise has been kept, and this is what it looks like when it is.

The fourfold phrase — nation, tribes, peoples, languages — is the one from 5:9, where the Lamb was praised for having ransomed people from every one of them. This chapter is the receipt for that transaction. The purchase was made in chapter 5; here are the purchased, standing in the room.

And they are standing. Chapter 6 asked who can stand? while kings and generals crawled into caves. Here is the answer, and it is not a class of person anyone would have picked: a crowd with no rank, no army and no leverage, drawn from every obscure corner of the world, upright before the throne while the great ones of the earth are face down under the rocks.

Clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands. The robes have been promised since 3:5 and worn since 6:11, and verse 14 will say where they came from. The palms are the more interesting detail. Palm branches belonged to the Feast of Tabernacles, the week each autumn when Israel moved out of its houses and lived in booths made of branches to remember the wilderness (Lev. 23:40–43) — a festival of harvest home, of a journey finished. And palms were what the crowd waved on the road into Jerusalem, shouting Hosanna, which means save now (John 12:13).

Which makes the cry in verse 10 the answer to the shout on that road. Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! They asked save now; they are here saying that salvation belongs to him — it is his, it comes from him, it is his to give and nobody else’s to supply.

Take the word belongs seriously, because everything in the Christian life depends on it. The multitude has come out of the great tribulation. Some of them died under torture. Every one of them held on when it would have been easier not to. And when they open their mouths in front of the throne, not one syllable of the song is about what they did. They do not sing we endured. They sing that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and there is no second clause.

That is the test of whether a person has understood the gospel, and it can be run quietly at any moment. If everything you are were suddenly explained out loud in front of the throne, whose name would the account turn on? The people who have suffered most for Christ are, on the evidence of this verse, the least inclined to mention it.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God.

Note the seating plan, because John gives it carefully. In the middle, the throne. Around it, the living creatures and the elders. And in the outer ring, all the angels — the myriads of myriads from 5:11. But the multitude of verse 9 is described as before the throne and before the Lamb, which puts the redeemed nearer than the angelic host. Ransomed sinners stand closer to God than the beings who never fell.

And what the angels do is fall on their faces. They have been standing throughout; now they go down. What has just happened to prompt it? The multitude sang. The angels of God hear a crowd of forgiven human beings say that salvation belongs to God, and they put their faces on the floor.

Their doxology has seven parts: Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever. Seven, which in this book is the complete set — everything there is to give, given. And the list is almost the same as the sevenfold ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving here in place of wealth. The change is not accidental. Wealth is what a conqueror receives; thanksgiving is what a redeemed people offer.

The whole thing is bracketed by Amen, at the beginning and at the end. The word means it is firm, it is so, and it is the only word in the verse that is not itself a gift. To say Amen is to agree with what somebody else has said. The angels open and close by adding their agreement to a song they cannot sing on their own account, because nobody has ever ransomed an angel.

There is something in that arrangement that is easy to miss and difficult to get over once seen. The order of events in these two verses is: the redeemed sing, and then heaven agrees. The song that sets the whole company of angels on their faces was started by people who had been slaves, shopkeepers, soldiers, prostitutes and thieves, out of every language on earth. Peter says the angels long to look into these things (1 Pet. 1:12). Here they are looking, and this is what looking does to them.

Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honour and power and might be to our God for ever and ever. He was on that throne when the seals were breaking and the horses were riding and the winds were straining against four angels’ hands. He is on it still. And everything that exists in heaven, from the creatures covered in eyes to the last angel in the outermost ring, is on its face in front of him, saying it is so.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An elder turns to John and asks him a question he cannot possibly answer: Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?

It is a teacher’s question, asked to give the answer rather than to get one, and John knows it. Sir, you know is not evasion; it is the honest reply of a man who has been asked something above his pay grade and does not intend to guess. Ezekiel gave the same answer standing in a valley full of dry bones: O Lord GOD, you know (Ezek. 37:3). There is a kind of ignorance that is a form of faith, and Scripture records both men practising it.

The answer comes in two halves, and each half settles something.

These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. Two features of that clause are argued over, and both should be given plainly. First, the tense. The Greek participle is present and continuous — the ones coming out, not the ones who came out. Whatever the tribulation is, people are still emerging from it while John watches, in a steady stream.

Second, the definite article: the great tribulation. In the dispensational reading this is the technical term for a defined seven-year period still future, in which case the multitude are those converted and martyred during it, and the article is doing exactly what it looks like it is doing. In the amillennial reading the phrase describes the whole pressure the church lives under between the two comings — John has already called himself their partner in the tribulation in the first chapter (1:9), using the same word of his own present situation, and Jesus said flatly that in the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33). On that reading the great tribulation is not a fortnight in the diary of the future; it is the era, and the multitude is everyone who has come through it since Pentecost.

Both are held by serious readers. What neither reading permits is the idea that Christians are promised a smooth passage. Under both, the people in the white robes went through something, and the something was severe enough to be called great.

Then the second half of the answer, and it is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward: They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

Read that slowly, because it is an impossible sentence and it is meant to be. Blood does not whiten cloth. Anyone who has ever tried to get blood out of a shirt knows exactly what it does, and every first-century hearer had killed animals with his own hands and knew better still. The image is deliberately, flagrantly wrong — and that is the point. There is one substance in the universe that reverses its own nature at this one job, and the effect is not a stain but a colour that nothing else produces.

And the verb is active: they washed. Not their robes were washed for them. There is something a person must do, and Revelation is not shy about it — the whole book is an appeal to repent, hold fast, conquer, come. But look at what the washing consists of, because the sentence contains its own safeguard: they washed in the blood of the Lamb. The action is entirely theirs; the detergent is entirely his. Nobody in that multitude contributed a drop of what makes them white.

Which is the answer to the elder’s second question, and it is the more important one. He asked not only who are these but from where have they come. They came from every nation on earth, and out of the great tribulation, and from under the executioner’s sword in some cases — and none of that is the answer. They came from the blood of the Lamb. Every person in a crowd nobody can count arrived there by the same road, and there is no second road, and no one of them can tell a better story about the journey than the person next to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they are before the throne of God. The word therefore carries the entire logic of the gospel. Not because they endured, though they did. Not because they were faithful under torture, though many were. Therefore — because of the washing in the previous verse, and because of nothing else — they are standing where they are standing.

And serve him day and night in his temple. The verb is latreuō, which is not general helpfulness but priestly service — the word for what a priest did at the altar. In the temple in Jerusalem, only priests entered the holy place, and only one man went behind the veil, once a year, with blood, having washed. Here a crowd from every nation on earth is inside, permanently, doing priestly work. The promise of 1:6 has arrived: he made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father.

The phrase day and night should not be hurried past either. It is the phrase used of the living creatures who never cease (4:8). But there is no night in the city at the end of this book (21:25; 22:5), which means the expression is not measuring hours. It means without interruption. Nothing ever again breaks it off — no fatigue, no distraction, no sin, no need to stop and earn a living, no Monday.

And then a clause the English can only half carry: he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence. The Greek is skēnōsei ep’ autous — literally, he will spread his tent over them. It is the word for the tabernacle, the tent God pitched in the middle of Israel’s camp so that he could live among them in the wilderness (Ex. 25:8; 40:34). It is the same word John used in the first chapter of his Gospel: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us — pitched his tent among us (John 1:14). And it is the word that will be used at 21:3, when the loud voice from the throne announces that the dwelling place of God is with man.

So the picture is not chiefly of protection from something. It is of proximity. God puts his tent over these people, the way a father pulls a blanket over a child, the way the cloud stood over the tabernacle in the desert. They are not being kept at a safe distance from the throne and defended; they are being covered by the one on it.

Set that beside where the chapter started. In 6:16 the great ones of the earth begged the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne. Here, the same throne, the same one seated on it — and a crowd with no rank at all is being sheltered under him. The identical presence is the thing one company cannot bear to look at and the thing the other company lives inside.

And the difference between the two, once again, is not in the people. It is in verse 14. One company is standing in front of the face because their robes were washed in the blood of the Lamb, and the other is under the rocks because they were not.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with five promises and one of the most beautiful sentences in Scripture, and almost every word of it is quoted from Isaiah 49:10, where God promises to bring his exiles home: they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. John takes the promise made to a people in exile and gives it to a multitude out of every nation.

They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. Notice how specific and how bodily the list is. Hunger. Thirst. Sunstroke. These are not spiritual metaphors to the people first hearing them. The black horse rode out with a pair of scales in chapter 6, and a labourer’s whole day bought one man’s ration of wheat. Believers under economic boycott in Smyrna were poor in the beggar’s sense. And a slave working a field in Asia Minor in August knew precisely what scorching heat does to a man who cannot stop.

So the promise is not vague comfort about a better place. It answers, item by item, the exact things that had made their lives hard: the empty stomach, the dry throat, the sun on the back of the neck at the fourteenth hour.

That plainness is doing theological work, and it cuts against an instinct most Christians have absorbed without noticing. Ask a congregation what heaven will be like and the answers come back weightless — light, peace, spirits, somewhere else. The Bible almost never talks that way. It promises a body that works, food, water, shade, a city with streets in it, and a Lamb who has to lead people to springs, which means there is somewhere to walk and something to arrive at. The Greeks wanted deliverance from the body. Scripture promises deliverance of it.

And there is a reason the promises are stated as negatives — no hunger, no thirst, no striking sun. A negative is the only honest way to describe a condition nobody alive has experienced. No one can picture a body that never tires, because everybody reading this has been tired every day of his life. What can be pictured is the absence of a specific misery, and that is what John gives: not an abstraction, but the removal, one by one, of things the reader could name from this week.

Try the same move with whatever is currently wearing you down — the diagnosis that has to be managed daily, the pain that decides what you can and cannot do, the arithmetic at the end of the month that never quite works, the exhaustion that sleep no longer touches. Each of those is a hunger of some kind, and each has its own line in this verse. The promise is not that you will stop minding about them. It is that they will not be there.

One more thing about the shape of the sentence. Every one of the four clauses describes something being taken away, and none of them names what is put in its place. That comes in the next verse, and it is not a condition or a climate. It is a person.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last verse of the chapter contains three promises, and the first of them is a sentence no one but John would have dared write: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd.

The Lamb will be the shepherd. Lambs are shepherded; they do not shepherd. And this is the third of the great reversals in this book — the Lion who is a Lamb (5:5), the Lamb who has wrath (6:16), and now the Lamb who is a Shepherd. Every one of them works the same way: the image that ought to be weak turns out to be the strong one, and the strength is of a kind nobody was looking for.

And the shepherd is one of us. That is the force of it. Psalm 23 says the LORD is my shepherd, and Ezekiel promised that God himself would come and search for his sheep (Ezek. 34:11–16), and Jesus said I am the good shepherd and that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Here all of it arrives at once: the shepherd who leads this flock is the one who was himself led to the slaughter (Isa. 53:7). He has been where they have been. He is not directing the flock from a height; he is walking in front of it, and he has scars.

And he will guide them to springs of living water. The Greek is literally springs of waters of life — not a cistern, not a well that has to be drawn from, but water coming up out of the ground under its own pressure and not stopping. It is the offer he made to a woman at a well at noon (John 4:14), and it is where this book will finish, with the river of the water of life flowing from the throne (22:1).

And then, last: and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

Think about what that sentence requires. It requires that there be tears in the first place — the promise is not that nothing bad happened but that something is done about it afterwards. It requires that God knows which ones and whose; every tear, not the general average of human sorrow. And it requires that he does it himself. Not an angel with a cloth. Not time healing it. God, personally, close enough to touch a face.

Anyone who has sat with somebody dying, or stood at a small grave, or gone on getting up in the morning after the worst thing, should take this verse exactly as it is written and not one degree weaker. The tears were real, and they were counted, and every one of them will be dealt with by the hand of God on a human face — and the hand doing it belongs to the Lamb who was slaughtered, who is the shepherd, who has come through worse and has the marks to prove it.

The question at the end of chapter 6 was who can stand? Here is the answer, and it has taken seventeen verses: a crowd nobody can count, from every nation and tribe and people and language, sealed before the winds were let loose, washed in blood that makes cloth white, standing before the throne with palm branches, sheltered under the tent of God, led by a Lamb to water that never runs dry, with a Father wiping their faces. They can stand. And there is nothing in the list that any of them did.

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal does not release a horseman or a cosmic catastrophe. It releases silence. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the unceasing worship of chapters 4–7, after the thunder and lightning of the throne room, after the cries of the martyrs and the acclamation of the great multitude — silence. Heaven holds its breath. The silence of the seventh seal is more terrifying than any of the sounds that preceded it, because it signals that something of ultimate gravity is about to happen.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before the trumpets sound, another angel offers incense before the altar — and the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God. This is the answer to the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (“How long, O Lord?”): the prayers of God’s people are not lost. They have been gathered. They are being presented before the throne. And now fire from the altar is thrown to the earth — the prayers of the saints become the fire of divine judgment.

The trumpets follow the pattern of the Exodus plagues, but escalated. Hail, fire, blood — the first trumpet echoes the seventh plague of Egypt. The sea turning to blood — the second trumpet echoes the first plague. Darkness — the fourth trumpet echoes the ninth plague. The Exodus pattern is deliberate: the God who judged Egypt to liberate his people is now judging the new Egypt (Rome, Babylon) to liberate the new Israel (the church). The judgments of Revelation are not arbitrary cruelties; they are the exodus of the new covenant people on a cosmic scale.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the last seal is opened and nothing happens. There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Everything the reader has heard for four chapters — the ceaseless holy, holy, holy of the living creatures (4:8), the myriads crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12), a multitude nobody could number (7:10) — stops. Scripture repeatedly commands exactly this silence before God acts in judgment (Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13), and the crowd outside the temple prayed in silence while the incense was offered (Luke 1:10). Both are probably in view.

Verse 2: seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets — the second of the book’s three sevens. A trumpet in Israel sounded at Sinai (Ex. 19:16), brought down Jericho (Josh. 6:16–20), raised the alarm (Joel 2:1), announced Jubilee (Lev. 25:9) and will sound at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52).

Verses 3–4: before a trumpet sounds, another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints, and the smoke rises before God. This is the payoff of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls which John identified as those prayers. Three details matter: all the saints; the incense is added from the other side, so the prayers do not go up on their own account; and they arrive.

Verse 5 turns everything over. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, followed by thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake — the Sinai signs of 4:5 with an earthquake added. The same censer that carried the prayers up now carries fire down. The trumpets are the answer to the church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as the Mechanism of History

The martyrs under the altar cried how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? and were told to rest a little longer (6:10–11). Verse 5 is the little longer coming to an end. Prayer in this book is not a private exercise with private effects; it is the means by which the judgments of God are set in motion. The most powerless people in the empire — slaves, widows, boycotted tradesmen, prisoners awaiting a hearing — are shown to have been operating the levers of history from their knees the whole time, without knowing it and without seeing a single result.

Much Incense, Given

Verse 3 says the incense was given to the angel and offered with the prayers. Something is added to them at the altar before they rise. Anyone honest about praying knows his prayers are not impressive — the mind wanders, the motives are mixed, the words run out. This verse says they are not offered as they left the mouth. There is a mediator at the altar and incense in his hand, and it is his and not yours.

The Silence Is Not Absence

For a believer who has prayed about one thing for a year and heard nothing, this half hour says something about the nature of heaven’s quiet. It is the pause of a court before sentence, and it comes immediately before the prayers of the saints are carried up and then thrown back down as fire. God being quiet and God being idle are not the same thing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: When the censer of incense was offered in the temple, the whole congregation stood outside and prayed while the smoke went up, and nobody spoke. Luke describes it at the beginning of his Gospel. A congregation in Asia hearing chapter 8 read aloud would have recognised the scene immediately — and would then have heard the censer come back down.

Now: The commonest objection a Christian raises against his own prayer life is not doctrinal but experiential: it appears to do nothing. Verse 5 answers that with a picture rather than an argument. A man kneels by a bed at eleven at night, says something short and inadequate about a son who is not speaking to him, and gets up feeling that nothing has occurred. On the evidence of these verses, something has occurred. The words went up. They were mixed with much incense from the hand of another. They stood before God. And the fire on that altar comes back down.

That is the reason this chapter puts the censer before the trumpets. The judgments that follow are not an interruption to the prayers of the church. They are the reply.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

Everything in this book has been building to the opening of the last seal, and what happens is nothing. No trumpet, no throne, no announcement. Heaven stops.

Consider what has to stop for that sentence to be true, because the reader has been in this room for four chapters. The four living creatures have been saying holy, holy, holy day and night without ceasing since before the world was made (4:8). Myriads of myriads of angels have been crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12). A multitude nobody could number has been shouting that salvation belongs to God (7:10). All of it goes quiet. The most continuous sound in the universe is interrupted, and John — who has been describing thunder and voices and songs for four chapters — has nothing to write down.

Why? Several answers have been given and more than one of them is likely to be right.

The most probable is that this is the silence Scripture repeatedly commands before God acts in judgment. The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (Hab. 2:20). Be silent before the Lord GOD! For the day of the LORD is near (Zeph. 1:7). Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling (Zech. 2:13). In all three the silence is the hush before a verdict, and in all three what follows is God rising to act.

A second reading is bound up with the next four verses. When the censer of incense was offered in the temple, the crowd outside prayed in silence — Luke describes it exactly, the whole multitude praying outside at the hour of incense (Luke 1:10). And what happens immediately after this silence is an angel offering incense with the prayers of all the saints. On that reading heaven falls silent so that the prayers of the church can be heard.

Either way, and both may be true at once, the effect is the same. The silence is not empty. It is loaded.

For about half an hour. The vagueness of about in a book of exact numbers is itself striking; John is describing what it felt like, the way a man says a wait went on for about twenty minutes. And half an hour is long. Try it. Half an hour of silence in a room is close to unbearable, and it is very much longer than any pause in any human ceremony. Whatever is coming, heaven considers it worth stopping everything for.

And there is something here for the believer who has been on the other end of a silence — who has prayed for a year about the same thing and heard nothing back, and drawn the natural conclusion. This verse does not explain that experience away, but it does say something about the nature of heaven’s quiet. The silence here is not absence and it is not indifference. It is the pause of a court before sentence, and it comes immediately before the prayers of the saints are carried up and then thrown back down on the earth as fire. God being quiet and God being idle are not the same thing, and this half hour is the proof.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. The definite article — the seven angels — suggests a particular known order, and Jewish tradition named seven archangels who stood in the immediate presence of God; one of them introduces himself to Zechariah as Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). Their trumpets are the second of the book’s three sevens.

A trumpet in Israel was never a musical instrument in the modern sense. It sounded at Sinai, so loud that the people trembled (Ex. 19:16). It brought down the walls of Jericho on the seventh day (Josh. 6:16–20). It was the alarm blown when an army was coming (Joel 2:1). It announced the year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves went free (Lev. 25:9). And it will sound at the end, when the dead are raised (1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16). A trumpet means: attention, something is about to happen, and you cannot sleep through it.

But before a single trumpet is blown, the vision stops and does something else entirely. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne.

This is the payoff of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls of incense which John explained were the prayers of the saints. Now the incense is being burned. The picture comes straight from the temple: twice a day a priest went into the holy place and put incense on the golden altar in front of the veil, and the smoke went up while the congregation stood outside praying.

Three details in these two verses deserve slowing down for.

The first is all the saints. Not the prayers of the notable ones, not the prayers that were well phrased or persevered in longest. All of them — which includes prayers prayed by people who did not know how to pray, in the dark, badly, and then forgot about.

The second is much incense, and it is given to him. The prayers do not go up on their own account. Something is added to them at the altar, from the other side, before they rise. Any honest person who has prayed knows that his prayers are not impressive; the mind wanders, the motives are mixed, the words run out. What this verse says is that they are not offered as they left the mouth. There is a mediator at the altar, and there is incense in his hand, and it is his and not yours.

The third is the direction. And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel. They arrive. That is stated flatly, as a fact about what John saw. The prayers of the church reach the presence of God — not as a general principle, not as an encouragement, but as a thing happening in front of a man’s eyes while he watches.

Consider what that does to the ordinary experience of praying. A believer kneels by a bed at eleven at night, says something short and inadequate about a son who is not speaking to him, and gets up feeling that nothing has occurred. On the evidence of this verse, something has occurred. The words went up. They were mixed with much incense from the hand of another, and they stood before God, and God is not deaf and does not mislay things.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the verse turns, and it is one of the great surprises of the book.

Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.

The same censer. The one that a moment ago was carrying the prayers of all the saints up to God is now filled with fire from that same altar and hurled down. What went up as incense comes back as fire. The trumpets that follow are the answer to the church’s praying, and the answer arrives in the form of judgment on the world that made the praying necessary.

Go back and hear what those prayers had been. Under the altar in chapter 6, the martyrs cried O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? (6:10). They were told to rest a little longer. This is the little longer coming to an end. The how long of chapter 6 is answered by the censer of chapter 8, and the seven trumpets are the answering.

Take that as concretely as John means it. Prayer, in this book, is not a private spiritual exercise with private spiritual effects. It is the mechanism by which the judgments of God are set in motion. The most powerless people in the Roman empire — slaves, widows, boycotted tradesmen, prisoners awaiting a hearing — are shown to have been operating the levers of history from their knees the whole time, without knowing it and without seeing a single result.

Set that against the way praying usually feels. The commonest objection a Christian raises against his own prayer life is not doctrinal; it is that it appears to do nothing. Verse 5 answers that with a picture rather than an argument. The prayer that seemed to evaporate went into a golden bowl. The bowl went to an altar. The altar had fire on it. And the fire came back down.

The four phenomena that follow — thunder, rumblings, lightning, earthquake — are the Sinai signs from 4:5, where they came out of the throne. John will use this same list twice more, at 11:19 and 16:18, each time at a hinge in the book, each time with something added. Here the earthquake is new. It is his standing signal that God has begun to act.

And note who never leaves the room. The angel offers the incense, the angel fills the censer, the angel throws it — but the fire is from the altar, and the altar is before the throne. The seven trumpets do not begin because an angel decided something. They begin because the prayers of ordinary Christians reached the throne of God, and God answered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6: the seven angels prepare to blow. Verse 7: the first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, and a third of the earth, a third of the trees and all green grass are burned. Verses 8–9: the second brings something like a great mountain, burning, thrown into the sea — the image Jeremiah used of Babylon as a burnt mountain (Jer. 51:25) — and a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of its creatures die, a third of the ships are destroyed. For seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was the economy, not the scenery.

Verses 10–11: the third trumpet drops a blazing star, Wormwood, on the fresh water, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. Apsinthos is bitter rather than poisonous, and it is the prophets’ standing image for judgment that makes the sweet unswallowable (Jer. 9:15; 23:15; Lam. 3:19) — most pointedly in Amos, where men turn justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7) and here find their own wells undrinkable.

Verse 12: the fourth strikes a third of the sun, moon and stars, so that a third of the light is darkened — the ninth plague on Egypt (Ex. 10:21–23), aimed at a nation whose chief god was the sun and whose Pharaoh was his son.

Verse 13 closes with an eagle at the zenith, where everyone can see it, crying Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth — one woe for each trumpet still to come. Four trumpets have struck earth, sea, fresh water and sky, the whole created order. The remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire (Ex. 9:23–25), water to blood (Ex. 7:20–21), darkness (Ex. 10:21–23), locusts to come at the fifth trumpet (Ex. 10:12–15), and a sixth that ends with people refusing to repent exactly as Pharaoh did. The plagues on Egypt had two stated purposes: on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments (Ex. 12:12), and let my people go. Dressing the trumpets in exodus clothing tells seven small congregations something enormous — the empire grinding them is Egypt, the God who broke Egypt is not retired, and the purpose is the same: to expose the gods that cannot save, and to bring his people out.

A Third Is a Mercy

The word third beats through the sequence, five times in v. 12 alone. In chapter 6 the horsemen were given a fourth; here it is a third; at the bowls the limits come off. The escalation is the argument: these are not the end but warnings getting louder because they are not being heard, and 9:20 says so in as many words. Two thirds is untouched, and somebody is holding that line.

“Those Who Dwell on the Earth”

The eagle’s phrase becomes a technical term in this book, used about ten times, and it never means simply everyone alive. It means those whose whole account is settled here, who have no other citizenship and want none — the ones who in 6:16 would rather be crushed by a mountain than look at the face on the throne. The saints live on the earth too, and are never called earth-dwellers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Grain came to Asia from Egypt by ship, and Ephesus and Smyrna were harbours. A third of the sea life dead and a third of the ships destroyed is not an ecological note but a commercial collapse — the same merchants who will stand weeping at a distance in chapter 18 because no one buys their cargo any more (18:11), discovering that the system they trusted was never load-bearing.

Now: A caution that applies to the whole trumpet sequence. Every generation has matched these verses to its own headlines — volcanic ash, wildfire, chemical warfare, industrial pollution — and every generation has been confident and wrong. It is widely repeated that Chernobyl is the Ukrainian word for wormwood, and therefore that v. 11 is about 1986. The linguistic claim is roughly right; the interpretation is not. On that logic any place named after a bitter herb is a candidate, and the verse would have had nothing to say to the churches John wrote to, or to any generation before that year.

What is permanent about these images is not the mechanism but the argument: the created order turns against a humanity in rebellion against its Maker, the things people depend on become the things that fail them, and none of it happens outside the throne room. Notice what actually gets struck — not temples and armies, but the earth a man farms, the sea he trades on, the water he drinks and the light he works by. These judgments land on the ordinary infrastructure of confidence, the things that make it possible to believe tomorrow will be much like today.

And there is a plain word in v. 11 for anyone who has been made bitter. Wormwood is not lethal; it is unbearable, which is a different thing and in some ways worse. A person can live for decades on water made bitter — by an injustice never put right, a marriage that went wrong, a betrayal nobody was called to account for — and go on functioning, and never taste anything sweet again. Scripture takes that seriously enough to name a trumpet after it, and this book ends with a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, free to anyone who is thirsty (22:1, 17).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. One verse of pure anticipation. Seven angels lift seven trumpets. And then the first sounds, and what follows is the plagues of Egypt happening again on a larger stage.

That parallel governs the whole trumpet sequence and should be established at the start. The first trumpet brings hail and fire — the seventh plague (Ex. 9:23–25). The second turns a third of the sea to blood — the first plague (Ex. 7:20–21). The fourth darkens the lights — the ninth plague (Ex. 10:21–23). The fifth trumpet will bring locusts (Ex. 10:12–15), and the sixth will end with people refusing to repent, exactly as Pharaoh did.

The point of the parallel is not decoration. The plagues on Egypt were not random cruelty; they had two purposes, both stated in Exodus. They were aimed at the gods of Egypt — on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments (Ex. 12:12) — each plague striking at something Egypt worshipped. And they were aimed at getting a people out: let my people go. So when John dresses the trumpets in the clothes of the exodus, he is telling seven small congregations something enormous. The empire that is grinding you is Egypt. The God who broke Egypt is not retired. And the purpose of what is coming is the same purpose it was then: to expose the gods that cannot save, and to bring his people out.

The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.

Three things are struck: the land, the trees, the grass. And two of the three are measured. A third of the earth. A third of the trees. In chapter 6 the horsemen were given a fourth; here it is a third; at the bowls in chapter 16 the limits come off altogether. The judgments escalate in stages, and the escalation is the argument: these are not the end. They are warnings that get louder because they are not being heard, and chapter 9 will say so in as many words — the rest of mankind… did not repent (9:20).

A fraction is a mercy, and it is easy to read past. Two thirds of the earth is not burned. Somebody is holding the line at a third, and the same hand that holds it wrote the number down. Judgment that stops is judgment that still intends to be answered.

One caution about reading these verses, and it applies to the whole trumpet sequence. Every generation has matched them to its own headlines — volcanic ash, wildfire, chemical warfare, industrial pollution — and every generation has been confident and wrong. The images here are quarried from Exodus, not from the newspaper. What is permanent about them is not the mechanism but the argument: the created order itself turns against a humanity in rebellion against its Maker, the things people depend on become the things that fail them, and none of it happens outside the throne room. That was true in Egypt, it was true under Rome, and it has been true in every century since without needing to be decoded.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

Note the hesitation in the wording: something like a great mountain. John is again describing what he has no vocabulary for, and he says so rather than pretending. Whatever it was, it looked like a burning mountain and it went into the sea.

The image has an Old Testament address. Jeremiah, pronouncing doom on Babylon, wrote: Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain… I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain (Jer. 51:25). A mountain in prophetic language is a kingdom — something immovable, dominating the landscape, permanent. And the burning mountain thrown down is an empire coming to an end.

What is struck this time is the sea, and for the seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was not scenery. It was the economy. Ephesus and Smyrna were harbours. Grain came from Egypt by ship, and so did every luxury on the list that chapter 18 will read out over the fall of Babylon. A third of the sea life dead and a third of the ships destroyed is not primarily an ecological note; it is a commercial collapse. Trade routes fail, cargoes are lost, and the merchants of the earth — who in chapter 18 will stand weeping at a distance because no one buys their cargo any more (18:11) — discover that the system they trusted was never load-bearing.

And the sea in this book carries a further weight. It is where the beast comes from (13:1). It is the ancient image of chaos, restless and untameable, which is why the throne room has it frozen into glass under God’s feet (4:6), and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1). The second trumpet strikes the thing the world sails on and the thing the beast rises out of, and does it with a measured third.

There is a question a working reader will ask here, and it should be answered rather than avoided: what has any of this to do with me? The answer is in what gets hit. The trumpets do not fall on temples and armies. They fall on the earth a man farms, the sea a man trades on, the water a man drinks and the light a man works by. God’s judgments in this chapter land on the ordinary infrastructure of confidence — the things that make it possible to believe that tomorrow will be much like today.

Anyone who has watched a business fail, or a savings account evaporate in a crash he did not cause, has met the second trumpet in miniature. The point is not that such an event is a punishment aimed at that person; Scripture is careful about that (Luke 13:4–5). The point is what it reveals. Every one of these systems is holding up somebody’s confidence, and every one of them can be taken down by a third in a single afternoon. The only thing this book has shown that cannot be taken down is the throne, and it was shown first, on purpose, before any of this began.

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.

Fresh water this time — rivers and springs, the thing no settlement can exist without. And this is the first trumpet where the text says plainly that people died.

Wormwood is apsinthos, a shrub of the Middle East with an intensely bitter taste. It is not, in fact, poisonous; that is part of the point. In the Old Testament wormwood is the standing image for what happens when God’s judgment turns something sweet into something a person cannot swallow. Jeremiah twice records the Lord saying of a rebellious people, I will feed them with wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink (Jer. 9:15; 23:15). Lamentations describes affliction as wormwood and gall (Lam. 3:19). And Amos accuses those who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth (Amos 5:7).

That last one is the key to the trumpet. In Amos, men make justice bitter, and here God makes their water bitter. The judgment matches the crime exactly. A society that has poisoned what should have refreshed people finds its own wells undrinkable. This is the shape of divine judgment throughout Scripture: not an arbitrary penalty attached to an offence, but the offence itself, served back.

A word about a claim many readers will have met. It has been widely repeated that Chernobyl is the Ukrainian word for wormwood and that the 1986 disaster is therefore this verse. The linguistic claim is roughly right — the name relates to a variety of the plant — and the interpretation is not. On that logic, any place in the world named after a bitter herb becomes a candidate, and the verse would have nothing to say to the churches John actually wrote to, or to any generation between them and 1986. The trumpet is not a coded reference to one accident. It is the standing biblical picture of a world whose own water turns against it, and it has been true in every century, including that one.

And a third of the waters, again. Two thirds of the springs are still sweet. The restraint in this chapter is monotonous by design: a third, a third, a third, a third. Somebody is counting, and the counting is happening on the earth as well as in heaven.

There is a plain application in it for anyone who has been made bitter. Wormwood is not lethal; it is unbearable, which is a different thing and in some ways worse. A person can live for decades on water that has been made bitter — by an injustice never put right, by a marriage that went wrong, by a betrayal that nobody was ever called to account for — and go on functioning, and never taste anything sweet again. Scripture takes that condition seriously enough to name a trumpet after it. And this book ends with a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and free to anyone who is thirsty (22:1, 17).

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.

The word third occurs five times in one verse. The repetition is not clumsy writing; it is the drumbeat of the whole sequence, and by now a reader hearing this read aloud would be waiting for it.

The ninth plague on Egypt was a darkness that could be felt, lasting three days, so that nobody rose from his place — while the people of Israel had light where they lived (Ex. 10:21–23). And the gods being judged were unmistakable: Egypt worshipped the sun. Ra was the head of the pantheon, and Pharaoh was his son. To darken the sun over Egypt was to demonstrate publicly that the chief god of the empire could not keep his own lamp lit.

The same argument runs in the province of Asia. The emperor was routinely associated with the sun in imperial art and poetry; Nero had himself depicted with the sun’s rays around his head. And the heavenly bodies were what everyone in the ancient world steered by, planted by, and read their fortunes by. The fourth trumpet strikes the calendar, the compass and the horoscope in a single stroke.

What is being taken away, in other words, is not light in general but reliable light — the confidence that the day will behave as days have always behaved. There is something more disturbing about a sun that is a third dimmer than about no sun at all. Total darkness announces itself as a catastrophe. A partial failure of the light is worse, because it says that the machinery is not as fixed as everyone assumed, and nobody can be sure what it will do next.

Then the chapter ends with a warning nobody could sleep through. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

An eagle, alone in the sky at the zenith, where everyone on the ground can see it. The Greek word covers both the eagle and the vulture, and both associations are working: the eagle was the standard of the Roman legions, and the vulture is what circles above the dying. Jesus used the same ambiguity: wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matt. 24:28).

Three woes, one for each of the three trumpets still to come, and the escalation is explicit. Four trumpets have struck the earth, the sea, the fresh water and the sky — the whole created order, in the four-part division the ancient world used. The remaining three will not fall on the environment. They will fall on people, and chapter 9 opens the shaft of the bottomless pit.

And the phrase the eagle uses is one to watch, because it becomes a technical term in this book: those who dwell on the earth. It occurs about ten times, and it never means simply everyone alive. It means the people whose whole account is settled here, who have no other citizenship and want none — the ones who, in 6:16, would rather be crushed by a mountain than look at the face on the throne. The saints in this book live on the earth too. They are never called earth-dwellers.

So the eagle’s cry is a mercy in the shape of a threat. It is announced in advance, in daylight, at the top of the sky, in a loud voice, to people who still have time to do something about it. Every warning in Revelation is an act of patience, and the God who sends an eagle across the sky before the fifth trumpet is not a God who wants anybody caught unawares.
