And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.<sup>8</sup>The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood.<sup>9</sup>A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.<sup>10</sup>The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.<sup>11</sup>The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.<sup>12</sup>The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.<sup>13</sup>Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is among the most vivid and terrifying in Revelation. The fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss — creatures drawn from Joel 2 and shaped like scorpions, with the faces of humans and the hair of women and the teeth of lions. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the great Euphrates river, who command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The devastation escalates from the bounded third of the earlier trumpets to something more comprehensive and more personal: now humanity itself is directly targeted.

The two woe-trumpets of chapter 9 share a common theme: demonic power unleashed. The fifth trumpet releases the army of the abyss, led by “the angel of the bottomless pit” whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon — “Destroyer.” The sixth releases an army from beyond the Euphrates — the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies (Assyria, Babylon) had always come. The locust-army of the fifth trumpet torments but does not kill; the cavalry of the sixth kills a third of humanity. The escalation is purposeful: God is turning up the pressure on a world that refuses to repent.

The chapter’s most sobering verse is its final one: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent.” The purpose of the trumpet judgments — like the purpose of the Exodus plagues — was to break the hardness of heart that keeps humanity from turning to God. Pharaoh’s hardness repeated in every generation: even faced with the unmistakable signs of divine judgment, even watching a third of their companions die, the survivors “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons.” The judgment does not automatically produce repentance; only grace can break what judgment cannot.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a star fallen from heaven — a perfect participle, an event already complete — who is immediately a he, and who was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opens it, and before anything comes out the light goes: smoke like the smoke of a great furnace darkens the sun and the air (cf. Gen. 19:28).

Verses 3–4: locusts come up out of the smoke with the power of scorpions — and are told not to touch grass, plant or tree, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Their only target is those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads: the first cash-out of chapter 7, and the doorpost of the Exodus Passover moved from the house to the person (cf. Ex. 8:22; 10:23).

Verses 5–6: they are allowed to torment for five months — about the life cycle of a locust swarm — but not to kill. And then the hardest sentence in the chapter: people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them (cf. Job 3:21; Jer. 8:3).

Verses 7–10 describe them in nine comparisons, seven of which begin with like: horses prepared for battle (Joel 2:4), what looked like crowns of gold, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth (Joel 1:6), iron breastplates, wings like many chariots, and scorpion tails in which their power to hurt resides.

Verses 11–12: Proverbs 30:27 says locusts have no king; these have one — the angel of the bottomless pit, named in both languages, Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction, Job 26:6; 28:22; Prov. 15:11) and Apollyon (Greek for destroyer). Then a line of bookkeeping: the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything Here Is on a Permission

He was given the key. They were told what not to harm. They were allowed five months. The divine passive has governed every judgment since chapter 6, and it answers a fear thoughtful Christians carry more often than they admit — that good and evil are two matched powers wrestling for the world with the outcome genuinely uncertain. Revelation never allows it. The destroyer is the subject of passive verbs; there is only one place in this book where keys are kept (1:18); and the abyss has a shaft, which means it has a mouth, and a mouth can be shut.

Abaddon, Apollyon, and Domitian

The Greek name almost certainly carries a barb the first hearers would have caught. One of the emblems of the god Apollo was the locust, and the emperor Domitian — under whom this letter was most likely written — presented himself as Apollo’s earthly manifestation. Naming the king of the abyss Apollyon tells a Christian in Ephesus that the god the empire boasts in has a name one letter from destroyer, and that what he actually rules is a pit. And destruction is the whole of his competence: he makes nothing. Set that beside 4:11 — you created all things — and the asymmetry is total.

What the Seal Does Not Do

The seal of v. 4 does not exempt anyone from the great tribulation; 7:14 says they came out of it, and it did not spare the martyrs of 6:9. What it does is set a boundary on what can be done to a sealed person, and the boundary was drawn before the shaft was opened. Christians get cancer, lose jobs, are lied about and die. What the seal guarantees is that nothing reaches past it to touch what they actually are.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A locust swarm is heard before it is seen — a dry roar filling the whole sky — and people who lived through one described the sound as the thing they never forgot. Joel had built a prophecy on it. John takes the most feared plague in the ancient world and makes every detail wrong: locusts that will not eat grass, horses that are not horses, crowns that are only like crowns. Every category the mind reaches for slips, which is what comes up out of the abyss.

Now: Verse 6 is a verse some readers will study from the outside and others will recognise as a country they have lived in. There are Christians who have lain awake wishing quite specifically not to wake up. If that is you, this verse is not describing your condemnation and must not be allowed to sound as though it is.

Three things stand. Wanting to die is not the same as being abandoned by God, and Scripture proves it by the company — Job wanted it, Moses asked God to kill him (Num. 11:15), Elijah asked to die the day after the greatest victory of his life (1 Kings 19:4), and Jonah asked twice; God rebuked none of them for it, and fed Elijah and let him sleep.

The torment here falls expressly on those who do not have the seal of God (v. 4) — it is the logical end of refusing him, not a warning to his own struggling children. And despair says the darkness is permanent and there is no door; this whole book announces a door opened from the other side at enormous cost, by someone who holds the keys of Death and Hades. Anyone in that territory should say so out loud to another Christian this week rather than carry it alone. That is what the body of Christ is for.

And the last word of the section is the first woe has passed. The five months ended. Every affliction in this book is announced, measured, and then reported finished, by someone who has never once lost count.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four trumpets have struck the earth, the sea, the fresh water and the sky. An eagle has crossed the sky crying three woes. Now the fifth sounds, and the target changes: from here on the trumpets fall on people.

And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit.

The grammar does half the work. John does not say he saw a star fall; he saw a star fallen — a perfect participle, describing a completed event whose result is still standing. The falling is not happening in front of him. It happened, and this is the aftermath. And the star is immediately a he: the pronoun switches from an object to a person in the same sentence.

Who is he? Two readings are held. Many take this to be Satan, and the case is strong: Jesus said I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18); Isaiah’s taunt against the king of Babylon — How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! (Isa. 14:12) — has been read that way since the early church; and in 12:9 this book will describe the dragon being thrown down to the earth. Others take him to be an angel on commission, since 20:1 shows an angel coming down from heaven with the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain, and that one is plainly no enemy.

The text does not settle it, and on the point that matters it does not need to. He was given the key. Whoever holds it received it, and there is only one place in this book where keys are kept: I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Even the opening of the abyss is a delegated act. Nothing gets out of that shaft on its own authority.

The bottomless pit is abyssos — the abyss, the deep. In the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2 and for the waters under the earth. In the New Testament it is where demons are kept and where they do not want to go: the legion in the Gerasene man begged Jesus not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31). Peter and Jude both describe rebel angels held in gloomy chains until judgment (2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 6). And it has a shaft — a well, a narrow neck — which means it has a mouth, and a mouth can be shut. It is shut for the whole of history except when it is opened, and it is opened by permission.

From the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft. Before anything comes out, the light goes. That is the first effect of the abyss being opened, and it is exactly right as a description of what evil does. It does not usually arrive arguing. It arrives as a haze — things that were clear stop being clear, distinctions that used to be obvious go soft, and after a while nobody can see far enough to be sure of anything.

The comparison is to a furnace, and the reader is meant to hear Sodom, where Abraham looked down and saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace (Gen. 19:28). The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun by direct judgment. The fifth darkens it by pollution from below. Both take the light; only one of them comes up out of a hole.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth.

Locusts were the standard ancient image of total devastation, and Joel had built a whole prophecy on them: an army of locusts that darkens the land, runs like war-horses, leaps over walls, and leaves a garden of Eden looking like a desert behind it (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11). Anyone who has seen a swarm knows why the image works. There is nothing to fight. They come as a shadow on the horizon, and when they lift there is nothing green left standing.

But these locusts are wrong in every particular, and the wrongness is the point. They come out of the abyss rather than off the fields. They are given the power of scorpions, which locusts do not have. And the next verse tells them not to touch a single blade of grass, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Whatever John is describing, it is not an infestation. It is what comes up when the pit is opened, wearing the shape of the most feared plague in the ancient world.

A scorpion’s sting is rarely fatal to a healthy adult, and it is agonising. Rehoboam threatened Israel with it as an image of intensified cruelty (1 Kings 12:11). The comparison sets the terms for the whole trumpet: this is a judgment that does not kill, and is not therefore a lesser judgment.

They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

Three restrictions in one verse, and the pattern of the whole book is in them. They were told — the divine passive again, which has governed every judgment since chapter 6. There is a fence around the vegetation. And there is a fence around people, drawn along one line: the seal of God.

This is the first time the sealing of chapter 7 is cashed out, and what it does and does not do needs care. It does not exempt anybody from the great tribulation; 7:14 said they came out of it. It did not spare the martyrs under the altar. What it does is set a limit on what can be done to a sealed person and by whom. The powers that come up out of the abyss have a list, and the list has a boundary, and the boundary was drawn before the shaft was opened.

Behind this is Egypt again. When the plagues fell, God drew a line through the land: I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there (Ex. 8:22), and in the darkness all the people of Israel had light where they lived (Ex. 10:23). And when the destroyer went through at the Passover, the doorposts of the sealed households were marked with blood. The seal on the forehead in Revelation is the doorpost of Exodus, moved from the house to the person.

Which is where a believer’s honest fear should be answered rather than flattered. The seal is not a promise that nothing will happen to you. Christians get cancer, lose jobs, are lied about, go to prison, and die. What the seal guarantees is that nothing can reach past it to touch what you actually are. There are torments in this chapter that go on for five months and cannot be escaped, and a marked person is not on the list, and the reason is not his courage.

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone.

Allowed — again. And two boundaries: a duration and a limit. They may torment; they may not kill. Five months, and not a day more.

Why five months? The most likely answer is the plainest one: the life cycle of a locust swarm, from hatching to death, is about five months, roughly May to September. The number is not a code. It means one locust season — a real, bounded, recognisable stretch of time with a beginning and an end that everybody in an agricultural society could measure. It will feel endless while it lasts. It is not endless.

Then verse 6, which is the most terrible sentence in the chapter and one of the hardest in the Bible: And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.

Job said something close to it out of his own ash-heap, of people who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures (Job 3:21). Jeremiah said the survivors of a judged nation would choose death rather than life (Jer. 8:3). This is the condition in which existence itself has become the punishment, and there is no exit, because the one exit a person would take has been closed.

Some readers will read that verse from the outside as a description of a future horror. Others will read it and recognise the country. There are Christians who have lain awake and wished quite specifically not to wake up, who have found that the only thing they could imagine wanting was for it to stop. If that is you, this verse is not describing your condemnation, and it should not be allowed to sound as though it is.

Three things need saying plainly. First, wanting to die is not the same as being abandoned by God, and Scripture proves it by the company: Job wanted it, Moses asked God to kill him (Num. 11:15), Elijah sat under a tree and asked to die the day after the greatest victory of his life (1 Kings 19:4), and Jonah asked twice. God did not rebuke one of them for it. He fed Elijah and let him sleep.

Second, look at who is in this verse and who is not. The torment of verse 5 falls expressly on those who do not have the seal of God (v. 4). This is a judgment on people who have refused God and are being handed the logical end of that refusal — existence without him — not a warning issued to his own children who are struggling.

Third, the direction of travel matters. Despair says the darkness is permanent and there is no door. This whole book is the announcement that there is a door, that it has been opened from the other side at enormous cost, and that the one who opened it personally holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Death does not have the last word on anybody who belongs to him. Anyone in this territory should say so out loud to another Christian this week, and not carry it alone; that is not weakness, it is what the body of Christ is for.

And the horror of the verse, rightly read, is not that God is cruel. It is that there is a state worse than dying, and that human beings can arrive at it by their own steady choosing. The most merciful thing in the chapter is that it has a five-month fence around it, and that the fence was put there by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the description, and it is deliberately impossible to draw. John piles up nine comparisons in four verses, and seven of them begin with like or as. He is not filing a report on a species. He is telling a congregation what it felt like to look at.

In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. Joel said the same: their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like war horses they run (Joel 2:4). Anyone who has looked closely at a locust knows why: the head is startlingly like a horse’s in miniature, and the Italian and German words for the insect both mean little horse.

On their heads were what looked like crowns of gold. Not crowns — what looked like crowns. This is a counterfeit, and John will not let it pass for the real thing. Everything in this book that is genuinely crowned is crowned by God.

Their faces were like human faces, their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth. Three details in ascending order of menace. The human face is the worst of them: whatever this is, it has intelligence and intention, and it looks back at you. The long hair suggests the streaming antennae of a locust and perhaps, to a first-century ear, the loose hair of a warrior. The lions’ teeth are Joel again, of the locust nation with the teeth of a lion (Joel 1:6).

They had breastplates like breastplates of iron — there is no attacking them; nothing gets through. And the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. A locust swarm is heard before it is seen, a dry roar that fills the whole sky, and people who have lived through one describe the sound as the thing they never forgot.

They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails. The sting is in the back end, and the sixth trumpet will repeat it: those horses too have power in their tails (9:19). Twice in one chapter the injury comes from behind, after the thing has apparently passed. That is a fair description of how a great deal of evil actually works. The damage is rarely done at the moment of the encounter. It is done afterwards, by what was left in the wound.

Stand back from the portrait and the effect is exactly what John intends. It has a man’s face and a lion’s teeth. It wears armour and a crown that is not a crown. It is a locust that will not eat grass and a horse that is not a horse. Every category the mind reaches for slips. That is what comes up out of the abyss, and it is why every generation that has tried to identify these creatures with a particular weapon — cavalry, cannon, helicopters, drones — has been confident and has been left behind by the next generation’s equally confident identification.

What is permanent here is not the mechanism. It is the anatomy of spiritual evil given a body: intelligent, armoured, unkillable by the people it torments, crowned with an authority it did not earn, deafening, and stinging from behind. A congregation in Pergamum living under the shadow of Satan’s throne did not need the picture decoded. They needed to be told that it comes up on a permission and goes down on a timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon.

Proverbs says that locusts have no king (Prov. 30:27), and it is one of the things that makes a swarm so unnerving — a vast coordinated destruction with nobody in charge. These locusts have one. The chaos is organised, and it has a commander, and John gives his name twice so that neither half of his congregation misses it.

Abaddon is Hebrew for destruction, and in the Old Testament it is a name for the realm of the dead, paired with Sheol and with the grave: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering (Job 26:6; cf. Job 28:22; Prov. 15:11). Apollyon is the Greek participle meaning the destroyer, the one who ruins. The two names say the same thing in two languages, which is John’s way of saying that this figure is not a local problem.

There is very probably a barb in the Greek name that the first hearers would have caught at once. The god Apollo was one of the great deities of the Greek world, and one of his emblems was the locust. More to the point, the emperor Domitian — under whom this letter was almost certainly written — presented himself as Apollo’s earthly manifestation, and imperial propaganda made the association freely. So when John names the king of the abyss Apollyon, a Christian in Ephesus hearing it read out would have made the connection without being told: the god the empire boasts in has a name one letter away from destroyer, and the thing he actually rules is a pit.

And that is the only thing this figure can do. Not create, not build, not make anything at all. His entire competence is destruction, and his name is his job description. Set that beside the one seated on the throne, whose title in chapter 4 is you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created, and the asymmetry is total. One of these two makes things out of nothing. The other unmakes what somebody else made, and can be shut in a shaft.

Which is the answer to a fear that troubles thoughtful Christians more than they usually admit — the sense that good and evil are two roughly matched powers wrestling for the world, with the outcome genuinely uncertain. Revelation never allows it. The destroyer is a subject in a passive sentence: he is given a key, he is allowed five months, he is told what he may not touch. He is not the opposite number of God. He is a creature with a leash and a name.

The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come. A single verse of bookkeeping, and it does two things. It confirms that the eagle’s three woes in 8:13 map onto the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets. And it says has passed. The five months ended. Whatever came up out of that shaft went back down, and John is already speaking of it in the past tense while two more are still to come.

That is not a small thing to say to people who are inside something. Every affliction in this book is announced, measured, and then reported finished. The one who keeps the register is the one who holds the keys, and he has never once lost count.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–14: the sixth trumpet, and a voice from the four horns of the golden altar — the incense altar, where the prayers of all the saints were offered in 8:3–4 and from which fire was thrown down in 8:5. The order it gives is Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. They are bound; they must be released; the order comes from the altar where the church prays. The Euphrates was the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from.

Verse 15: the four had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year — one article in the Greek governs all four, so this is a fixed moment rather than a duration — and are released to kill a third of mankind. The fraction has moved from things to people. Verse 16 gives the number of mounted troops as twice ten thousand times ten thousand, with the telling clause I heard their number, exactly as at 7:4.

Verses 17–19: breastplates the colour of fire, sapphire and sulfur — the same three things the horses breathe. Lions’ heads; fire, smoke and sulfur from their mouths, the substance of Sodom (Gen. 19:24) and of the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10). A third of mankind killed by these three plagues. And the power is in mouths and in tails, the tails being like serpents with heads — the word John reserves for the dragon (12:9; 20:2).

Verses 20–21 give the verdict the whole sequence was building toward. The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent — not of the works of their hands, not of worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood which cannot see or hear or walk (Ps. 115:4–8), and not of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality or thefts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar Where the Church Prays

Three times in two chapters John makes the same connection: the incense of the saints’ prayers (8:3–4), the fire from that altar thrown down (8:5), and now the voice from its horns releasing the sixth trumpet. The judgments of God on the world are not arbitrary spasms; they are the answer to the praying of his people, issued from the place where that praying is received. The horns were where a man grasped for refuge (1 Kings 1:50) and where atoning blood was smeared (Lev. 4:7).

A Diary Entry, Not an Accident

Verse 15 is the most steadying sentence in the chapter. The four angels were prepared — made ready and standing ready — for the hour of the day in the month of the year. The catastrophe that arrives without warning and seems to prove nobody is steering carries a time stamp applied in advance. That is not to say the catastrophe is good; Scripture never says so. It is to say that history is not a series of accidents occasionally interrupted by providence.

Two Hundred Million

A myriad was the largest number Greek had a word for, so a myriad of myriads is the language reaching its ceiling (5:11; Dan. 7:10), and doubling it is not a census. The clause that fixes it is I heard their number — John did not count, he was told, exactly as with the 144,000 at 7:4. A reader who takes one of those figures as overwhelming completeness should take the other the same way. The population of the whole Roman empire was perhaps sixty million.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The terror on Rome’s eastern frontier was Parthia, the one power Rome had never subdued, whose mounted archers had destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae and who were famous for shooting backwards over the horse’s rump as they rode away. A reader in Asia hearing about cavalry from beyond the Euphrates whose power was in their tails would have needed no explanation — and would then have heard that the whole host was tied up, on the far side of the river, waiting for a word from an altar.

Now: Verses 20–21 answer a question a great many people carry unspoken: surely if God made himself unmistakable, people would believe. Send a real catastrophe and the world would turn. Revelation says it has been tried. The sky has gone dark, the water has turned bitter, a third of the human race has died, and the survivors go back to what they were doing. Suffering hardens as often as it softens, and Pharaoh — whose plagues these are — is the standing proof: after every one of the ten he hardened his heart, and the last thing he did was drive into a sea that had opened.

The sting in the psalm John quotes is its last clause: those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:8). You become what you worship. Serve something blind and deaf and in the end you cannot see or hear either — which is precisely what this chapter has described. And note that sorceries is pharmakeia: magic, spells, and the drugs used in them. It is not a verse about medicine, and reading it that way misuses it. What it names is the attempt to control life, luck, love and death by technique instead of by trusting God.

There is a test here that is more searching than it looks, and it is not do I own a statue? An idol is whatever you would be unable to give up. Take the thing you have already been warned about — by your body, by your bank, by your wife, by a friend who took a risk in saying it — and notice how expertly you have explained the warning away. That is verse 20 happening in a life, at a scale where it can still be repented of. The whole chapter is finally about a door that stayed open and was not used: the judgments were fractional so that somebody would be left to turn, and the last word is that they did not repent — not that they could not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God.

Of all the places a command could come from, this is the one that matters. The golden altar is the incense altar, and the reader has been there twice already. In 8:3–4 an angel stood at it and offered much incense with the prayers of all the saints. In 8:5 the fire from that altar was thrown down on the earth. Now a voice speaks out of its four horns, and what it says releases the sixth trumpet.

The horns of an altar were the four projections at its corners, and they were the part a man grasped when he fled to the sanctuary claiming protection (1 Kings 1:50–51). Blood was smeared on them at the great atoning sacrifices (Lev. 4:7–18). They were the place of refuge and the place of blood. The order to release four destroying angels comes from between the horns of the altar where the prayers of the church are burned.

That is the third time in two chapters the same connection has been made, and it is the argument the trumpets exist to make. The judgments of God on the world are not arbitrary spasms. They are the answer to the praying of his people, issued from the place where that praying is received. A congregation that has prayed for years about wickedness that nobody seems to be doing anything about is being told where its prayers went and what they are doing.

Saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

Two things. They are bound — and have been, presumably for a long time, since somebody had to bind them. And they must be released, by an order, from an altar, at a specified moment. The reader is now four chapters into a pattern that does not vary: nothing hostile in this universe moves except on a permission, and every permission is issued from the throne room.

The Euphrates was the eastern boundary of the Roman empire and the frontier of Israel’s world before that. Every invasion that ever destroyed Jerusalem came from beyond it: Assyria, then Babylon. In John’s own day the terror on that frontier was Parthia, the one power Rome had never subdued, whose mounted archers had annihilated a Roman army at Carrhae and whose cavalry was the standing nightmare of the eastern provinces. To say the Euphrates to a first-century reader was to say what the border says in any country that has been invaded across one. It is the direction the end comes from.

And on the far side of that river, in this vision, are four angels who have been tied up and are now being untied by name. Whatever a reader thinks about the invasions of history, this verse says something specific about all of them: the horde crossing the border was on a rope, and the rope was in God’s hand, and the hand let go at a moment of its own choosing.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind.

Four units of time, and the Greek has a single article governing all four, which makes them one appointed moment rather than a span. Not for a year and a month and a day and an hour, as though the killing lasted that long. For the hour, which falls on the day, in the month, of the year. This is a diary entry.

Sit with the implication, because it is the single most steadying sentence in the chapter. There is a moment fixed for this, and it was fixed before the angels were bound. They were prepared for it — a perfect participle again, made ready and standing ready. The catastrophe that arrives without warning and appears to prove that nobody is steering has a time stamp on it, and the stamp was applied in advance.

That is not the same as saying the catastrophe is good, and Scripture never says so. It is saying that history is not a series of accidents interrupted occasionally by providence. Every hour in it has been counted, including the ones nobody would have chosen.

And the fraction moves again. The horsemen of chapter 6 had a fourth. The first four trumpets took a third of the earth, the sea, the water and the light. Now a third of mankind. The judgments are escalating from things to people, and still — still — two thirds are untouched, and the reason will be stated with brutal clarity in verse 20.

The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.

Two hundred million, if it is arithmetic. It is almost certainly not. A myriad — ten thousand — was the largest number Greek had a word for, so a myriad of myriads is the language reaching its ceiling, and John has used it already of the angels around the throne (5:11) and Daniel before him of the attendants of the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7:10). Doubling it is not a census; it is a way of saying and then twice that again. The population of the entire Roman empire was perhaps sixty million.

The detail that fixes it is the last clause: I heard their number. John did not count them and does not claim to have. He was told, and he is reporting what he was told, exactly as he did with the 144,000 in 7:4 — I heard the number of the sealed. The two numbers are given the same way, and a reader who takes one as a figure of overwhelming completeness should take the other the same way.

What the number is doing is a matter of proportion. The church in Asia was a few thousand people in seven towns, meeting in houses, with no standing whatever. The forces arrayed against them are being described in a figure that runs off the end of the counting system. And the whole of that host is on the wrong side of a river, tied up, waiting for a word from an altar.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them. John reminds the reader, in the middle of the description, that this is a vision. He is not claiming to have watched cavalry through a telescope.

They wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur. Three colours: red, dark blue, and the sickly yellow of brimstone. And they are the colours of the three things that come out of the horses’ mouths in the next clause — fire, smoke and sulfur. The riders are wearing what the horses breathe.

And the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. Sulfur is theion, brimstone, and in Scripture it has one address: the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven (Gen. 19:24). It is the smell of judgment, and this book will use it again for the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8). What comes out of these mouths is the substance of hell.

By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed. The word for the three is plagues — the Exodus vocabulary, which has governed the whole trumpet sequence. And the killing is done by what proceeds out of a mouth, which in this book is never accidental: the weapon of Christ is the sword that proceeds from his mouth (1:16; 19:15). Two mouths, two kinds of word, and both of them decisive. What comes out of a mouth kills or saves, and there is no third category.

For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.

Twice now the tail has been the dangerous end — the scorpion-locusts of verse 10 and these horses. And here the tails are given heads of their own. It is a grotesque image and a precise one: the thing bites in both directions, and the second bite comes after you have decided it has gone past.

The word for serpents is opheis, and in this book that word has a single owner: the dragon is that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan (12:9; 20:2). John has quietly signed the picture. Whatever historical shape this army takes — and Parthian archers were famous precisely for shooting backwards over the horse’s rump as they rode away, which any reader in Asia would have thought of at once — the tail that stings from behind belongs to the serpent.

That is a fair description of how ruin actually arrives in a life, and it should be said plainly for the reader who is living in the aftermath of something. The moment of the encounter is rarely the moment of the damage. The affair ended years ago; the consequences are only now walking through the door. The drink was put down; the liver was not consulted. The words were said in one bad evening; the son has not called since. Evil does its worst work with its back turned, and the person it wounds usually thought the danger had passed.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the sentence the whole trumpet sequence has been building toward, and it is the most sobering diagnosis of the human heart in the New Testament.

The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

Start with the two words that carry the weight: the rest. Two thirds of mankind survived. Every fraction in the last four chapters — a fourth, a third, a third, a third — existed for the sake of the people who were left, and this verse says what the survivors did with the mercy of being alive. They did not repent.

That is the answer to a question a great many people carry, usually unspoken: surely if God made himself unmistakable, people would believe. Send a real catastrophe, something undeniable, and the world would turn. Revelation says it has been tried. The sky has gone dark, the water has turned bitter, a third of the human race has died, and the survivors go back to what they were doing. Suffering does not automatically produce repentance. It hardens as often as it softens, and Pharaoh — whose plagues these are — is the standing proof: after every one of the ten he hardened his heart, and the last thing he did was drive into a sea that had opened.

What they will not give up is listed in two groups, and the order is not accidental. First, the idols. John pauses to describe them with what can only be called contempt: gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk. It is a quotation of the Psalms almost word for word — they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see… those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:4–8; cf. Dan. 5:23). The last clause of that psalm is the sting. You become like what you worship. Worship something blind and deaf, and in the end you cannot see or hear either — which is exactly what this chapter has just described.

And John says these idols are demons. Paul said the same about meat sacrificed in temples: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Cor. 10:20). The statue is wood. What is being served through it is not nothing.

Then the second list, and it is startlingly ordinary: murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, thefts. Four sins, and the second needs a word. Sorceries is pharmakeia, from which we get pharmacy — it covered magic, spells and the drugs and potions used in them. It is not a verse about medicine, and reading it that way is a misuse. What it names is the attempt to control life, luck, love and death by technique rather than by trusting God: pay the right practitioner, use the right substance, say the right words, and bend reality your way.

Set the two lists together and the diagnosis is complete. Idolatry is the root; murder, manipulation, immorality and theft are the fruit. A person who has replaced God will end up destroying his neighbour’s life, body, marriage or property, because there is nothing left to stop him. And none of these four is exotic. Every one of them is available on an ordinary Tuesday.

There is a test in this verse that a reader can run on himself, and it is more searching than it looks. It is not do I own a statue? An idol is whatever you would be unable to give up. Take the thing you have already been warned about — by your body, by your bank, by your wife, by a friend who took a risk in saying it — and notice how expertly you have explained the warning away. That is verse 20 happening in a life, at a scale where it can still be repented of.

Because the whole chapter is finally about a door that stayed open and was not used. The judgments were fractional so there would be somebody left to turn. The trumpets were warnings and not the end. An eagle flew overhead in daylight shouting three woes before the first of them landed. God went to extraordinary lengths to be heard, and the last word of the chapter is that they did not repent — not that they could not.

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the second great interlude of Revelation — this one inserted between the sixth and seventh trumpets (as chapter 7 was inserted between the sixth and seventh seals). The interlude performs the same function: it pauses the judgment sequence to reorient the reader to the prophetic commission of the church. Before the seventh trumpet sounds and the final woe arrives, John is given a little scroll to eat and recommissioned to prophesy.

A mighty angel descends from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun, his legs like pillars of fire — imagery that deliberately echoes the description of Christ in chapter 1. He stands on sea and land (claiming sovereignty over the whole earth), holds a little open scroll, and cries out with a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders respond — and John is told not to write what the thunders said. This is the only thing in Revelation that is sealed rather than revealed: some of God’s purposes remain hidden until their time.

John eats the little scroll at the angel’s command. It is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach — an echo of Ezekiel’s commissioning (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3) and Jeremiah’s experience of the word (Jeremiah 15:16). The word of God is sweet to receive — it is the good news of grace, the promise of the kingdom, the comfort of the gospel. But the prophetic task is bitter: to speak God’s word to a world that does not want to hear it, to witness to the truth in the face of hostility, to suffer for the testimony of Jesus. The whole book of Revelation is this little scroll: sweet with the glory of the Lamb, bitter with the suffering of faithful witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mighty angel of chapter 10 is one of the most majestic figures in Revelation. His description borrows directly from the vision of Christ in chapter 1 (face like the sun, voice like thunder) and from the description of God’s theophany in the Old Testament (cloud, rainbow, pillars of fire). Whether this is Christ himself or a high-ranking angel reflecting the glory of the one he represents is debated — the Reformed consensus tends to see him as a glorious angel, since the book distinguishes between Christ and angels throughout; but the christological imagery is unmistakable. Whatever the identity, the angel’s appearance announces that what is about to happen carries the full weight of divine authority.

The seven thunders that speak after the angel’s lion-roar are a unique feature of this vision. John is about to write what they said — and is told not to. The sealed thunders are a reminder that not everything about God’s governance of history is disclosed. Revelation is an unveiling, but it is not a total disclosure. Some things remain sealed. Deuteronomy 29:29 applies: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever.” The Christian interpreter must resist the temptation to speculate about the sealed thunders — if God chose not to reveal them, the appropriate response is worship, not curiosity.

The angel’s oath (vv. 5–7) is one of the most solemn moments in the book: he swears by the living Creator that “there will be no more delay.” When the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he announced to his servants the prophets. The delay is over. The patience of God that has held back judgment for the sake of the elect will be exhausted. The “mystery of God” that will be fulfilled is the redemptive plan announced through the prophets — the new creation, the final kingdom, the consummation of all things in Christ. This is the end of the delay, not the end of hope.

The eating of the scroll completes John’s recommissioning. He must “prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.” The book of Revelation does not end at chapter 10; the prophetic task continues. The sweet-and-bitter experience of the scroll is the experience of every Christian who has genuinely engaged with the word of God: the sweetness of the gospel in the heart, the bitterness of the cost of faithful witness in the world. These two are inseparable. You cannot have the sweetness without accepting the bitterness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sealed thunders raise the question of divine hiddenness alongside divine revelation. Revelation is the great book of divine disclosure — the apokalypsis, the unveiling. But within the unveiling, something remains sealed. God reveals what we need for faithful endurance; he does not reveal everything. This is the epistemological shape of the Christian life: we know enough to trust, not enough to be self-sufficient. “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully” (1 Corinthians 13:12). The humility to leave some things sealed is part of the posture of faith.

The angel’s oath by the Creator recalls God’s oath in Genesis 22 and the oath of Hebrews 6:13–18 — God swearing by himself because there is no higher authority. The solemnity of the oath signals that the declaration of “no more delay” is absolutely certain. God’s patience is real and genuinely prolonged; it is also finite. The interplay between God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9) and God’s decisive action at the appointed time is the rhythm of redemptive history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bitter-sweet scroll is the experience of every preacher and witness. The gospel is “the sweetness of the knowledge of him” (2 Corinthians 2:14–16) — and it is the aroma of death to those who are perishing. Speaking truth costs. Prophesying “about many peoples and nations and languages and kings” means confronting powers that would prefer silence. John is recommissioned for this task not after the suffering has ended but in the middle of it. The church is always being recommissioned in the middle of the battle.

The sealed thunders are the comfort of every believer facing a question about suffering that has no answer. God knows what the thunders said. He has not revealed it. But he has revealed enough: the Lamb is on the throne, the scroll is being opened, the delay will end, the mystery of God will be fulfilled. That is sufficient for faithful endurance, even without knowing everything. The Christian’s confidence is not in having all the answers but in knowing the one who holds all the answers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land, and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mighty angel’s posture — right foot on the sea, left foot on the land — is a claim to universal sovereignty. He spans the whole earth. The sea and land together constitute the entire created world; by standing on both simultaneously, the angel declares the authority of the message he carries over every domain of creation. This is the prelude to the declaration that there will be no more delay — the whole earth is within the scope of the judgment that is coming.

The little scroll that is “open” in his hand contrasts with the sealed scroll of chapter 5. The great scroll of history was sealed with seven seals; this little scroll is already open. Its contents are immediately available — indeed, John is commanded to eat it. The little scroll is most likely the prophetic commission that John must fulfill: the content of the rest of the book of Revelation, the word he must speak to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down." And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seven thunders and their sealed content are the most tantalizing feature of this vision. John hears them, understands them (he is about to write them down), and is commanded not to. This is divine self-restraint in revelation: God chooses how much to disclose and when. The interpreter who speculates about the sealed thunders is overriding a divine prohibition. The lesson is the humility of revelation: the book of Revelation reveals much and conceals this. Both the revealing and the concealing are acts of the sovereign God.

The oath formula — raising the right hand to heaven and swearing by the living Creator — echoes Daniel 12:7, where a heavenly figure raises his right hand and swears by the one who lives forever that a time period will come. The angel’s oath parallels Daniel’s oath, positioning the events of Revelation as the fulfillment of Daniel’s prophecies. The “mystery of God” fulfilled at the seventh trumpet is the hidden redemptive plan now brought to completion — the “mystery” of Ephesians 3:3–6 (Jews and Gentiles together in one body in Christ) extended to its cosmic consummation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter. And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eating of the scroll draws on two Old Testament prophetic commissions. Ezekiel was given a scroll written on front and back — words of lamentation, mourning, and woe — and commanded to eat it; it was as sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3). Jeremiah “found” God’s words and ate them; they became a joy and the delight of his heart (Jeremiah 15:16) — even though Jeremiah’s prophetic ministry was the most painful in the Old Testament. Eating the word is the classic image of internalizing the prophetic message so completely that it becomes part of you, inseparable from your identity.

The sweetness and bitterness together are not a contradiction but a simultaneity. The gospel is sweet: it announces the victory of the Lamb, the redemption of the nations, the new creation, the end of tears. It is honey. And the prophetic task of declaring that gospel — to peoples, nations, languages, kings who may not want to hear it — is bitter: it involves suffering, rejection, the cost of witness, the grief of watching the world refuse what is offered. Every faithful preacher knows both at once. The sweetness does not dissolve the bitterness; the bitterness does not cancel the sweetness. John is told: you must prophesy again. Again. The commissioning is renewed precisely because the task is hard.

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar, and those who worship there — but not the outer court. The measuring is a sign of preservation (Zechariah 2:1– 5; Ezekiel 40–43, where measuring signals God’s claiming of the space). The outer court is given to the nations for 42 months. The 42 months — also expressed as 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, times, and half a time” (12:14) — is the symbolic duration of the church age, drawn from Daniel’s “half seven” (Daniel 7:25; 9:27; 12:7). Three and a half years is exactly half of seven — the number of completeness. The church age is the incomplete half, the time between the two comings, the time of testing and tribulation that precedes the full consummation.

The two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days clothed in sackcloth — the garment of lamentation and repentance, like Elijah on Carmel and John the Baptist in the wilderness. Their testimony is urgent, costly, and counter-cultural. They are described as the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth — imagery from Zechariah 4, where the two olive trees supplied oil to the lampstand, representing the Spirit’s empowerment of God’s witnesses (Zechariah 4:6: “not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”). The church’s witness is not a human achievement; it is Spirit-empowered testimony that flows from the inexhaustible supply of the anointing.

After completing their testimony, the beast from the abyss makes war on them and kills them. Their bodies lie in the street of “the great city that is symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.” The great city is Jerusalem in the immediate reference — it is where Jesus was crucified — but it is called Sodom (for its wickedness) and Egypt (for its slavery and idolatry), transforming it into the symbol of every city and every civilization that opposes the witness of Christ. The world celebrates the witnesses’ deaths for three and a half days, sending gifts to one another in their glee.

After three and a half days, the breath of life from God enters them, they stand up, terror seizes those who see them, and a loud voice from heaven says “Come up here!” — and they ascend to heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch. An earthquake kills seven thousand; the rest are terrified and give glory to God. The pattern is unmistakable: the death, resurrection, and ascension of the two witnesses mirrors the death, resurrection, and ascension of their Lord. The church that is killed for its witness participates in the pattern of the one whose witness it sustains.
verseByVerse.theology:
The death, resurrection, and vindication of the two witnesses is the pattern of all faithful witness. The church does not overcome by winning on the world’s terms — by accumulating political power, cultural credibility, or social influence. It overcomes by being faithful to the point of death and being vindicated by the God who raises the dead. This is the theology of the cross applied to the church’s mission: the apparent defeat of faithful witness is not the end of the story. Three and a half days after the world celebrates, the witnesses stand up.

The great city being symbolically called Sodom and Egypt even though it is “where their Lord was crucified” is a theological claim of permanent importance: the city of God becomes the city of the world when it rejects the testimony of God’s witnesses. Jerusalem is not exempt from the judgment that fell on Sodom and Egypt simply because the temple stands there. Presence of the institutions of religion does not equal the presence of God. This judgment applies to the church in every age.
verseByVerse.examples:
The three and a half days of the witnesses’ unburied bodies — the world celebrating, exchanging gifts, gloating over the silencing of the prophetic word — is the experience of the church whenever it has been apparently crushed. The Reformation was “dead” for seasons. The Chinese church appeared “dead” after 1949. The Ugandan church appeared “dead” under Idi Amin. In every case, after three and a half days, breath returned. The witnesses stood up. The celebration of the enemies was premature.

The two witnesses in sackcloth are not a triumphalist church claiming political power and cultural dominance. They are a prophetic church, urgent in witness, costly in faithfulness, willing to be silenced and to rise. The church that is comfortable and celebrated is probably not in sackcloth. The church in sackcloth may be the most faithful church of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The measuring of the temple echoes Ezekiel 40–43 (the measuring of the restored temple as a sign of God’s renewed presence) and Zechariah 2:1–5 (the measuring of Jerusalem, where God himself is the protective wall). To measure is to claim, to assess, to protect. God is declaring: this community is mine; I have measured it; I know exactly what it is and where it is; I am preserving it.

The outer court given to the nations for 42 months is the church’s visible vulnerability. The outer court of the Jerusalem temple was accessible to Gentiles; only Jews could enter the inner courts. In the spiritual reading, the outer court represents the church’s visible life in the world — its institutions, its buildings, its social standing — all of which are subject to worldly power and can be trampled. The inner sanctuary — the true worshipping community before God, the souls of the redeemed — is preserved. The world can destroy the visible church; it cannot destroy the church that God has measured.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The witnesses prophesy “clothed in sackcloth” — not in triumph and glory but in lamentation, urgency, and the garment of repentance-preaching. Elijah wore a garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8); John the Baptist wore camel’s hair and a leather belt (Matthew 3:4). The prophetic ministry is not a comfortable ministry; it calls the world to repentance, which the world does not appreciate.

The two olive trees and two lampstands from Zechariah 4 represent Spirit-empowered witness. In Zechariah’s vision, the two olive trees supply the lampstand with oil continuously — the Spirit without measure. The church’s witness is not dependent on human eloquence, political access, or social acceptability. It is dependent on the one who says “not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). The fire from the witnesses’ mouths is the word of God as judgment (Jeremiah 5:14: “I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them”). The word that saves those who receive it judges those who reject it.

And who are the two witnesses? Readers have long divided, and the text pulls two ways. The miracles point to individuals: shutting the sky recalls Elijah (1 Kgs. 17:1), and turning water to blood and striking the earth with plagues recalls Moses (Ex. 7–12) — which is why some expect two end-time prophets, often named as Moses and Elijah, or Enoch and Elijah (the two men in Scripture who never died). Yet John calls them “two lampstands,” and lampstands, he has just told us, are churches (1:20); “two” is also the number Scripture requires for valid testimony (Deut. 19:15). So others read them as the whole witnessing church. Either way, the emphasis falls where the passage does: their God-given message, their divine protection until the work is done, and their share in their Lord’s death and vindication.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast from the abyss makes its first appearance here — it will be described more fully in chapter 13. The timing is precise: the witnesses are killed “when they have finished their testimony.” Not before. They are invulnerable while their prophetic task continues; only when that task is complete does God permit their death. This is the sovereignty of God over the martyrdom of his witnesses: no one can silence the church before it has said what God appointed it to say.

The refusal of burial is the ultimate insult in the ancient world — it left the dead without honor and without the hope of proper passage to the afterlife in the surrounding culture. The gloating of the “those who dwell on the earth” — Revelation’s consistent phrase for those whose ultimate orientation is toward earthly things rather than the kingdom of God — reveals the true depth of the world’s hostility to the prophetic word. The prophets were “a torment” to them: not because the prophets were cruel but because truthful witness torments those who are determined to live in a comfortable lie.

One line rewards a careful reader: the bodies lie in “the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.” The city where the Lord was crucified is Jerusalem — yet John will not simply name it, because it is behaving like the world at its worst. He calls it Sodom (the byword for moral corruption, Gen. 19) and Egypt (the byword for enslaving God’s people, Ex. 1–14). The point is character, not geography: wherever God’s witnesses are put to death, that place — even a holy city — has thrown in its lot with Sodom, Egypt, and the crucifiers. “The great city” becomes Revelation’s name for the whole world in its rebellion against God (cf. 17:18).

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them. And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The breath of life from God entering the witnesses echoes Ezekiel 37:10, where the breath of God entered the dry bones and they stood on their feet — the resurrection of Israel from the death of exile. The pattern is unmistakable: death, resurrection, ascension. The witnesses mirror their Lord in the pattern of their defeat and vindication. The “Come up here!” echoes 4:1, where the same words summoned John into the heavenly vision — but here it is the vindication of the martyred witnesses before the eyes of their enemies.

The earthquake and the falling of a tenth of the city and the death of seven thousand produce terror — and “the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.” Whether this “glory to God” represents genuine repentance or merely terrified acknowledgment (as in 6:16, where the kings call on the mountains to fall on them) is contested. The Greek allows either reading. The context of chapter 9’s non-repentance suggests the latter — but the interlude of chapter 11 may be designed to offer a note of eschatological hope: even from the ruins of judgment, some come to give God glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventh trumpet does not release a further woe upon the earth. It releases instead the final declaration of the kingdom. Loud voices in heaven cry: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship. The temple in heaven is opened, and the ark of the covenant appears within it, accompanied by lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

This is the climax of the trumpet series and, in a sense, of the whole book. Everything that follows in chapters 12–22 is the unpacking, the elaboration, the showing of what this declaration means. The kingdom has come. Christ reigns. The nations are angry; God’s wrath has come; the time for judging the dead and rewarding the saints and destroying those who destroy the earth has arrived. All of this is stated as accomplished fact at the seventh trumpet, even though the bowls and the final judgments remain. The pattern is the same as the Lamb taking the scroll in chapter 5: the authority is declared in heaven before it is fully executed on earth.

The opening of the temple and the appearance of the ark of the covenant is the culminating revelation of the chapter. The ark — which disappeared from history after the Babylonian destruction of the temple in 586 BC, its fate unknown — is revealed in the heavenly temple. It was never lost. It was never destroyed. It was in the heavenly sanctuary all along, where Moses’ earthly tabernacle was only “a copy and shadow” (Hebrews 8:5). The ark is the throne of God’s presence, the place of atonement, the heart of the covenant. Its appearance signals: the covenant has been kept. God has been faithful. The promises stand.
verseByVerse.theology:
The declaration “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” is the fulfillment of Daniel 2:44 (the stone that becomes a great mountain filling the whole earth) and Daniel 7:14 (the Son of Man given dominion, glory, and a kingdom that shall not pass away). It is also the fulfillment of the Lord’s Prayer: “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” The kingdom for which the church has prayed across twenty centuries is declared a reality at the seventh trumpet. From the throne’s perspective, it is done. From earth’s perspective, the working out continues.

The wrath of God that has “come” (v. 18 — again the aorist, completed action) alongside the rewarding of the saints and the judging of the nations is the two-sided verdict of the final judgment: the wicked face God’s wrath; the righteous receive the reward of the kingdom. Both are expressions of the same justice. The reward of the saints is not a sentimental addition to the judgment of the wicked — it is the flip side of the same verdict: God declares what is true and gives to each what is due.
verseByVerse.examples:
The seventh trumpet is the basis for the church’s confidence in prayer and witness. When we pray “Your kingdom come,” we are praying into something that has already been declared from the throne. The kingdom is not a project the church is building from the ground up; it is a reality that the Lamb has already established and that the church is proclaiming and living into. This does not eliminate the urgency of mission; it grounds it in certainty rather than anxious effort.

The appearance of the ark of the covenant in the heavenly temple is the assurance that no covenant promise has been lost. Everything God promised Abraham, everything God promised David, everything God promised through the prophets — it is all preserved in the heavenly sanctuary, all intact, all still in force. The apparent losses of history — the temple burned, the ark gone, the covenant people scattered — are provisional. The heavenly reality has never wavered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The loud voices (plural — a great choir of heavenly beings) proclaim the kingdom in the past tense: it “has become.” In the prophetic vision, what is certain is declared as accomplished. The kingdom that will be fully manifest at the second coming has been, from God’s eternal perspective, always certain; the declaration at the seventh trumpet is the announcement of its irreversible arrival. “He shall reign forever and ever” — the eternal reign is the counterpoint to every temporal power that has claimed sovereignty over the earth.

The twenty-four elders’ thanksgiving focuses on the fact that God “has taken your great power and begun to reign.” This is not a new development — God has always reigned. It is the eschatological manifestation of that reign in undeniable, universal clarity. The one who has always ruled is now seen to rule by all. The hiddenness of God’s governance that has allowed the wicked to prosper and the righteous to suffer is now dissolved: the kingdom is manifest.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying those who destroy the earth. Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourfold action of the seventh trumpet — the nations raging, God’s wrath coming, the dead being judged, and the saints being rewarded — parallels Psalm 2 almost exactly: the nations rage (Psalm 2:1), the LORD laughs and judges (Psalm 2:4–5), the Son receives the nations as his inheritance (Psalm 2:8), and the kings are warned to submit (Psalm 2:10–12). Revelation 11:18 is the fulfilment of Psalm 2. The small and the great are rewarded equally — kingdom status is not determined by earthly prominence.

The ark of the covenant appearing in the heavenly temple is the culminating revelation. The earthly ark was the footstool of God’s throne, the place where the blood of atonement was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement, the container of the law that the people had broken. In heaven, the ark is intact, the covenant is unbroken, the atonement is complete. The lightning and thunder and earthquake and hail that accompany its appearance echo the Sinai theophany (Exodus 19:16–19) — the giving of the law is here shown to have its heavenly completion in the keeping of every covenant promise that the law pointed toward.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring.
